sections.text: You played the Italian solidly: 3...h6 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Nxd4 7.Qxd4 c5 8.Qd1 Be7, and 9.Bf4?! and 10.O-O?! were small inaccuracies (9.e5 was stronger).
11.Re1 Ng4 12.h3 Nxf2?? was a blunder, and 13.Kxf2! won the knight. 13...Bxh3 14.gxh3 Bh4+ 15.Bg3 left you well ahead in material.
You finished cleanly: 16.Kg2 Qg5 17.Qg4 Qd2+ 18.Re2 Qg5 19.Bxh4 Qxg4+ 20.hxg4, and you were up a lot in material when Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 12...Nxf2?? was a blunder, and 13.Kxf2! took the knight.
review.focus: At 9.Bf4?! and 10.O-O?! you drifted; 9.e5 was stronger. Look for forcing moves first.

review.headline: An early piece blunder, then a comeback built on White's errors and a mating finish

sections.text: This was a Three Knights Petrov that you won despite a rough opening. After 3.Nc3 you played 3...Nxe4, but 4.Nxe4 simply took the knight back, so you were a piece down for a pawn almost at once (-3.2). The calmer 3...Nc6 would have kept things level.
You fought back with 4...d5, 5...e4 and 6...c5, and the queen trip with 8...Qa5+ and 10...Qxb2 won a pawn. 7...f5 loosened your own position, though, and the engine preferred 7...h5.

White then went wrong several times. 11.Bxb8 traded a bishop for a knight and you recaptured correctly with 11...Rxb8. 12.Qb1 offered a queen trade that you declined with 12...Qa3, and then 13.Nf4 was the real blunder (13.Qb3 was needed). After 14.Ke2 you found 14...Bd6, which hit the knight on f4 and was the engine's top reply.

From there the attack grew. 17...Re8+ chased the king, 18.Kd1 only made things worse for White, and although 18...Be6 let some of the advantage slip (+7.1 to +2.8), 19...b5 and 26...Bxe4+ kept the pressure on until 30...Rb2# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 13.Nf4 swung the evaluation from -1.7 to +1.1 in your favor, and once your queen was out with 13...Qa5+ and 14...Bd6 followed, you were in control.
review.focus: 3...Nxe4 is the move to learn from: before grabbing a central pawn, check whether the capturing piece can be taken, because 4.Nxe4 left you a knight down for a pawn. 3...Nc6 develops safely.

review.headline: A tidy French where you punished a loosening pawn grab and converted cleanly

sections.text: This was a controlled French Defense in which you stayed ahead from start to finish. Black's setup with 2...c6 and 3...a6 was slow, and 4...Qb6 gave you something to aim at. Your 4.Bc4 and 5.b3 were a touch loose (the engine liked 4.Bd3 and 5.Nc3), but nothing was lost.

You traded pieces sensibly with 6.exd5, 10.Qxe2 and 11.O-O and kept a small edge. Then your opponent cracked with 13...dxc4. You answered at once with 14.Nxc4!, which hit the queen on b6 and gained a tempo.
15.d5 gained space and opened lines toward the black king. After 15...O-O? you found 16.dxe6!, and after 16...fxe6 17.Qxe6+ Rf7 Black's position was falling apart (+6.8).
The technical phase was handled well. 18.Qxd6 was a small inaccuracy (18.Nxd6 kept slightly more), but the queen trade, 20.Bxf6 and 23.Nxd7 kept you far ahead in material, and 35.Nxc2 ended the game.

review.turning_point: 16.dxe6! after 15...O-O? opened the f-file and the black king's cover, taking a good position to a clearly winning one.
review.focus: Your opening moves 4.Bc4 and 5.b3 each gave back about a pawn of advantage. Against a quiet reply like 4...Qb6, simple development such as 4.Bd3 and 5.Nc3 keeps your edge without weakening anything.

review.headline: A Sicilian where one careless bishop move nearly cost you the game, then a perpetual saved the half point

sections.text: This was a Sicilian where you took the early initiative with 5.Nf5. After 6...Bxf5 7.exf5 the position was balanced, and the trades continued with 10.Nxe7+ Nxe7, which was a slightly generous swap (-0.7).

The decisive mistake came with 11.Bg5. Your bishop on b5 was undefended, and 11...Qa5+ gave check while also attacking it. Playing 11.O-O first would have kept everything safe. After 12.Qd2 Qxb5 you were a piece down (-3.9).

You kept fighting. 13.Bxf6 gxf6 broke up Black's king cover, and 14.Qxd6 and 15.Qxf6 kept the queen active against a king with few defenders. Then your opponent blundered with 15...Nd4??, when 15...Qb4+ was needed to keep the edge.
You found the only resource: 16.Qg5+ Kh8 17.Qf6+ Kg8 18.Qg5+ Kh8 19.Qf6+ Kg8, a perpetual check that turned a lost game into a draw.

review.turning_point: 11.Bg5 dropped the evaluation from -0.5 to -3.7, because 11...Qa5+ attacked the loose bishop on b5 with check. Your opponent's 15...Nd4 gave it all back.
review.focus: Before every developing move, check which of your pieces are undefended. After 11.Bg5, the bishop on b5 had no protection, so 11.O-O was the safer choice.

review.headline: A long win where your opponent's bishop blunder opened the door to a huge edge

sections.text: This was an Italian where Black chose the unusual 3...h6. You played the natural 4.d4 and 5.Nxd4, and after 5...Bc5? you had the chance to hit f7 with 6.Bxf7+. Instead 6.Nxc6 gave up some of your advantage (+2.3 to +0.5). It was your one real slip in the opening.
You kept developing with 7.O-O, 8.Nc3 and 9.Bb3, and 10.Qe2 and 12.Qc4 kept the pressure on. 12.Qc4 was slightly inexact, but it set a trap that your opponent walked into with 12...Be6??.

13.Qxc5! was excellent, a discovered attack from your bishop on b3 toward e6 once the queen moved away. Black could not save everything, and the engine had you at +5.8. 15.e5 and 19.Bxf6 then kept Black on the back foot.
From there you steadily converted, trading rooks with 20.Rad1 and 21.Rxd1+, then pushing the h-pawn all the way with 32.h8=Q+. The game ended on the clock after 58.Q8e8, with you far ahead.

review.turning_point: 13.Qxc5! after 12...Be6?? was a discovered attack that won material and took the evaluation to +5.8.
review.focus: 6.Nxc6 let Black off the hook; 6.Bxf7+ was the stronger idea. When your opponent leaves a piece loose on c5 and f7 is under pressure, check forcing captures like 6.Bxf7+ before trading pieces.

review.headline: A wild King's Gambit where you built a won position and then lost it on the clock

sections.text: This was a King's Gambit Accepted that you handled well early on, picking up the pawn with 2...exf4 and developing with 4...Be6. But 7...b5?? was a real mistake (+0.2 to -1.9): after 8.Bxe6 fxe6 9.axb5 cxb5 you had weakened your own queenside. 7...d5 was the engine's pick.

White then blundered with 12.Nbd4??, and you found the strong 12...e5!. Combined with 16...Bxd4+ and 17...O-O you got back into the game, though 18...Rc8?? gave White a chance. Both sides then traded errors: 19.e5?? Nf5! and 20.e6?? Nxh6! were good replies by you.

The decisive mistake came with 23...Qc7??, which swung the evaluation from +2.4 to -4.2. 23...Bf2 was the move. After 24.Rf7+ Nxf7 25.Qxf7+ Kh6 26.Qxe8 you were in trouble, but 27...Nc6! was the best defense and White missed the strongest 28.Qxa8, playing 28.Qf7??.
At the end you were winning again, but short of time. In the final position 49...Qa6?? missed 49...Qf1#, a mate in one, and 50.d8=Q+ ended the game for White.

review.turning_point: 23...Qc7?? dropped you from +2.4 to -4.2 in one move, when 23...Bf2 would have kept your advantage.
review.focus: 49...Qa6 is the painful one: 49...Qf1# was mate in one. When the clock is short, make your first move check every check and capture, because forcing moves are the quickest to calculate.

review.headline: A balanced Sicilian where resigning was far too early

sections.text: This was a Löwenthal Sicilian where you played the first moves sensibly: 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 and then the trade 5.Nxc6 bxc6. That left Black with doubled pawns on the c-file, which is a small structural gain for you.
6.Nc3 Bb4 7.Bd2 Nf6 8.Bc4 are all normal developing moves, and your accuracy was 92.8 without a single inaccuracy. The engine only had the position at -0.5 after 8.Bc4, which is essentially level.

The game ended with you resigning after just 8 moves. Nothing in the position called for that. Even a small disadvantage can be played on in blitz, where your opponent may blunder, as happens often at this level.

review.turning_point: There was no turning point on the board: after 8.Bc4 the position was about equal at -0.5, and the game was decided by the resignation.
review.focus: After 8.Bc4 you had a perfectly playable position, so the work here is not a chess move but a habit: keep playing until the position is clearly lost. Resigning at -0.5 gave away a game you could have fought for.

review.headline: A quiet Bishop's Opening ruined by a pawn grab and a hanging bishop

sections.text: This was a Bishop's Opening where you equalized easily with 2...d6 and 3...Be6, and 4...Bxc4 5.dxc4 simplified things. Your development with 5...Nf6 and 6...Be7 was fine, and 7...c6 prepared a solid center.

The problem was 8...Nxe4??. After 9.Nxe4 you were a piece down for a pawn (-2.9). You partly recovered with 9...Bxh4, taking the knight on h4, and when White replied 10.f4?? the position was close to level.

Then 10...Qb6+?? gave it back (+0.0 to -5.5); 10...d5 was the move. White answered with 11.Kh1??, a mistake in return, and you found 11...O-O!, but after 12.fxe5 dxe5 13.Qg4 you played 13...Bf6??, and 14.Nxf6+ cost you the bishop.
From there White's pieces were simply more active, and 15.Nh5, 17.Qh4 and 19.Nxh5+ closed in on your king before 20.Qh6+ ended the game.

review.turning_point: 13...Bf6?? dropped you from -3.5 to -8.0, since 14.Nxf6+ took the bishop with check.
review.focus: 8...Nxe4 came from grabbing a pawn without checking the recapture: 9.Nxe4 left you a piece down. Before any capture, ask what recaptures are possible. 8...g6 was the quieter choice.

review.headline: An Italian where a well-timed exchange sacrifice crashed through to mate

sections.text: This was a Giuoco Piano where both sides played slowly. You kept the center under control with 6.d3 and 7.Be3, and 8.fxe3 opened the f-file for your rook. A little inaccurate was 11.Qd2, but it worked out when your opponent replied 11...Qd7?.

12.d4? was the one real slip (+1.6 to +0.3); 12.Nh4 was better. After 12...Bxf3 13.Rxf3 your opponent made two more mistakes with 13...exd4? and 14...Rae8?, and you punished both with accurate play: 14.exd4! and then the key shot.
15.Rxf6! was a strong exchange sacrifice. After 15...gxf6 16.Qxh6 you had given up a rook for a knight and a pawn, but Black's king was open and you were at +4.9. 17.Rf1 added a second attacker.
The finish was clean: 18.Qg5+ Kh8 19.Rf4, then 20.Nxe2 and 21.Rh4# ended the game with mate.

review.turning_point: 15.Rxf6! gave up an exchange to rip open the black king, and from there the attack could not be stopped.
review.focus: 12.d4 was premature: with your knight on f3 and Black's bishop on h5 hitting it, 12.Nh4 was the better way to handle the pressure. Check what your pawn push does to your own pieces before playing it.

review.headline: A good opening and a winning position that was lost on the clock

sections.text: This was a Three Knights Petrov where Black played the Philidor-style 3...d6. You took the pawn with 4...exd4 and 5.Nxd4 was met by 5...Bd7?!, which was slightly slow; 5...Be7 was the engine's choice.
7...Nxe4?! was a tactical try (7...Nc6 was safer), but it worked. 8.Nxe4 Bxg5 9.Nxg5?? was a blunder, and you punished it with 9...Qxg5!, regaining the material and leaving you up a pawn (+0.9).
10.Qe2+ was met by 10...Qe5?!, which was slightly inexact (10...Qe7 was better), but 11.Nb5? gave you the chance to trade queens: 11...Qxe2+! 12.Bxe2 left you with a comfortable edge (+1.8).
The game ended there on the clock: you lost on time in a position the engine liked for you. In blitz this happens, but it is avoidable.

review.turning_point: 9...Qxg5! reversed the result of the earlier tactics and turned a worse position into a better one.
review.focus: You were ahead at +1.8 and still lost, so clock management matters here. Moves like 10...Qe5 (where 10...Qe7 was simpler) cost thinking time you did not have; in known positions, play faster and bank the time.

review.headline: A trap-filled Petrov that ended with a surprise mating blow

sections.text: This was a Three Knights Petrov in which White traded early with 5.Bxe6 fxe6 and you recaptured to keep your pawns healthy. After 6.d4 exd4 7.Nxd4 Qd7 you were doing fine, and 9.e5 Nxe5 won you a pawn.
10...Be7?! and 11...O-O?! were slightly inexact, and 12...Nfg4?? was a real blunder (-0.3 to -2.9). 12...Nf7 was the engine's idea. After 13.Bxe7 Qxe7 14.fxe5 you were a piece down.
But you found 14...Qh4, aiming your queen and the knight on g4 at h2, and White fell into it with 15.Nxe6??. 15...Qxh2# was checkmate, since the king on g1 had no defenders left.

review.turning_point: 15.Nxe6?? missed the threat on h2, allowing 15...Qxh2# in one move.
review.focus: 12...Nfg4 hung your knight on e5 for nothing: 14.fxe5 left you a piece down. Before a flashy move like 12...Nfg4, check whether your other pieces are still defended.

review.headline: An uneven Scotch Gambit that you turned around with sharp rook play and a mating attack

sections.text: This was a Scotch Gambit where the opening went slightly wrong. 5.Nxd4?! Nxe4 left you behind, and 7.Qf3? was a further mistake (7.Bxf7+ was suggested). You traded queens with 12.Qxf6, doubling Black's pawns, which was a useful structural gain.
Black was solid for a long time, and 18.Re3?? gave away a big chance: after 17...c5?? the engine liked 18.Rxe7 (+4.8). Luckily Black replied with 19...Bxg3?, and you recaptured well with 20.Rxg3+!.
20...Kh7? let you in. 21.Re7! put the rook on the seventh, and 21...Ra6?? was the final error. 22.Bxf7! brought your bishop into the attack (+6.9).
The finish was neat: 24.Rh7+ Kg8 25.Be4+ Bg4 26.Rxg4# was checkmate.

review.turning_point: 21...Ra6?? let in 22.Bxf7!, which took the evaluation from +2.1 to +6.9 and left Black's king with no safe squares.
review.focus: 18.Re3 gave back nearly all your advantage (+4.8 to -0.7) because 18.Rxe7 was available. When your opponent errs, look for the forcing capture first, as 18.Rxe7 was.

review.headline: A promising Italian that fell apart after a bishop was left loose

sections.text: This was a Classical Italian where you played the main line with 4.c3 and 5.d4. After 5...Bb6 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.dxe5 Nxe4 the position was about equal, and you had a good chance on the next move.
8.O-O?? was a blunder (+1.5 to -0.3): the engine suggested 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.Qd5+. Later you played 11.Re1?!, giving Black time, and 11...Qh4 started to create problems against your bishop on c4.

12.g3?? was the decisive mistake (-0.9 to -4.9). It attacked the queen, but 12...Qxc4 simply captured your undefended bishop. 12.Qe2 would have kept everything protected. After 13.exd6 cxd6 you were down a piece.
From there you tried 15.Re7 and 17.Qxg4, but 17...Qxe7 won more material. By 19.Rf1?! you were lost and resigned.

review.turning_point: 12.g3?? attacked the black queen but left the bishop on c4 undefended, and 12...Qxc4 won it.
review.focus: 12.g3 is the move to remember: a threat against the queen is only useful if your own pieces are safe. The bishop on c4 had no defender, so check what the opponent's queen already attacks before making a threat.

review.headline: A near-lost London that you rescued with a string of accurate tactics

sections.text: This was an Accelerated London in which White got greedy early. 4.Be5? gave you the chance to trade bishops, but 4...Nc6?? (the engine preferred 4...Bxe5) allowed 5.Bxg7 and 6.Bxh8, and you were suddenly far behind in material (-4.4).
You kept playing well. 5...Qg5 and 6...Nf6 created counterplay, and when White played 14.cxb4? you found 14...Bxb4+!, bringing the bishop back into the game with a check.
White's mistakes kept coming: 18.Ke2?? 18...d4! and 19.f3? dxe3! were strong replies. 19...dxe3 was a discovered attack that opened the d-file for your rook toward the knight on d2.
20.Qb3?? was the final blunder (20.Ne4 was needed). 20...Rxd2+! 21.Ke1 Rb2+ 22.Kd1 Rxb3 won the queen, and after 23.Rxb3 Qa1+ White resigned.

review.turning_point: 20.Qb3?? walked into 20...Rxd2+!, and the sequence won the white queen.
review.focus: 4...Nc6 is the move to learn from: 4...Bxe5 simply took the bishop and kept you ahead. When an enemy piece lands on e5 next to your bishop, check the capture first before developing.

review.headline: A chaotic Scotch where both sides blundered and your attack finally prevailed

sections.text: This was a Scotch Game where you brought your queen out early and then spent time on slow moves like 6.b3?! and 9.f4?!. Even so, you were at +2.0 at one point, with Black's knights misplaced.
Then 10.Qa4?? threw the advantage away (+2.0 to -1.7). 10.Qf2 was the safer choice. 11.Bb5?? and 12.Bc4?? followed, and 12...b5 attacked your bishop.

13.Bxb5! was a good practical answer, giving a bishop for two pawns, and 15.O-O! kept you in the game after 14...h5??. Black's 18...c5?? gave you a chance again, though 19.e5?? was a mistake in return.
Black replied 19...dxe5??, and you punished with 20.fxe5! g6?? 21.exf6! Rh5? 22.Rae1+! Be7 23.Qg8#, checkmate.

review.turning_point: 20...g6?? swung the evaluation from +0.2 to +5.2 in your favor, after which 21.exf6! and the mating attack followed.
review.focus: 10.Qa4 started the trouble: your queen went to a square where it could be harassed, and 12.Bc4 then dropped more time. Keep your queen safe and your pieces coordinated before making attacking moves.

review.headline: A long English game where a missed mate in time trouble decided it

sections.text: This was a Symmetrical English in which you played the setup with 2...b6 and 3...Bb7. 4...e5?! and 8...f6?! loosened your position slightly, but the trade of queens with 14.Qxd7+ Kxd7 kept the game balanced.

White made several errors in the middlegame, including 18.g4?, 24.Rfe1? and 29.Ng3?, and you found 24...Bd2! as a good reply. You could have pressed harder at points, but the position stayed around equal.
Time trouble then took over. 38...Kg5?? and 42...Re1?? were both errors, and after 43.Ng3?? you had a forced mate: 43...Bd2+ was a discovered check, and after 44.Ne2 Rxe2# it was over.
Instead you played 43...Bg1+?? and the chance was gone. 44...Kh4?? and 45...Kxg4?? followed, and you lost on time.

review.turning_point: 43...Bg1+?? missed the forced mate with 43...Bd2+, a discovered check that would have ended the game at once.
review.focus: 43...Bg1+ is the one to remember: in a won position, look at every check before choosing. 43...Bd2+ 44.Ne2 Rxe2# was mate. Playing faster in the opening and middlegame would leave you the time to find it.

review.headline: A solid Philidor undone by one hasty knight move

sections.text: This was a Philidor in which you played sensibly: 2...d6, 3...Be6 and 5...g6 with 6...Bg7 set up a fianchetto. 7...c6?! was slightly slow, and 9...Qb6? put the queen on a square where it could be harassed.
You traded bishops with 10...Bxb3 11.axb3, which was fine, and the position was close to level (+0.2).
Then 11...Nc5?? changed everything (+0.2 to -4.6). After 12.b4 Ng4 13.bxc5 Nxe3 14.cxb6 Nxd1 15.Rxd1 you ended up a piece and a pawn down. 11...Qc7 was the engine's choice.
You kept fighting through 44 moves against a 1481-rated opponent, but the material deficit never went away and the game ended on the clock.

review.turning_point: 11...Nc5?? let 12.b4 attack the knight while your queen was also loose on b6, and the sequence cost you material.
review.focus: 11...Nc5 is the key: before you play a move that attacks nothing, check what the opponent's pawn can attack. 12.b4 attacked the knight and the queen was also loose. 11...Qc7 would have moved the queen first.

review.headline: A Stafford Gambit game where you started well but gave it all away in a tactical middlegame

sections.text: This was a Stafford Gambit line in which White took the pawn with 3.Nxe5 and Black replied 3...Nc6?. You found 4.Nxc6!, which was the engine's top reply and left you comfortable at +1.8.
6.Be3? gave up some of that edge (+2.0 to +0.5), since 6.Be2 was better, and after 6...Bxe3 7.fxe3 Ng4 8.Qe2?! Qg5 Black had active pieces. 10.g3? and 11.Qd2? made it worse (-3.4).
Black helped you with 11...h6??, and you found 12.Be2!, which was a good defensive move. The game stayed tense, and 17.Rxf7 won a pawn.

Then 18.Rxf8?? was a blunder and 19.Qd2?? allowed 19...Qxd2+?? to be met by 20.Kxd2!, but then 21.Kc1?? and 22.b3? finished you off. The engine's 19...Rf1+ would have shown the back rank problem after 19.Qd2.

review.turning_point: 19.Qd2?? dropped the evaluation from -1.6 to -6.9, leaving your king on e1 exposed.
review.focus: 19.Qd2 is the move to study: the king was still on e1, so checks like Rf1+ were always possible. Before moving your queen from defence, count the checks your opponent has.

review.headline: A Sicilian against a 1955-rated player that slipped away after the opening and ended on the clock

sections.text: This was an Accelerated Dragon setup against a much stronger opponent. You played the first moves well, 5.Be2 and 6.Be3 and 8.O-O, and the position was fine at +1.4 after 7...a6.

10.e5?! was a risk and Black replied 10...d6?, a mistake. 11.Nxc6 was the right way to punish it, but 11.Nf3?? let Black off (+1.7 to -0.7). After 11...dxe5 12.fxe5 Nxe5 13.Nxe5 Bxe5 you were suddenly worse.
14.Bh6?? was another mistake (14.Qxd8 was suggested), and although Black replied 14...Bg7?, 15.Bxg7 Kxg7 16.Qd3 left you at -2.2. 17.g4?! and 18.Kh1?! made it harder.
The rest was a long grind against a strong player. 29.Nd6?! and other errors brought the evaluation to around -5. You played on to move 44 but lost on time.

review.turning_point: 11.Nf3?? swung the evaluation from +1.7 to -0.7, since 11.Nxc6 kept your advantage.
review.focus: 11.Nf3 is the key: when your opponent plays a mistake like 10...d6?, look for the immediate capture. 11.Nxc6 was the move. Stop and ask what the knight on d4 can capture before retreating.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined with strong resilience that was undone by the clock

sections.text: This was a Queen's Gambit Declined with the Bg5 line against a 1731-rated opponent. You developed smoothly through 7...Nbd7 and 8...b6, but 9...Ba6? was inexact (-1.8): 9...dxc4 was the engine's choice.
Your opponent replied with 10.O-O??, a blunder, and you punished it with 10...dxc4!. After 14.Bxc4 Bxa4 15.bxa4 Nb6?? 16.Bb3 Rc8 17.Ne5 c5? you gave back the edge again.
You then found strong defence with 18...Nbd5! after 18.a5??. The sequence 20.Bxf6 gxf6? (20...Bxf6 was better) 21.Nc6?? Nc3?? was messy, but you stayed in the game.

In the endgame, 31...Rd7?? was a blunder (-1.2 to -5.3) with the clock low, but White returned the favour with 32.Rxd7??, and you found 32...Kxd7!. You lost on time at move 36 in a position that was close to level.

review.turning_point: 32.Rxd7?? gave back the advantage that 31...Rd7?? had handed over, and 32...Kxd7! restored equality.
review.focus: 9...Ba6 is where it started: 9...dxc4 first would have kept things simple. Spending your time in the opening on a clear plan leaves you more minutes for the endgame, where the clock decided this game.

review.headline: A fast Italian win: a developing queen recapture and a one-move mating shot

sections.text: This was a classical Italian where you played the main line without a single inaccuracy (96.2). 4.c3 and 5.d4 challenged the center, and 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 met the check by developing a piece.

8.h3 asked the bishop on g4 a question. After 8...Bxf3 you recaptured with 9.Qxf3, which developed your queen with an eye on f7, already supported by your bishop on c4. That put quiet pressure on Black's weakest square.
Black went wrong with 9...Nxd4??, grabbing a pawn when 9...Qf6 was needed. You saw the shot at once: 10.Qxf7# was checkmate, with the queen protected by the bishop on c4.

review.turning_point: 9...Nxd4?? left f7 defended only by the king, and 10.Qxf7# ended the game on the spot.
review.focus: This was a clean game, so the lesson is to keep doing what worked: the queen recapture 9.Qxf3 kept an eye on f7. Make a habit of checking the f7 square for such shots in every Italian.

review.headline: An Italian where you were well ahead, until two early slips and then the clock

sections.text: This was a sharp Italian where you came out of the opening well. After 3...h6 you played 4.d4 and 5.Nxd4, and black's 5...Qe7? put the queen on the e-file right in front of its own king. You found the right answer with 6.O-O!, got castled and held about +1.8.

Then the game turned. 10.Qd2? let the evaluation drop from +1.8 to +0.4, because 10.Be2 was the cleaner way to deal with the bishop on g4. Your opponent missed 10...Nxc4 and went 10...O-O-O?, but your 11.fxe5?? took the evaluation all the way to -2.4. The quieter 11.Qc3 would have held your edge.

You did not fold. 13.Bxf7 and 14.cxd4 kept things tangled, and black's 15...Bd6?? helped you back to about -2.1 when 15...Ne4 was the better defence. Later 22...Bd6? gave you +0.8, but 23.g3? handed it straight back.

The decisive swing came with 29...Nc5??. You punished it at once with 30.Rxf7!, came out clearly ahead, and by 33.Rxg7 you were around +5.4. Sadly the clock ran out after 37...Kb5 while you were still better than +6.

review.turning_point: 29...Nc5?? gave you a huge advantage and 30.Rxf7! cashed it in, but the earlier 11.fxe5?? was where you let go of your opening edge.
review.focus: Slow down on natural-looking captures such as 11.fxe5 and protect your clock, since you were low on time by 23.g3 and then flagged in a position worth over +6.

review.headline: Queen's Gambit Declined where a gift on move 15 decided everything

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with the classical 1...d5 and 2...e6, and the opening was balanced. After 4.Bg5 4...Be7 5.Nf3 you played the freeing 5...Ne4, trading off pieces and heading for a comfortable game.

Then you pushed too hard. 8...e3?! opened the position, and after 9.fxe3 your 9...Qh4+? sent the queen out early, while 9...e5 was the better idea. White got a pleasant edge, around -1.4, and 10.g3 followed by 11.Qb3 kept you under pressure.
The knight jump 14...Nxd4 looked dangerous because it also opens the bishop on b7 toward f3 with a discovered attack, but objectively it was a blunder, down to -3.8. The calm 14...O-O-O was better.

You were rescued. White answered with 15.Nxd4??, which swung the game to +2.6 for you, when 15.Rxd4 was fine. You found 15...Bxh1! at once, and after 16.Nf3 16...Bxf3 17.exf3 you were well ahead and the game was essentially over. The ending was straightforward, and 24.Kb1 24...Rxg2 finished it off.

review.turning_point: 15.Nxd4?? by your opponent. Taking with the knight let 15...Bxh1! win the rook and turned -3.8 into a big plus.
review.focus: Check which recaptures your opponent has before a knight sacrifice like 14...Nxd4. It worked only because 15.Rxd4 was not played.

review.headline: A French where a bold bishop sacrifice and a late queen win decided it

sections.text: Your opponent chose an unusual 2...Ne7 setup and later pushed the h-, g- and f-pawns on the kingside. You played sensibly with 5.Nc3, 6.O-O and 7.e5 to get space, but 11.Rad1?! and 13.Ne2? let black's pawns roll. After 13...f4 you were about -0.9, and 13.exf6 was the cleaner alternative.

Your best moment in the middlegame came right away. 14.Bxf4! was a bold bishop sacrifice that opened black's king, and after 14...gxf4 15.Qxf4 you got your queen into the attack, followed by 16.Qf7. You were behind on the board, but black's king on c8 was exposed.

Things went wrong at 22.Qf3??, which dropped you to -4.7. The simple 22.Nxe7+ was the move. After 23.Qh3, black's 23...Kb8?? was a gift though, and your 24.Ng3! was the best way to keep the pressure on.

Then came the knockout. Black's rook on f5 was shielding the queen on d7 from your queen on h3, so 24...Rg5?? opened a discovered attack and you answered with 25.Qxd7!. You took the queen, reached a decisive +6 edge, and 26.c3 sealed it.

review.turning_point: 24...Rg5?? moved the rook that was blocking the diagonal, and 25.Qxd7! took the queen.
review.focus: Before moving a piece like 22.Qf3, count what your opponent can capture. 22.Nxe7+ was available and would have kept you out of trouble.

review.headline: A Petrov where you won a piece, then let the win slip in a rook ending and on the clock

sections.text: In the Petrov you followed the usual plan, 4...Nxe4 and 5...d5, and built up naturally. 7...Bf5?! gave up a little ground and 8.Nd4? was an inaccuracy by white, but 8...Nxc3?! and 9...Bg6?! let the pressure ease.

Then white blundered. 12.Nh4?? put a knight on a square where 12...Qxh4! just won it. You took it, and after 13.Bxg6 13...Qxf2+ and 14.Kh1 14...fxg6 you were up to +5. That was a strong, clean finish to the middlegame.
Even better was 17...Bxg3!, which tore open the white king, and you followed with 18...Bxh2 and 20...Qxe3. By 24...Qxg2+ the queens were off and you held about +6.7.

The ending went wrong at 30...Rxc3??, which turned +5.5 into about -0.3 when 30...h5 kept the win. After 35.Rg3?? and your 35...Nxd4!, white played 36.c3?? and you were close to winning again. But 36...Ne6+? and the time pressure produced 38...Ke5??, which dropped you to -5.3, and the clock ran out on move 47.

review.turning_point: 30...Rxc3?? let a +5.5 position slip to equality, and low time then ruined the later chance.
review.focus: In a winning endgame, take a breath before a capture like 30...Rxc3. The quiet 30...h5 would have kept everything under control.

review.headline: A quick Petrov loss where one castling decision cost a pawn and the game

sections.text: You met 1.e4 with the Petrov, and white played 3.Nc3 and 4.d4 exd4 5.Qxd4. That centralised queen is annoying but your development was fine, and 5...Nc6 was a reasonable way to challenge it. The evaluation stayed small until around move 9.

After 9.O-O-O h6 10.Bh4, 10...g5?! was the first drift (-0.6 to -1.4). It loosened your king's cover for no clear gain. Then 11...Qd7?! put your queen behind the d6 pawn, and with white's queen on d4 this was a pin on the d6 pawn.

12...O-O-O?? was the blunder. White's queen on d4 already looked at a7 along the diagonal, so putting your king on c8 allowed 13.Qxa7, which won a pawn and tore open lines at your king. Castling the other way with 12...O-O, followed by 13.Qd3, would have kept you in the game.
After 13.Qxa7 b6 white played 14.e5, and 14...Ne4?! left you at -5.8. You resigned, which was sensible.

review.turning_point: 12...O-O-O?? walked the king toward the queen's diagonal, and 13.Qxa7 had an easy target.
review.focus: Before castling, check which enemy pieces eye the squares around your king. The queen on d4 made 12...O-O-O a mistake, and 12...O-O was safe.

review.headline: A quick Italian win after black grabbed a pawn and walked into a queen attack

sections.text: You played a classical Two Knights line with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4, and after 4...Bd6 you opened the centre with 5.dxe5 5...Bxe5 6.Nxe5 6...Nxe5. Then 7.Bb3 was a calm move that kept the bishop aimed at f7 while black's knight sat loose in the centre.

Your opponent grabbed the pawn with 7...Nxe4??, a blunder that moved the evaluation to +3.4 for you. Your 8.Qe2 was understandable because it attacks the knight on e4, but it gave up some of the edge (+1.7). The stronger idea was 8.Qd5, hitting both knights at once, on e4 and e5.

Black then went wrong again with 8...Nd6??, which moved the knight off e4 but left the one on e5 undefended and facing a check on the e-file. You spotted it straight away. 9.Qxe5+! won a knight and put you at +5.6.
The rest was clean. 10.O-O, 11.Bd5 and the final 12.Qxd6+ picked up another piece. You kept making forcing, sensible moves, and the game ended with an overwhelming position.

review.turning_point: 8...Nd6?? left the e5 knight undefended, and 9.Qxe5+! won it with check.
review.focus: Look for the double attack first. After 7...Nxe4, 8.Qd5 hit both knights and would have kept more of the advantage than 8.Qe2.

review.headline: A Cochrane Gambit where you were far ahead, then lost it in time trouble

sections.text: Your opponent tried the Cochrane Gambit with 3.Nxe5 and then 4.Nxf7? against your Petrov. You answered correctly with 4...Kxf7!, taking the knight, and after 5.Bc4+ 5...Ke8? 6.d4 6...Nxe4 you were comfortably ahead with your king back on e8. 7.Qh5+ g6 8.Qd5 8...Qe7 was reasonable.

You played the middlegame well. 9...c6 and 10...d5 gave you solid control of the centre, and white's 12.f3? was a mistake because it gave you time for 12...Nd6. By 16.Re3 16...Bxd4 you were around +4.5.
Your best trick came at 21...Rxe3!, which punished 21.Nf4?? and left you far ahead. After 22.Bxe3 22...Qd1+ 23.Kf2 you were completely winning.

There was one earlier slip, 19...Bxe3+??, since 19...Qd8 was the better route. But the real problem was time. 27...Ke8??, 30...Qd3?? and 31...Nf6?? all happened with the clock low, and by 32.Qe5+ the game was lost.

review.turning_point: 30...Qd3?? and 31...Nf6?? gave away a hugely winning position under time pressure.
review.focus: Convert while you still have time. At 30...Qd3 the check 30...Qe1+ kept your queen active, and a calmer approach would have held the win.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann Exchange won by early tactics, with a messy middle that nearly gave it back

sections.text: You played the Exchange Caro-Kann solidly with 4.Nc3 and 5.Nf3, then 6.Bb5 and 7.Ba4?! was a slightly awkward bishop manoeuvre. After 8.Bb3 your bishop sat on the b3-d5 diagonal, pointing at black's centre.

The game turned at 9.Ne5. Black took with 9...Nxe5?, and you recaptured with 10.dxe5!, hitting the knight on f6. Black's 10...Ne4?? left the d5 pawn hanging, and 11.Qxd5! jumped on it with the bishop on b3 behind. 12.Qxf7+ and 13.Qxf5+ then took black's position apart and you were up past +6.

You kept control until the endgame got messy. 23.Rd1?? was a blunder, since 23.Rd7 kept the attack. Then 25.Bxh8?? gave away your advantage after 24...Rxf2??, with 25.Rcd7 being the right idea. The evaluation fell to -0.9.

Black returned the favour with 27...Kb6??, and you saw 28.Bd4+!, a fork of the king on b6 and the rook on f2. After 29.Bxf2 29...Bxf2 you were winning again, and the rook endgame with extra pawns was an easy finish.

review.turning_point: 28.Bd4+! forked the king on b6 and the rook on f2, putting you back at +5.3.
review.focus: Stay calm when you are far ahead. 23.Rd1 and 25.Bxh8 gave away a +3.5 lead, and 23.Rd7 and 25.Rcd7 were straightforward and strong.

review.headline: A Philidor draw where you let a +4.7 advantage slip away

sections.text: You played the Philidor with 3.Bc4 and 5.O-O, and 6.Nd5 followed by 7.Nxe7 simplified into an easy opening. Your opponent's 8...Bg4 and 9...Bh5 aimed at your knight on f3, but you stayed solid until 10.g4 10...Nxg4 11.hxg4.

The game then became tactical. 13.c3?? was a blunder that dropped you to -2.0, since 13.Be2 was needed. Black's 14...Bxf3?? gave it back, and 15.Qxf3! brought you back to +1.1. You also kept up the pressure with 16.d4 and 18.Be3.
Your opponent drifted with 19...Rf6? and 20...Raf8?, and your 22.dxe5! left you at +4.7. That was your big chance.

Then the slip. 23.f3?? dropped you to +2.1, because 23.Bg5 kept the attack going. 25.Rd1?? and 27.Rd3?? followed, and black's queen began checking, so the game ended in perpetual check with 28.Bh4, 29.Kf2 and 30.Ke3.

review.turning_point: 23.f3?? threw away your +4.7 advantage, because 23.Bg5 was the stronger move.
review.focus: When you reach +4.7, look for forcing continuations instead of quiet pawn moves. 23.Bg5 was the best choice instead of 23.f3.

review.headline: A quick French win built on one clean capture of a knight

sections.text: Black chose a fianchetto setup against your French structure, and you answered with 3.Nf3, 4.Be3 and 5.Nc3, just developing. 6.h3?! was a slightly slow move, since 6.Qd2 was more purposeful, but your position was still comfortable.

You pushed 7.e5, attacking the knight on f6. Black's 7...b6?? was the mistake that decided the game, because it left the knight to be taken. You took at once with 8.exf6!, and after 8...Bxf6 you were up a piece for a pawn.
You then kept making useful moves: 9.Bb5, 10.Bxc6 to remove a defender, and 11.Bh6, which attacked the rook on f8 and cramped black's king. 12.O-O finished your development.

Black went for complications with 12...Bxf3 and 13.gxf3, a little weaker than 13.Qxf3, but the extra piece still counted. Black's 13...Bxd4?? lost a piece, and 14.Qxd4! put you at +5.3 and ended the game. You played a clean, clear game.

review.turning_point: 7...b6?? left the knight on f6 to be taken, and 8.exf6! won the piece.
review.focus: A small point: 6.h3 and 13.gxf3 were both fine but not best. Keep looking for the most active move, such as 6.Qd2 and 13.Qxf3.

review.headline: An English Opening where you survived a bad position and escaped with perpetual check

sections.text: In the Whale line you played 1...e5, 3...c6?! and 4...Qc7, building a classical set-up against 1.c4. White got a small edge, around -0.7 to -1.5, but after 6...d5 7.Qe2? the queen was misplaced and you were close to equal.

Then you slipped. 8...Be7?! and 10...Be6?? were mistakes, with 10...Qa5+ being the right way to keep things under control. After 11.Nxe6 fxe6?! the evaluation dropped to -3.7, and 12.Qh5+ 12...Kd7 13.O-O-O+ drove your king into the open.
White's attack kept growing. 14.Qf7 and 16.Bf5+ pushed you to about -7. 17.Qg7 and 20.Qxh7 went after pawns, and you were in serious trouble.

Your resilience paid off. White played 24.Rd3??, a big mistake, since 24.Rxe7 was far stronger. You grabbed the chance, and 25.Bxc5 25...Qxc5 brought the evaluation close to equal. Another white error, 28.Rd7??, allowed 28...Qxc4+! and a perpetual check with 29.Kb1 29...Qf1+, 30.Kc2 30...Qe2+ and so on.

review.turning_point: 28.Rd7?? let you play 28...Qxc4+! and escape with a perpetual check.
review.focus: At 10...Be6 you were in a playable position, but the bishop move lost ground. 10...Qa5+ was the safer, forcing option.

review.headline: A Pirc where you won big early, gave it back, and finished with perpetual check

sections.text: Your opponent met 3.e5 with 3...g6??, which was a blunder, since 3...dxe5 was needed. You took the chance with 4.exf6!, which won a piece for a pawn, and followed with 6.Bb5+ and 7.Bxd7+ to simplify while you were ahead. At +4.8 you were doing everything right.

The first slip was 12.Nd5??. After 11.Bg5 11...Qd7, 12.Bxf6 was the correct move, and your knight jump let black take a piece, dropping you from +4.8 to -1.7. After that the position became hard to hold.

You fought on with 13.c4, 21.Ne5?! and 23.Bxh6?!, but black took the lead. Your biggest chance came when black played 26...Ra4??. The right idea was 27.Re8+, a back-rank shot, but 27.Rxb7?? dropped you from +3.5 to -3.8.

You still saved the game. After 30...Rg4?? you found 31.Qxf7+!, the key move, and repeated with 32.Qe8+, 33.Qe7+, 34.Qe8+ and 35.Qe7+. 36.Qe8+?? was a slip, since 36.Qe6+ was right, but black's 36...Kg7?? missed 36...Nf8, and 37.Qe7+! forced the draw.

review.turning_point: 26...Ra4?? gave you a winning chance with 27.Re8+, a back-rank shot, but 27.Rxb7?? threw it away.
review.focus: When you are far ahead, look for the safe capture. At 12.Nd5 you had 12.Bxf6, and at 27.Rxb7 you had 27.Re8+.

review.headline: A Scandinavian that turned sour after a knight went to e4, and you were mated by move 12

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 and 3.Nc3, then 4.d4 4...Nc6 5.Bd2. Black grabbed the d4 pawn with 5...Nxd4, and at this point 6.Nf3 was the natural move, keeping you in an easy position.

Instead 6.Ne4?? was a blunder, going from +1.0 to -1.1. It looks active but black's 6...Qe5 and then 7.f3 7...Bf5 left your knight under pressure. 8.Bf4?! made it worse, because 8...Qxf4 won your bishop outright.

Black returned the favour with 9...Rd8??, a blunder that put you at +4.5. The right move was 9...Bxe4. After 9...Rd8 you had 10.Nf6+, a discovered attack that uncovered your queen on d4 against the queen on f4, and it would have kept you winning.
You played 10.Qf2?? instead, and after 10...e6 11.Nc5? 11...Bxc5 12.Qxc5? came the knockout. 12...Qd2# ended the game. 12.Bb5+ was the last chance to avoid mate.

review.turning_point: 10.Qf2?? turned a winning +4.5 into -3.7. 10.Nf6+ was the move.
review.focus: After a gift like 9...Rd8, stop and list every check and capture. 10.Nf6+ was available and 10.Qf2 missed it.

review.headline: A Bishop's Opening where you won a bishop for free and let a huge lead slip

sections.text: White played 3.Bxf7+??, a huge blunder, and you took the bishop with 3...Kxf7!. Then 4.Nf3 h6 5.Nxe5+ came, and your king was in the open. 5...Kg8 would have been safe and good, but 5...Ke6?? dropped you to -0.8.

White's 6.d4 took the centre, and 6...Bd6?? missed the better 6...Qe8. Fortunately 7.Nf3?? was a gift from white. You went back to equal, and 12.Ne4?? was an even bigger gift, which you took at once with 12...Rxe4!, winning a piece.
You kept the pressure with 15...Nxf3+, 16...Re6 and 17...gxh6. Even with 18...Rxd6?! and 20.Qd5+ you were around +3, with a lot of extra pieces.

Then the end. 22...b6?? dropped you from +4.1 to -7.4 because 22...Qg6 was the move. White's 23.f3?? and 24.Qxd7+?? gave you chances, but 23...Ba6?? and 25...Qb7?? stepped onto the diagonal where white's queen on c6 hits both your queen and the rook on a8, a skewer, and 26.Qxf6 was crushing.

review.turning_point: 22...b6?? turned +4.1 into -7.4 in a single move.
review.focus: When you are far ahead, check your own king and loose pieces before each move. 22...Qg6 was the safe move, and 25...Bb7 kept everything defended.

review.headline: A messy King's Pawn game rescued by a missed mate and a final queen trap

sections.text: In this quiet setup you traded early with 7...Bxf3?! and 8.Bxf3, then reached a slightly worse but playable position after 10...Nxd5 and 12.Bxd4 exd4. Your opponent kept the initiative, and 15...c5?? was the first real blunder, going to -3.3.

After 15.e5 c5 16.Bxa8 you were down a lot of ground, and 16...Rb8?! and 17...Rxb2 did not fix it. By 18.exd6 the evaluation was around -5, and 19.Qh5, 20.Qd5 and 21.f4 kept your king under fire. For a long stretch you were just worse.

But you kept finding the toughest defensive moves. 28...Qg7! was a trap. White had 29.Qxg7#, a mate, but played 29.Rb8+?? instead, a back-rank check that you answered by taking, 29...Bxb8!. From then on you were safe.
White's last blunder was 32.Qxg6??. You took the queen with 32...Qxg6!, and the game ended in your favour. A lucky win, but you earned it by setting problems and staying calm.

review.turning_point: 29.Rb8+?? missed 29.Qxg7#, and 29...Bxb8! flipped the game.
review.focus: Avoid 15...c5. After 15.e5, the quieter 15...Rab8 kept you level, so look for a quiet move before opening the position.

review.headline: A Stafford Gambit where you built a bind and then dropped a knight to a loosened pawn

sections.text: Your opponent tried the Stafford Gambit. You answered with 3.Nxe5, and after 3...Nc6? you found 4.Nxc6! dxc6 5.d3 5...Bc5, which gave you a pleasant edge, around +1.9. 6.Be3? was a small mistake and 6.Be2 was cleaner, but 6...Qe7? gave it back.

You found 7.Bxc5!, which traded off black's active bishop, and after 7...Qxc5 you were comfortable. 8.Nc3 and 9.Qe2 were solid and 11.O-O-O was a sensible way to castle. 11...Be6? let you continue, and you were around +2.4.

Then 13.b3?? ruined the position. Your knight on c3 had been defended by the b2 pawn, so moving it let black take with 13...Qxc3, a swing from +2.4 to -2.9. 13.f4 was a good alternative. After that you pushed forward with 15.g5?! and 19.hxg6?, trying to attack.
You did find 20.gxh7+!, but 21.Qf1?? and 24.g6?? threw away your chances. After 24...Qxh6 the game was gone.

review.turning_point: 13.b3?? removed the defender of the knight on c3 and handed black the capture on c3.
review.focus: Before a pawn move such as 13.b3, ask what it stops defending. 13.f4 kept the knight on c3 protected.

review.headline: A French where you built a winning attack and lost on time after a pawn check

sections.text: Black played an odd setup with 2...a6, 3...b5 and 5...h6, and your calm 4.Be2 and 5.Nbd2 were fine. When black pushed 6...g5 and 7...g4, 8.Ne5 was a good answer, and 9.Bxg4 won a pawn straight away. You were clearly better, around +2.0 and then +3.0.
Your attack grew with 12.f4, 13.f5 and 14.Bxh5, which kept black's king uneasy, and 16.g3 held the structure together. Everything was going to plan.

Then 17.Kh1?? was a slip that dropped you to -1.5. 17.Rf2 was the better idea. Black missed the strong 17...Qxg3 and played 17...Rh3??, and your 18.Bg2! was the correct answer. Later 19.fxe6 and 20.exf7+! kept you in control.

You reached 23.Qxd7 and the evaluation read +9.3 after 23...Rd8. But under time pressure 24.e7+?? looked like a fork of the rook on d8 and the king on f8, yet the knight just took it with 24...Ngxe7. 24.Ba3+ was the move. 25.Qe6?? followed and the flag fell.

review.turning_point: 24.e7+?? let the knight take the pawn and threw away a +9.3 position, when 24.Ba3+ was needed.
review.focus: In time trouble, play the forcing check you have already calculated. 24.Ba3+ was the move, not the pawn push 24.e7+.

review.headline: A Petrov where you were outplayed for 30 moves, then won on the clock with a pawn race

sections.text: You played the Three Knights Petrov solidly: 3...d6, 4...Be7, 5...Nbd7 and 6...exd4. The early moves were fine. 10...b5? was the first slip, since 10...d5 was cleaner. After 11.Nc6 and 12.Nxe7+ you were about -2.5.

Then 13...Nxd5?? was a blunder, since 13...Nb7 was better. After 14.Nxd5 14...Qe5, 15.c3?? gave a little back, but after 15...Na4?! 16.Bf4 16...Nxc3?! 17.Bxe5 17...Nxd1 the queens were off and you were still around -4.
You defended stubbornly. White spent time with checks like 29.Rc8+ and 30.R2c7+ before 31.Rxf7 and 33.Rxd1 left white with the better ending at about -4.9. The key was to keep your pawns moving.
White's collapse started with 34.Rb1??. You found 34...b4! and then 35...b3!, then 38...Nxb1!, winning the rook. Your pawns ran with 43...b2 and 44...b1=Q, and white lost on time.

review.turning_point: 34.Rb1?? let you push the b-pawn, and 38.Kf4?? allowed 38...Nxb1! to win the rook.
review.focus: Look at 13...Nxd5, where the knight capture lost ground. 13...Nb7 was the calm choice that kept the position level.

review.headline: A messy Zukertort where your opponent's pawn storm collapsed and you finished with mate

sections.text: White played the London-style 3.e3, 4.h3 and 5.g4, chasing your bishop. You went to g6, and after 7.Nxg6 hxg6 the structure was fine. 8.f4 f5? was a risky response, though, and the game became sharp very quickly.

You made many small slips in the middle: 13...Ng3? (13...e5 was better), then 18...Qa5?, 19...O-O-O? and 20...Rh7?. The evaluation stayed within a pawn or two most of the time. A good moment was 16...Ne4!, which led to 17...Nxd2 and a useful trade of your knight for the dark bishop.
Then white overpressed. 25.g6?? was a blunder, and you found 25...Rxh5! to take the rook. After 26.Rxh5 26...Nxg6 27.Rxh8+ 27...Nxh8, the evaluation went from -2.4 to roughly equal.

Slips continued with 31...g6?? and 32.a5?, but you stayed solid. White's king drifted, and you won pawns with 36...Nxg5 and 41...Nxe3. Your passed f-pawn ran home with 47...f3 and 49...f1=Q, and 51...Bd2# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 25.g6?? by white and your answer 25...Rxh5! swung the game from -2.4 to nearly equal, and later errors by white gave you the edge.
review.focus: Keep a close eye on structural weaknesses, such as 31...g6. The better 31...Nf7 would have kept the endgame simple.

review.headline: A Blackmar-Diemer where you were nearly lost and then won through a long endgame mate

sections.text: Your opponent offered a gambit and you took it with 3...dxe4. White played 4.f3? but 4...Nf6? gave back the edge, and 6...a6?? was the first big blunder, since 6...c5 was cleaner. After 7.Nf3?? you answered 7...c5! to get back into the game.

Then 8...c4?? went wrong, falling to -2.6, because 8...cxd4 was needed. 9.Bxc4 9...Nb6?! made it worse and 11...Ke7?? moved the king to a risky spot, with 11...e5 the safer choice. 12.d6+ 12...Qxd6 13.Qxd6+ 13...Kxd6 left you in a long defensive endgame.

You kept surviving. 14...Kc7?? was another mistake, and 15.Bf4+, 16.Ne5+ and 17.Be3+ chased your king up the board, the evaluation reaching about -9. But your king reached a5 and survived, and trades like 18...Bc5+ and 19.Bxc5+ simplified things.

White erred late. 34.Nxa4?? let you play 34...Rxd2!, and 36.Nb6?? allowed 36...Rxd2! again. From there your rook and passed pawns won everything: 40...Rxc5, 42...Rxa3 and 43...Rxc3. The pawn race ended with 57...a2#.

review.turning_point: 36.Nb6?? allowed 36...Rxd2!, swinging the evaluation from -2.8 to over +5.
review.focus: Review 8...c4. After 8.O-O the simple 8...cxd4 kept the position level, but the pawn push cost a pawn and the initiative.

review.headline: Italian attack that finished with a queen mate on f7

sections.text: This was a clean Italian Game where you took the centre and held the initiative. After 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4, your opponent chose 6...Bb6?, and you answered with exactly the right idea. 7.e5! kicked the knight off f6 with tempo and sent the evaluation to +1.7.

Black's knight then spent several moves being chased around, from 7...Ng4 to 8...Nh6 and 9...Ne7. Your 9.Bg5 and 11.g4 kept it from settling anywhere comfortable. 10.Qd2?! was a little slow, but you were still about two pawns up in the evaluation.
12.Bxe7? was your one real slip. Swapping your active bishop for a knight released the pressure, and the evaluation fell from +1.9 to +0.3. Keeping the bishop with 12.Bf4 maintained the grip.

Your opponent then handed the game back. After 14.Qf4, the move 14...Ng6?? walked into 15.Qxf7#. The queen takes on f7 with check, the king on e8 has no escape, and the queen also attacks the knight on g6, a fork of king and knight that finishes the game on the spot.

review.turning_point: 14...Ng6?? allowed 15.Qxf7#, a mate that was also a fork of the king on e8 and the knight on g6. Before that, 7.e5! was the move that took control of the opening.
review.focus: At 12.Bxe7? you gave up a good bishop for a knight when you were clearly better. When you have the edge, ask whether a trade helps you or just relieves your opponent; 12.Bf4 kept the pressure on.

review.headline: A winning position thrown away by a queen blunder on move 24

sections.text: A Queen's Pawn game that started fine for you. You were slightly better after 7.c3, but 7...Ba5? let the advantage slip, since 7...Bd6 was the engine's choice. At 11...Nd3? you slipped again. After 11.O-O you stood at +1.0, but taking on f3 with 11...Nxf3+ was the better capture, and the evaluation dropped to -0.5.
Your opponent returned the favour with 13.Ned4??, a blunder, and then 15.Qxg6??. After 14.Nh4 Ne1 the white queen took on g6, and 15...hxg6! picked up the queen. From -0.5 you were suddenly at +3.9.

You then converted well for a while. 16.Rfxe1 Bb6 and 17...Bxd4 18.exd4 kept you comfortably ahead. 20...f6? was an inaccuracy (20...g5 was stronger), and 23.Bxe4?? gave you 23...dxe4!, which kept the advantage at around +4.

Then came 24...Qd5??, which dropped the evaluation from +4.1 to -7.2. After 25.Ne7+ the knight checks the king and attacks the queen at the same time. 24...Kf7 simply attacked the knight on g6 and kept everything safe.

review.turning_point: 24...Qd5?? turned a +4 position into a lost one, because 25.Ne7+ checks the king and attacks the queen. 24...Kf7 was the safe move.
review.focus: On 24...Qd5?? you moved the queen onto a square a knight check could hit. In a winning position, list every check and capture your opponent has before each move; 24...Kf7 would have been enough.

review.headline: A huge advantage thrown away by a blunder when the clock ran low

sections.text: You went into the Italian with 3.Bc4 and the position was fine, with 4.Nc3 Na5 5.Nd5 Qd6 giving you +1.7. But 6.d3?? threw most of it away. 6.Be2 was the safe move, and after 6...Nxc4 7.dxc4 the evaluation was -0.3.

Then Black blundered back. 8.c5?! was an overpush, but 8...Qxc5?? walked into 9.Nc7+!, a fork of the king on e8 and the rook on a8. After 10.Nxa8 you had won the rook, and the evaluation was around +4.

From here you collected material steadily, with 14.Bxe7+ Qxe7 and later 21.Rxa7 and 22.Rxg7?!. You were well ahead on the board. 23.Ng5?? is where low time hurt, as 23.Qb4 was the engine's pick, though 24.Rxg5 Rg8?? gave you 25.Rxg8+!, using the back rank against the king on b8.
Then 27.Qxf5?? lost on the spot to 27...Qxg2#. Your queen left the defence of g2 and nothing else covered it. 27.f3 would have kept everything protected, and you were still around +5.

review.turning_point: 27.Qxf5?? allowed 27...Qxg2# from a position where you were around +5. 27.f3 would have closed the door.
review.focus: With 27.Qxf5?? you grabbed a pawn without checking what the opponent's queen could do next. When ahead and short of time, ask first what your opponent threatens; 27.f3 covered g2.

review.headline: Accurate Queen's Gambit Declined that ended with a back-rank mate

sections.text: A model Queen's Gambit Declined from you. You developed with 3...Nf6 and 4...Be7, and met 5.Bg5 with ...h6 and ...Nbd7. After 9.cxd5 Nxd5 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 the trades left you comfortable, and 11.Qb3 Bb7 12.Bc4 N7f6 kept things level at around +0.2.

You played 14...c5 to open lines, and after 15.dxc5 Qxc5 your queen pressed on the c-file. White then played 16.Rad1??, which was a blunder, since 16.Nxd5 was the safe move. You took the chance with 16...Nxc3 17.Qxc3 Ne4 and were at +2.8.

After 18.Rxd8+ Rxd8 19.b4 Qc7 20.Qb2, your knight jumped to d2 with 20...Nd2, attacking the rook on f1 and the bishop on c4 together. 21.Rc1 Nxc4 won the bishop, and you went from +3.9 to +5.1 to +4.9.
White's last move, 22.Rxc4?, took the knight but pulled the rook off the first rank, and 22...Rd1# was a back-rank mate, with the king on g1 boxed in by its own pawns. A very accurate game from you.

review.turning_point: 16.Rad1?? gave you the initiative, and 20...Nd2 hit the rook on f1 and the bishop on c4 together. 22...Rd1# finished it with a back-rank mate.
review.focus: You played cleanly. The pattern to keep from this game is 20...Nd2 followed by 22...Rd1#: look for double attacks by knights and always check whether your opponent's king can be mated on the back rank.

review.headline: Ragozin that went wrong when the bishop retreated to a5

sections.text: You played a normal Queen's Gambit Declined setup with 2...e6, 3...Nf6 and 4...Bb4. After 5.a3 your bishop on b4 was asked a question, and the evaluation was still level at 0.0.

5...Ba5?? was the mistake and dropped the evaluation to -3.9. 5...Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 c5 is the standard answer and keeps things even. After 6.b4 the bishop on a5 was under attack and the position was already close to lost.
6...Bxb4 7.axb4 gave up the bishop for a pawn, and you were two points of material down. 7...Qd6 8.c5 pushed the queen away, and 8...Qf4?! walked into 9.Bxf4, which took the queen. You resigned.

review.turning_point: 5...Ba5?? was the decisive moment. After 6.b4 you lost the bishop for a pawn, where 5...Bxc3+ was the safe move.
review.focus: After 5.a3 your bishop has two options, to trade on c3 or retreat. Before retreating to a5, check what 6.b4 does; 5...Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 c5 kept the position equal.

review.headline: Wild Italian where you won material early, then let it slip

sections.text: A Two Knights style Italian where Black overreached. After 7.Nc3, 7...d5?? was a blunder, and you took advantage: 8.exd5 Nb4 9.Nxe5 Nbxd5 10.Nxd5 put you up material and at about +1.8.
Black played 10...Bxe3??, which raised the evaluation to +5.4. But 11.Nxf6+? let it slip away. The simple 11.Nxe3 took the bishop and kept the extra piece. After 11...Qxf6 you were at +2.7.

12.Ng4? was another slip, with 12.Nxf7 stronger. Then 12...Bxf2+?? was a blunder from Black, and 13.Nxf2! was the right reply, bringing you back to +4.6. After 13...Qxb2 14.Ne4 b5 15.Bb3 c5 you still had a good position.

16.Nxc5?? cost you about 2.4 pawns. After 16...Qd4+ 17.Rf2? things drifted to level. Then 23.Qg4?? gave Black a big edge (23.Rf5 was the engine's pick), and although 23...Kh8?? missed 23...Qxf2, 24.Qd7?? allowed 24...Qxf2, which took the rook on f2. You resigned.

review.turning_point: 11.Nxf6+? gave back a big advantage when 11.Nxe3 simply took the bishop. Later 23.Qg4?? and 24.Qd7?? ended it.
review.focus: At 11.Nxf6+? you went for a trade with the bishop on e3 still hanging. When your opponent leaves a piece en prise, take it first; 11.Nxe3 kept the extra piece.

review.headline: A good attack faded, then a queen walked into a free capture

sections.text: A Classical Italian where you reached a typical centre. After 6...Bb6? you found 7.e5!, hitting the knight, and 7...Ng8? drove it back to the edge of the board for +3.5.

8.Bg5? let Black back in. 8.d5 first, kicking the knight on c6, was the sharper move. After 8...f6 9.exf6 gxf6 you had a pawn, but 10.Bh4? slipped to +0.3. 10.Qe2+ was stronger, and Black's 10...Qe7+ 11.Kf1 d5 put you at +0.8.
12.Bxd5 grabbed a pawn, and 12...Nxd4?? lost a piece to 13.Nxd4!, pushing you to +4.1. After 13...c6 14.Bb3 Qc5 15.Qe2+ Kf8 you were at +4.4, with every piece better placed than your opponent's.
Then came 16.Qh5??, offering your queen where 16...Qxh5 simply took it for nothing. 16.Nf3 would have kept the advantage. The evaluation went from +4.8 to -5.3 on one move.

review.turning_point: 16.Qh5?? offered the queen on a square where the black queen could just capture it, turning +4.8 into a lost position.
review.focus: On 16.Qh5?? you moved the queen without asking what attacked the destination square. Check every square you move a major piece to; 16.Nf3 kept the winning position.

review.headline: Good counterplay against a pawn storm, spoiled by one knight check

sections.text: White opened with 1.e4 e5 2.d3 d6 3.f3 and a rapid pawn storm on the kingside, with 4.g4, 5.h4 and 6.h5. You handled it calmly; 6...Nbd7?! was a slight inaccuracy, but the real test came at 9.g5?, which pushed too far.

9...hxg5! was the right reply. After 10.Bxg5 Nxh5 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 you were a pawn ahead and your pieces were more active. 12...O-O-O put the king out of the way, and 13...Ng3?! used a discovered attack from the rook on h8 against the rook on h1.
After 14.Rxh8 Rxh8 15.O-O-O Rh2?! you kept up the pressure. 16.Qf2? was a mistake, and 16...Qh4! was the right reply, leaving your pieces ready to attack.

Then 17...Ne2+?? threw it away. The knight check forks the king on c1 and the knight on c3, and unmasks your queen against the white queen. But 18.Qxe2 simply took the knight and the idea collapsed. 17...Kb8 kept a clear advantage.

review.turning_point: 17...Ne2+?? looked like a fork plus a discovered attack, but 18.Qxe2 just captured the knight. The evaluation dropped from +2.9 to -1.6.
review.focus: At 17...Ne2+?? you saw a fork and a discovered attack but missed that the checked piece could simply capture the knight. Before any forcing move, ask whether your opponent can capture the checking piece; 17...Kb8 kept the advantage.

review.headline: A mate on g7 after a chaotic game with mistakes on both sides

sections.text: An Italian where Black played 3...h6, and you took the centre with 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4. Black's 5...Bc5? was a mistake, but 6.Be3? let it off the hook. 6.Bxf7+ was the engine's pick, and the evaluation dropped from +2.3 to +0.6.

After 7.c3?! d6 8.Nd2 Be6??, Black blundered, and 9.Bb3?? gave the advantage back at once. 9.Bxe6 fxe6 10.Nxe6 would have hit the queen and kept the edge. After 9...Bxb3 10.axb3 the position was level.
12.Qf3 Ne5 13.Qg3 followed, and now 13...Kh8?? was a blunder that allowed a forced win. 14.Bxh6 was not the best, as 14.Qxg7# was available at once.
But 14...gxh6?? made it easy, and 15.Qg7# finished the game. The queen on g3 mated on g7, supported by the knight on f5.

review.turning_point: 13...Kh8?? left the king on h8, and 14.Bxh6 gxh6 15.Qg7# ended the game. 14.Qxg7# was mate at once.
review.focus: At 14.Bxh6 you missed 14.Qxg7#, an immediate mate. Before each sacrifice, look at your checks first and see whether the queen alone can finish.

review.headline: A Pirc where a knight on h5 was punished, finished with a queen mate

sections.text: You went for 4.Bc4 against the Pirc, then 5.e5?! dxe5 6.Nxe5 was a speculative push and the evaluation dropped to -0.1. After 7.c3 Nbd7, 8.Qf3? was a mistake, as 8.O-O was the safe move, and 8...Nxe5 9.dxe5 left you at -1.9.
Black then blundered with 9...Nh5??, and you found 10.g4!. After 10...Bxg4 11.Qxg4 Bxe5 you had won a bishop for a pawn, and the evaluation was +3.0.
12.Bh6 Ng7 13.Nd2 a6 14.O-O-O b5 15.Nf3 Bd6 kept you pressing at around +4. But 16.Qd4?? was a blunder, dropping to +0.5. 16.Bb3 was stronger, hitting f7.
Black replied 16...bxc4??, and 17.Qxg7# was mate. The queen on g7 is supported by the bishop on h6, and the rook on d1 is unleashed on the bishop on d6 as the queen leaves d4, a discovered attack.

review.turning_point: 10.g4! punished 9...Nh5?? and netted a bishop for a pawn. Later 16...bxc4?? allowed 17.Qxg7#.
review.focus: At 16.Qd4?? the evaluation fell from +3.7 to +0.5. With a big lead, look for the most direct move; 16.Bb3 kept the pressure.

review.headline: A London where 17...exf3 let a bishop take the rook

sections.text: You set up solidly against the London with 2...e6, 3...Bd6 and 5...O-O. After 9.Bxd6 cxd6 10.Nbd2 Re8 11.h3 e5 12.dxe5 dxe5 the position was level at -0.1.
13.e4 dxe4?! took a pawn, and 14.Nxe4 Nb4 15.Nxf6+ Qxf6 16.cxb4 left you a knight down. But 16...e4 hit the knight on f3, and the engine had you roughly level.
17.Bb5 attacked your rook on e8, and 17...exf3?? was the blunder, dropping to -2.7. 17...Red8 was safe. After 18.Bxe8 the bishop took the rook, and 18...fxg2?! did not recapture the bishop.
19.Re1 Bf3 20.Qd7 Rd8? ended it. The queen on d7 and the bishop on e8 were too strong. 21.Bxf7+ Qxf7 22.Qxd8+ and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 17...exf3?? took the knight but left the rook on e8 en prise to 18.Bxe8. 17...Red8 would have kept the game balanced.
review.focus: At 17...exf3?? you captured a knight without checking that 17.Bb5 attacked your rook on e8. Before a capture, ask whether your opponent's last move created a threat.

review.headline: A reasonable Philidor spoiled by 10...Nxd5, dropping a knight

sections.text: A Philidor Exchange where you played carefully. After 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 Be7 6.Be3 O-O 7.Bd3 Re8 8.h3 c5 9.Nf3 you were only slightly worse, around -0.2.
9...d5? was a mistake. After 10.exd5 White had a pawn on d5 and a lead, and 9...a6 was the engine's choice. The evaluation dropped from -0.2 to -1.5.

10...Nxd5?? was the blunder, and the evaluation dropped to -5.1. After 11.Nxd5 you were a knight down. 11...Qa5+ 12.Qd2 Qxd2+ 13.Nxd2 traded the queens, and 14.Nxe7+ Rxe7 kept the extra piece. 10...Nbd7 was the safe move.
From there White pushed with 17.g4, 18.h4 and 19.h5 and 20.g5 to open lines. You held on for a while with 15...b6 and 16...Bf5, but the extra piece told. You resigned after 21.Bd5.

review.turning_point: 10...Nxd5?? lost a knight for nothing after 11.Nxd5 and the evaluation fell to -5.
review.focus: At 9...d5? you opened the centre while behind in development. Be careful with central pawn breaks; 9...a6 kept the position solid, and 10...Nbd7 was the safe reply.

review.headline: A winning endgame that slipped to a draw

sections.text: You played the Scotch and won a pawn early with 8.Qxg7!. After 7...Bc5?, you were at +2.0. 9.Qxf6?! traded queens but gave away some of the advantage, as 9.Qg3 was the engine's pick, and 10.Bg5? let Black back in.
12...d5?? gave you the chance, and 13.Bb5+! drove the king to f8. By 15.Rxd5 Rg8 you were at +5.0. Black's 23...Kg6? let you play 24.Bd3+!, a skewer on the king with the bishop on h7 behind it.
After 25.Bxh7 Rxg5 26.Rxg5+ hxg5 27.Re7 you were winning, and 32.f7 and 33.f8=Q queened. After 36.Qxg1+ Kxg1 you were a bishop up with pawns, at +5.7, and the position looked won.

But 50.Bd7?? threw it away, dropping from +6.3 to +0.3. 50.Bd3 would have guarded the c2 pawn. After 50...Kxc2 the position was drawn. Black blundered with 55...Kc5?? and 57...Kc5??, but 60.Ka4??, 61.Be8??, 63.Be8?? and 64.Bc6?? each let it go, and the game ended in a draw.

review.turning_point: 50.Bd7?? let the black king take the c2 pawn and turned a winning ending into a draw.
review.focus: At 50.Bd7?? you dropped the c2 pawn in a winning ending. In endings, check what each piece defends before moving it; 50.Bd3 kept c2 guarded.

review.headline: A messy Center Game you won on the back of opponent errors

sections.text: A Center Game where White's queen came out early. After 7.Bxc6 Bxc6 8.Qb4, 8...Qc8? was a mistake (8...d5 was better), and 9...Qg4?! kept the queen active but loose.
White blundered with 10.Qc4??, but 10...Nf6?? missed 10...Qxg2, a fork of the knight on f3 and the rook on h1. After 11.Qe2?? you found 11...Nxe4!, winning a pawn.
After 13.Qxe4+ Bxe4 14.Bd2 Bxc2? the evaluation went from +2.9 to +1.3. 14...Kd7 was stronger. 15.O-O?? was another miss, and 15...O-O-O put you in good shape.
You pressed for a long time. 29...Bd5?? dropped from +4.9 to +0.1, but White blundered with 39.h5??, and 39...a3! won. You were at +6.0 after 43...Kb2.

review.turning_point: 11...Nxe4! took advantage of 11.Qe2??, and 39...a3! won the pawn race after 39.h5??.
review.focus: At 10...Nf6?? you missed 10...Qxg2. When the opponent blunders, look first for forcing captures; 29...Bd5?? also dropped much of your advantage.

review.headline: A quiet opening spoiled by a knight move that blocked a queen's diagonal

sections.text: A Van't Kruijs where you played 2...Nf6 and 3...d5. After 5.a3 Be7? you slipped from +0.9 to -0.3, as 5...d4 was the engine's pick. 6.cxd5 Nxd5 7.Bc4 Be6 was fine.
White's 8.Qf3? was an error, and 9.Ne2? another, and your 9...b5! was a fine reply that hit the bishop on c4. After 10.Bd3 you were at +1.9.
10...Nf6?? was the blunder, dropping to -3.9. The knight on d5 was blocking the queen's diagonal from f3 to c6, and moving it opened the diagonal on your knight on c6. 10...Qd7 kept things safe.
11.h3?? missed 11.Qxc6+. But 11...Qxd3?? took the bishop, and 12.Qxc6+ Nd7 13.Qxa8+ won a rook with check. You resigned.

review.turning_point: 10...Nf6?? opened the diagonal from f3 to c6 and left the knight on c6 hanging, then 11...Qxd3?? let 12.Qxc6+ in.
review.focus: At 10...Nf6?? you moved a piece that was blocking an attack on your own knight. Before moving a piece, check what it was shielding; 10...Qd7 kept it safe.

review.headline: A London where a queen grab on g7 was punished

sections.text: You met the London with a solid setup, 2...e6, 3...Bd6 and 5...O-O. After 11.Ne5 Be7?! and 12.Ndf3 Nxe5 13.Nxe5 the position was balanced, around -0.3.
13...Nd7?? was a blunder, dropping to -3.3, since 13...Qc8 was better. White replied 14.Bc2??, a blunder, and 14...Nxe5! got you back to -0.5.
15...Bf6?! was an inaccuracy and 16.Qd3? a mistake by White, as 16.f4 was better. Then 16...c4?? lost control, since the queen and bishop battery was aimed at h7. 17.Qxh7+ Kf8 18.Qh8+ Ke7 followed.
19.Qxg7?? was the blunder, and you found 19...Bxg7!, winning the queen. After 20.Bxg7 f6 21.Bg6 Rg8 you were up material at +4.7, and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 19.Qxg7?? gave you the queen after 19...Bxg7!, turning a worse position into a winning one.
review.focus: At 16...c4?? you attacked the queen but ignored the battery aimed at h7. 16...g6 would have shut it down; always check what an attacked queen can capture.

review.headline: A strong Italian win, though two blunders nearly threw it away

sections.text: You played the Classical Italian and punished 6...Nxd4?? with 7.Nxd4!. After 7...Bxd4 8.Qxd4 you had won a piece for a pawn, at +4.5.
You kept the edge with 9.O-O d6 10.Re1 c5 11.Qd1 Bg4 12.Be2 Bxe2 13.Qxe2 and 16.Bxf6 gxf6 17.Qg4+. You were at about +5, and everything was working.
But 20.f3?? was a blunder, dropping to -0.5. 20.Qb2+ was the engine's pick. After 20...Qd4+ 21.Qe3 Qxa1 you were down material, and 23.Nd5?? made it worse, at -3.4.
Black blundered with 25...fxe4??, and you found 26.Nf6!. After 26...Qxf6 27.Qxf6+ Kg8 you had traded a knight for the queen and were back at +5.2. You won with 44.h8=Q and 63.Qa8#.

review.turning_point: 25...fxe4?? allowed 26.Nf6!, which won the queen for a knight and turned a worse position into a winning one.
review.focus: At 20.f3?? you weakened your king when winning. 20.Qb2+ kept everything under control; with a big lead, check forcing moves first.

review.headline: A French Exchange slugfest where you outplayed the opening, gave it back, then ran out of clock while worse

sections.text: This was a French Exchange that turned into an open fight. You gave up the bishop pair early with 7.a3 Bxc3 8.Bxc3 and pushed on the queenside with 9.b3 and 10.a4. The exchange 11.Ne5 and 12.Nxd7 was playable, but it cost you the nice initiative you had at 10...Bd7, and the game came back to roughly level.

Your opponent then slipped with 13...Na6, and you answered it well. 14.axb5 was a discovered attack: moving the a-pawn opened the a-file so your rook on a1 looked at the knight on a6 while the pawn took on b5. That put you at +0.7.

You gave much of that back immediately. 15.Ra5 was loose, and after 15...Qc6 the move 16.O-O let Black release the tension with 16...cxb3. The engine preferred 16.bxc4, keeping your structure intact. A similar chance appeared at 25.Re1, where 25.Bxd5+ was the move, and then 26.Re5 dropped you to -2.4 when 26.h3 was calm and fine.

You still showed fight: 30.Rxf5 brought the evaluation back to around -0.5 and the endgame was defensible. Then 37.f3 let Black's knight and rook become active again, and you lost on time at 41 moves with the game roughly -2.

review.turning_point: 26.Re5 turned a balanced rook endgame into a clearly worse one (+0.1 to -2.4), when 26.h3 kept everything protected.
review.focus: Before pushing a piece forward in a quiet position, such as 26.Re5, check what it leaves undefended and whether a waiting move like 26.h3 is safer.

review.headline: A reckless 4.Nxe5 that your opponent could not punish, followed by a tactical win

sections.text: You opened with a normal Two Knights Italian, then grabbed on e5 with 4.Nxe5. That was a real mistake: after 4...Nxe5 you were a piece for a pawn down (-3.2) and the engine wanted 4.Ng5 instead.
Credit to you for how well you used the next chances. Black replied 5...Bc5, and 6.d4! was the right shot. It forked the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5, which Black could not handle.

8.Qd5 created another fork on c5 and e5 and also pressured b7 and d7. Black's 8...Nxb3 was a blunder, and you took the best route with 9.Qxe5+. That check also hit g7 with the rook on h8 behind it, so Black had to trade queens with 9...Qe7 10.Qxe7+ Kxe7 and recapture with 11.axb3.

From there it was simple: you developed with 12.O-O and 13.Nc3, picked up pawns with 15.Nxc7 and 16.Nxa8, and finished with a steady rook and bishop attack. Black ran out of time at move 30 while you were far ahead.

review.turning_point: 8...Nxb3 was the decisive error from Black. You found 9.Qxe5+ and the evaluation jumped to +4.6.
review.focus: Look at 4.Nxe5: before capturing in the opening, ask what recaptures. 4.Ng5 was the safer way to keep the initiative.

review.headline: A wild attacking game where you had +5.6 and then threw it away

sections.text: You went for open play against 3...h6 with 4.d4 and kept the initiative, helped by 14...Bh3?, a Black blunder. You found 15.Rxe5+! and kept winning ground with 16.Qf3 and 17.Qxb7, then 18.Rxe7 put you at +5.6.

That was the moment to simplify, but 19.Qxc7?? went wrong. The engine liked 19.Bxf7+, a fork on the queen on g6 and the king on g8. Then 20.Bxf7+ also dropped the evaluation to -4.2, when 20.Qf4 would have kept control.

Black gave it back with 21...Rcf8, but 22.Ba3 missed 22.Rxf7 and 23.Re3 missed 23.Rxg7+, which carried a fork and a skewer. With each missed chance the position went from winning to lost, and then back again: 25.Kxh2!, 26.Kh1! and 27.Rxf3! were precise defensive moves that put you at +3.9.
Even at +7.1 after 27...Rxf3 you still had a win, but low on time you played 28.Rg1. The engine's 28.Qa8+ was a back rank check that kept everything under control. Instead 28...Rh3# ended it.

review.turning_point: 19.Qxc7 gave away a winning attack (+5.6 to +1.8), and 20.Bxf7+ and later 28.Rg1 completed the collapse.
review.focus: When you are far ahead, as at 19.Qxc7, look for the forcing move first: 19.Bxf7+ would have kept the attack going.

review.headline: Solid against the London until 19...fxg6 started a run of tactical oversights

sections.text: You met the London calmly. After 4.Bxd6 cxd6 you built a sound centre with ...e5 and ...e4, and White's early moves gave you equal chances through 15...Bb7.

The problems began with 18.Nf4 Ng6 19.Nxg6. Recapturing with 19...fxg6 was a blunder: 19...hxg6 kept your king safer and the f-file closed. White's 20.Rf4 then pinned the knight against your rook on f8. Your opponent missed 20.Nxe4, so you stayed in the game.

20...Qc7 let White add pressure, and 21...Nh5 opened the f-file for a discovered attack on your rook. 22.Rxf8+ cost you material, though White returned the favour with 23.Qd1 and 24.Qg4, so you got back some ground with 24...Nf6!
You still had resources, but White built up with 26.Rxf6 and 31.h3, and by move 37 the game was lost. The final mistake, 37...Qxg2+, gave up your queen for nothing (the engine suggested 37...Rxb2).

review.turning_point: 19...fxg6 was the moment the game tilted, going from +1.3 to -1.6 for White when 19...hxg6 was available.
review.focus: In 19...fxg6, 20...Qc7 and 21...Nh5, you reacted to threats move by move. Before recapturing, ask which recapture keeps your king safest.

review.headline: A dominating win on the board that ended on the clock

sections.text: Against the Nimzowitsch you played the main ideas well: 3.dxe5, 4.Nf3, 5.Bc4 and 6.Ng5, which set a trap. Black fell for it with 6...Be6?, a real blunder, and you collected with 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6.

9.Nxf8 was a mistake: it traded your knight for a bishop and your knight was recaptured, which only gained time for Black. The engine pointed to 9.Qd5, hitting b7 and the rook on a8. You were still better and played the next moves well, with 10.O-O, 11.Bg5 and 12.Qg4+.
The big moment came at 15...h6, which allowed 16.Bxe7!. It was a pin on the e-file (e6, e7 and e8), and it cost Black the queen trade at 17.Qxf7 Nxf7. After that you were around +5 or more.

You kept finding good moves: 28.Bxd6, 30.Bxd8, and 36.Rb8+!, a skewer along the eighth rank that was also a back rank idea, then 39.Rxf8. The position was easily winning at move 45, but the clock ran out first.

review.turning_point: 15...h6 and the reply 16.Bxe7! won the game on the board, taking the evaluation to +5.4.
review.focus: Time management: you were at +6.0 on move 45 and still lost on time. Look at 9.Nxf8, where a quick grab cost you the cleaner 9.Qd5, and plan to move faster in won positions.

review.headline: You punished a Bishop's Opening sacrifice, then let the advantage slip with 9...Ne7

sections.text: White opened with 2.Bc4 and sacrificed straight away with 3.Bxf7+??. You answered perfectly with 3...Kxf7!, and after 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qf3+ Ke8 you came out clearly ahead. 7...Qxf3 8.Nxf3 simplified into a position where you were up material and around +4.

Then came the key error: 9.Nd5 and 9...Ne7?. Instead of the quiet 9...Na6, this allowed 10.Nxc7+ Kd7 11.Nxa8, and the evaluation flipped from +4.3 to -1.6. After 12...Rf8? 13.Nxh7 you were fighting uphill.
You did get chances. 21.Ra3?? was a blunder from White and 21...Nxc1! punished it. 25...Bh6! was another strong reply. But 24...Rf2 and 27...Be3 let White off the hook; 27...Bxe4 was better.
Later 29...Rc2 put your rook on a square where it was taken by 31.Kxc2, though 31...Bxe4+ gave a fork and a pin as compensation. By then White was too far ahead, and the ending ended with 41.Ra8#.

review.turning_point: 9...Ne7 threw away a winning position, swinging the evaluation from +4.3 to -1.6.
review.focus: At 9...Ne7 you had a calm, safe move (9...Na6). When you are well ahead, check every knight jump on d5 or c7 before developing.

review.headline: You got a big edge from White's early errors, then blundered a piece with 14...Ng4

sections.text: In the London you played 3...Bd6 and 5...Ne4 in a standard way. After 6.Ne5 Nxg3 7.fxg3?, White chose the wrong recapture (7.hxg3 was better), and you steadily built an advantage with 7...Bxe5 8.dxe5 Qg5.

9...Nc6? was your first slip: 9...Nd7 kept the e5 pawn under control. The advantage shrank to +0.2, but White returned the favour with 10.Qf4??. You found 10...Qxe5!, which pinned the pawn on e3 against the king and won a pawn.
After 11...Nxe5 the position was clearly in your favour, and 12.Be2 Bd7 13.O-O O-O-O 14.Nc3 was normal development. Everything was fine until 14...Ng4??, which left a piece to be won.
15.Bxg4 simply captured it, and you resigned after the move. The engine's quiet 14...c5 would have kept the extra pawn and a stable position.

review.turning_point: 14...Ng4 dropped a piece (+2.9 to -3.8) in a position where you only needed to play something calm like 14...c5.
review.focus: Before every knight jump, as at 14...Ng4, check whether the knight is protected. If it is not, a quiet developing move is usually better.

review.headline: A one-move accident: 5...exf4 opened the long diagonal

sections.text: White played a quiet Van't Kruijs set-up with 1.e3, 2.b3 and 3.Bb2. You answered classically with 1...e5, 2...d5 and 3...Nc6, and 4...Bd6 was fine, so you came out of the opening about equal.
After 5.f4, you took with 5...exf4??. It looks natural, because it wins a pawn, but removing your e5 pawn opened the long diagonal for the bishop on b2.
6.Bxg7 took the pawn on g7 with the bishop attacking your rook on h8. That put you at -2.0 after one move, and you resigned.
The engine's answer was 5...Qh4+ 6.g3. Pushing the f-pawn weakened the e1-h4 diagonal, so a queen check was available and kept the e5 pawn in place.

review.turning_point: 5...exf4 cleared the e5 pawn out of the way of the bishop on b2, turning an equal position into a lost one.
review.focus: At 5...exf4, check what your capture opens up. Before taking a pawn, look at which of your pawns currently block enemy diagonals.

review.headline: A tactical Sicilian where you were winning easily and lost on time

sections.text: After 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5.Nf5 d6 you played 6.Qg4?, a blunder (the engine preferred 6.Nc3). Your opponent missed the right reply 6...g6 and played 6...Nd4?, so you got away with it.

You then played the tactics nicely. 7.Nxg7+ Bxg7 8.Qxg7! was a pin along the diagonal to d4, and after 9.Qxf6 Nxf6 you were well ahead. 12.Bg7! was a fork on f6 and h8, which took the evaluation to +4.0.
11.Bh6 was a mistake in between, since 11.f3 was safer, but Black's 11...Bb7 returned the favour. After that you kept winning material with 13.Bxf6, 14.Bh4 and 18.Bxg2 and stayed above +3 throughout.
