Your opponent gave you chances back. 16...Rxh3 was a blunder and 17.Rxh3 was the right answer. After 21...Qg3 you found 22.Qa6+ and 24.Qa5+, which set up a skewer on the king and the rook behind it and brought the game back to 0.0. In between, 23.c6 was a slip, since 23.Qb5+ kept the pressure.
Then 27.Rc1+ threw it away. The checking rook was simply captured by 27...Bxc1, and at -4.4 with the clock draining, the rest was damage limitation until your flag fell.

review.turning_point: 27.Rc1+ swung the game from +0.3 to -4.1, because the bishop on h6 could just take the rook. 27.Qc8+ kept the balance.
review.focus: Before you play a check, ask what can capture the checking piece, as with 27.Rc1+ Bxc1. Also notice that 9.Nh4 left the knight offside when 9.Ne5 was available.

review.headline: A messy Vienna where you survived early slips, won a piece, and finished with a back rank mate

sections.text: Against the Vienna you pinned the knight early with 3...Bg4, but it did not bring much. 5...Qd7 missed the better 5...Bxf3, and White settled into a comfortable game at -1.9 for you.

8...Bxf3 dropped to -3.2 when 8...dxe5 was better. Luckily 9.Bxf3 was a blunder by White (9.exf6 was the move), and you found 9...Bxe5 to get back to about -0.2. After 12...Bxc3 13.bxc3 Qc6 14.Bf3 Qxc3 you had also picked up a pawn.
White's 18.d7 and especially 19.Bf3 turned the game. You found 19...Nd4!, and after 20.Qb1 Nxf3+ you had won a piece. After 22...Rxd7 and the rook trade on d3 you were well ahead at +4 or more.

Your conversion wobbled. 27...Qd4 gave some back, and 31...Qxg3 dropped the evaluation from +5.0 to 0.0, as White got checks on e5 and e4. After 34...Kc8 you were objectively lost, but 35.Rxa7 walked into 35...Rd1+! and the back rank mate.

review.turning_point: 35...Rd1+ was a back rank shot that ended the game after White grabbed the pawn with 35.Rxa7 instead of playing 35.Rc1+.
review.focus: With a big lead, check what the opponent's checks lead to. 31...Qxg3 grabbed a pawn when 31...Qd4 kept everything under control.

review.headline: A scrappy Philidor-style game won on the clock after both sides traded blunders

sections.text: You went for a solid setup after 2.Bc4 d6 and traded bishops with 4.Bxe6 fxe6. The pawn break 8...d5 gave White the better chances at -1.5, but 10.Bd2 was a slip (10.d4 was better) and you found the good reply 10...Nf6!.

White kept up pressure with 14.Rhe1 and 15.Nf5, but 16.Ng3 let you off, since 16.Nxd6+ was stronger. Your tactical moment came at 19...Qxf2: after 20.Qxf2 Nxf2! the queens came off and you were a pawn up.

Both sides then swapped errors. 29...h5 was a blunder (29...Rf4 was needed), but 31.Rfxf2 gave it back and you found 31...Rxf2. 33...Rh5 let White back in, 34.Nf1 returned the favour and you answered with 34...g5!.
In the ending 37.Ne7 gave you +4.2, but 37...c6 threw it away; 37...g4 was the move. In time trouble 42...Rf1 and 44...Rg2 followed. After 45.Rxg2 hxg2 you were worse, but White's flag fell first.

review.turning_point: 37...c6 let a +4.2 position slide back to 0.0, when 37...g4 kept your edge.
review.focus: Under time pressure, look for forcing moves first, as with 37...g4 and 29...Rf4, rather than quiet pawn moves like 29...h5 that leave tactics behind.

review.headline: A Jerome Gambit that backfired, a long fight back, and a drawn ending lost on the clock

sections.text: You went for the Jerome Gambit with 4.Bxf7+, and the engine did not like it at -2.8; 4.c3 was the sound move. After 4...Kxf7 5.Nxe5+ Nxe5 6.Qh5+ Ng6 7.Qxc5 you had dragged the king out but were still at -2.4.
IronEagleBird made errors too. 12...Ng4 and 13...Bd7 gave you +2.1, but 14.Qh5 wasted it (14.Qc4+ was better), and 17.Bh4 simply lost a piece to 17...Nxh4, taking you to -5.4.

You kept fighting. 29...Qxh2+ 30.Kxh2! traded queens, and 33.Rg7+! set up a skewer on the king and the bishop on d7. Black answered 34...Rh8+ and later 41...Rd8, and your 40.e5! and 42.e6! brought you to +4.5.
Then the clock hurt you. 43.exd7 gave the win away (43.Rxd7+ was clear), 45.Kf2 was another slip (45.a4 kept the edge), and in the pawn ending 57.Kc2 lost where 57.a3 held.

review.turning_point: 43.exd7 fell from +4.5 to +0.1 when 43.Rxd7+ Rxd7 44.exd7 Kxd7 45.a4 kept a clear advantage.
review.focus: At 43.exd7 you picked the natural recapture and missed the forcing 43.Rxd7+. When you are winning, spend your time on the forcing line first.

review.headline: A Queen's Gambit Declined where you rode out early slips and White gave you a piece

sections.text: Against the London-style 3.Bf4 you played the Queen's Gambit Declined. After 4.Bxd6 you recaptured 4...cxd6, but 4...Qxd6 was better, and White had a small edge at -1.3.

The real mistake came at 10...Qb6, where 10...Nxc3 was the right idea. White answered with 11.Qa4, which missed 11.Nxd5, and then 11...Qc6 put your queen in front of the rook on e8 on the same diagonal as the queen on a4. 11...Bd7 was safer.

That was your lucky escape: 12.Qxc6 was another White error (12.Bb5 was better), and 12...bxc6! traded queens and left you only slightly worse at -0.6. After that you slowly improved your pieces with 13...Bg4, 15...Be6 and 16...Bf5. 17...Bg6 gave a little back, since 17...Nxc3 was better.
The decisive moment was 20.Bxe4, which swung the evaluation to +3.7. 20...Rxe4! won a piece, and you converted calmly with 22...c5 and 24...Rb8 until White resigned after 30...Nxa2.

review.turning_point: 20.Bxe4 was White's blunder, and 20...Rxe4! won a piece and swung the evaluation to +3.7.
review.focus: Look at 10...Qb6: 10...Nxc3 won a piece or more. Before you play a queen move, check whether a capture on the board wins material.

review.headline: A clean attacking win where one check led to a piece and then to mate

sections.text: A model game for you, accuracy 96. After 3.Bc4 Be7 you played 4.d4 and recaptured with 5.Nxd4, putting a knight on d4 in the centre. Black wandered with 5...Ne5, and 6.Bb3 kept your bishop on its best diagonal, while 8.f4 chased the knight back and gave you space.
After 9.Re1 and 10.Qd3 you were ready to strike. Black's 10...Nb4 (the engine preferred 10...Nxd4) set up your moment: 11.Qb5+! forked the king on e8 and the knight on b4.
12.Qxb4 won the knight, and you were suddenly a piece up at +2.5. Black tried 12...c5, hoping to chase the queen, but 13.Qc4 kept the queen safe and aimed with the bishop on b3 at f7.
13...cxd4 was the last mistake, and the engine says it lost by force. 14.Qxf7# finished it. Black's king had no way out because the bishop on e7 and the queen on d8 were blocking its own escape.

review.turning_point: 11.Qb5+ forked the king and the knight on b4, winning a piece and setting up the mate on f7.
review.focus: Keep hunting for forcing checks that hit two things at once, as 11.Qb5+ did here. Your play was clean, so the habit to keep is looking at every check before you play slowly.

review.headline: A Philidor where a strong start slipped away through loose queen moves and a final rook sacrifice that did not work

sections.text: You played the open 4.d4 against the Philidor and had a nice position, especially after 7...Be6, which was a blunder by Black (7...Bd7 was better). The engine gave you +3.2, and 8.Nxe6 fxe6 9.Bxe6 was the way to keep the edge.

Instead 8.Bb3 Bxb3 9.axb3 gave away the bishop pair and your evaluation fell to +1.0. You still got chances when Black played 13...g5. After 14.f4 Ng4 you needed 15.Nf5, but 15.fxg5 let Black back in with 15...Nxe3 16.Qxe3.

You then found a strong idea with 17.Nf5!, which pointed at g7 and brought you back to +2.6. 18.Nxg7 Kxg7 19.Rf5 kept the pressure, but 21.Qf3 was a slip (21.Qd4 kept +2.8) and you let Black untangle with 21...Ne5.
24.Qd5 was the final blunder, where 24.Qd3 held. 24...Ne3 hit your queen, and 25.Rxg5+ fxg5 simply lost material. You resigned at -3.6.

review.turning_point: 24.Qd5 dropped from +2.8 to 0.0 and 25.Rxg5+ then lost material; 25.Qxb7+ would have kept the balance.
review.focus: At 8.Bb3 you gave up the bishop pair when 8.Nxe6 fxe6 9.Bxe6 was ahead. Check forcing captures before retreating.

review.headline: A calm Bishop's Opening where you were fine until a missed fork and a last-move blunder

sections.text: Against the Bishop's Opening you played ...d6 and ...Be6, and after 4.Bxe6 fxe6 you had a solid if slightly passive structure. 6...c6 and 7...Be7 were small inaccuracies, but 9.dxe5 Nxe5 10.Nxe5 dxe5 traded off the central tension and left you only slightly worse.
The key moment came at 13.Na4, a mistake by White. The engine liked 13...Qb5, a fork of the knight on a4 and the queen on e2. Instead you played 13...Qa5, and the evaluation sank to -0.6.
You kept your composure. After 17...Bc5 18.Bxc5 Qxc5 you were back to about -0.6, and 20...Qxe4 21.Qxe4 Nxe4 22.Nxe6 Rxf2 simplified into an equal endgame at 0.0.
The end came at 23...Nd2. 23...Rf6 was the move, but instead 24.Kxf2 simply took your rook. The position was then at -5.8 and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 23...Nd2 turned an equal position into -5.8, since 24.Kxf2 took the rook that had just been left on f2.
review.focus: Before 23...Nd2, ask which of your pieces are loose: the rook on f2 needed support, and 23...Rf6 saved it. Also look for forks first, like 13...Qb5.

review.headline: A Center Game where a big early gift was missed, then a time-trouble loss

sections.text: White opened with the Center Game, and the early queen move 4.Qc3 was a blunder. 4...Bb4 would have pinned the queen on c3 to the king and given you +5.1. You played 4...d6 instead, and the advantage disappeared, down to -0.1.

You then played a solid middlegame, with 5...Bd7, 7...Be7 and 8...O-O, and after 11.Bxc6 Bxc6 you were fine. White overpressed with 15.h5 and 16.exd5, and you found 15...d5! and 16...Nxd5!, getting to +4.2.

17...Bb4 was the next error, where 17...Bxc4 was best. After 18.Qxd5, 18...Rxe2 was a blunder (18...Qxd5 was better), and 19.Qxd8+ made it -5.3. From there White pushed the a-pawn while you were down material.
The rest was a lost ending, and you flagged on move 56.

review.turning_point: 18...Rxe2 turned a good position at +1.4 into -5.1: after 19.Qxd8+ Rxd8 20.Rxd8+ you had lost a rook. 18...Qxd5 was the move.
review.focus: On 4.Qc3 you had a strong shot, the 4...Bb4 pin, and missed it. When the opponent's queen is out early, check for pins first.

review.headline: A big early edge wasted in time trouble and ended in mate

sections.text: Black opened with 2...Qf6, and you found the best reply 3.Nc3! to take advantage. After 4.d4 Bd6 5.Bg5 Qg6 you had a large edge, and 6.dxe5 Bxe5 7.Qd2 kept it.

A small slip came with 9.Be2 and 10.Be3, and you got into a long maneuvering phase. 14.Rhe1! pinned the knight on e7 against the rook on e8 and took you to +4.9. But 15.Re3 let some of the advantage go (15.Bd6 was better).
17.Bc4 Rxe3 18.fxe3 was fine, and Black's 18...b5 was a mistake, which gave you +6.1. Then 19.Bb3 Bb7 20.Qd3 Qxg2 started letting the attack flow to your king.
21.Qxh7 was the mistake, played low on time, because it left the knight on f3 to be won by 21...Qxf3. 22.Rg1 was the final blunder, and 23.Kb1 Qxg1# finished the game.

review.turning_point: 22.Rg1 turned a still-manageable position into -6.0; 22.e4 was the right defence, and 23...Qxg1# followed.
review.focus: With a big lead, slow down and check your king. 22.Rg1 and 21.Qxh7 were played low on time, while 22.e4 covered everything.

review.headline: A Sicilian where you kept finding good ideas and then missing the simple capture on c6

sections.text: You played the open Sicilian against the Accelerated Dragon, and 5.Bc4 and 6.Be3 were normal. 8.Qd2 and 9.O-O-O set up the Yugoslav-style attack, and 10.Bh6 was thematic.
11.h3 was the first slip, where 11.Bxg7 was needed. Black gave it back immediately with 11...b5, and the sequence 12.Nd5 Nxd5 13.Bxg7 Kxg7 14.Bxd5 gave you +1.9. Black's 14...Bb7 made it +4.3.
That was the moment: 15.Nxc6 was the move, and instead 15.h4 threw the advantage away (+0.1). 15...h5 and 16.g4 repeated the pattern, as 16.Nxc6 was again stronger, and 17.Qf4 missed 17.Nxc6.
After 17...e6 18.Bxe6 you were close to equal. 20.Qxd6 then simplified into an ending at -4.0, where 20.Rxd6 was the correct recapture. You flagged on move 34.

review.turning_point: 15.h4 threw away a +4.3 position (down to +0.1), when 15.Nxc6 b4 16.Nxb4 kept the advantage.
review.focus: At 15.h4, 16.g4 and 17.Qf4 the same idea, 15.Nxc6, was available three times. When the opponent leaves a piece pinned or attacked, take it before starting your own plan.

review.headline: A King's Gambit Declined where the opponent walked into a tactical net and you collected material

sections.text: Against the King's Gambit Declined you played 2...Nc6 and then 3...Nf6, which the engine liked less than 3...exf4. But 4.d4 was a blunder by White, and you found 4...exd4! at once.
5.Nxd4 was another error (5.e5 was better), and you replied with 5...Nxe4!. After 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 you struck: 7...Qh4+! pinned the pawn on h2 against the rook on h1.
8...Nxg3! was a lovely follow-up, a best move that puts a piece en prise. After 9.Kd2 Nxh1 you had won the exchange and more, with the material count at +7.

You converted without any hurry: 10...Qxf4+, 11...Qe5+ and 13...Qxh2+ kept White's king under pressure. After 14.Qf2 Qxf2+ and the bishop trade you were up a lot of material, and White resigned after 31...Re8.

review.turning_point: 7...Qh4+ and 8...Nxg3! won the rook on h1 and turned an equal position into +4.8.
review.focus: 3...Nf6 was your only real slip; 3...exf4 was cleaner. In the King's Gambit, taking the pawn with 3...exf4 keeps things simple before you start developing.

review.headline: A short Italian where you were doing well, and the game ended with your resignation

sections.text: You played the Italian with 4.c3 and 5.d4, a standard central plan. After 5...exd4 6.Bg5 Qg6, Black's queen was out early, and you used it.

7...h6 was a mistake by Black (7...d6 was better), and you found 8.Bh4!, which kept the bishop on the diagonal. After 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 d6 10.Nd5 Bb6 you had lots of development and attacking chances at +2.5.

11...Bh3 was another mistake by Black. The engine says 12.Nf4 was best, a fork of the queen on g6 and the bishop on h3. You played 12.Bg3 instead, which was only an inaccuracy and still left you at +2.8.
The engine had you better when the game ended. The result is recorded as a loss by resignation after 12.Bg3 Bg4, so I would look at why you resigned in a position rated about +3.5 in your favour.

review.turning_point: 11...Bh3 gave you the chance for 12.Nf4, forking the queen and the bishop; the game ended instead with your resignation.
review.focus: At 12.Bg3 look first for forcing options like 12.Nf4. Do not resign a position like this: check the material and the threats before you give up.

review.headline: A Colle-style game where one rook slip nearly cost you, and the opponent's blunder gave you the win

sections.text: You played a flexible Queen's Pawn setup and equalised easily with 6...c5 and 8...Qxd5. After the queens came off with 9.Qxd5 Nxd5 the game was balanced, though 15...b5 and 17...Bb7 were small inaccuracies.

Moein_doozande got the upper hand at 20.Nd7, which uncovered an attack from the bishop on b2 on your bishop on f6 and threatened your rook on f8. 20...Rfd8 was a blunder, while 20...Bxb2 was the move.
You were down to -3.1, but you kept playing. 21.Nxf6+ Nxf6 22.Rxd8+ Rxd8 23.Bxf6 gxf6 simplified, and White's 24.g3 was a mistake, which you punished with 24...Rd2!.

Your active rook and bishop caused problems: 25.Bf1 Ra2 26.Rb3 Ra1 and the decisive 29.Rb3 was a blunder by White. You found 29...Be2!, and 30.Kg2 Bxf1+ won the bishop. From there 37...Bxh5 and 41...Rh1# finished the job.

review.turning_point: 29.Rb3 was White's blunder, and 29...Be2! won a bishop and swung the game from +0.4 to +4.1.
review.focus: At 20...Rfd8 the right move was 20...Bxb2, which took the attacking bishop first. When your opponent makes a discovered attack, check what the uncovered piece is really hitting.

review.headline: An Owen Defense full of swings that ended in time trouble

sections.text: You played the Owen Defense with 1...b6, and White got a comfortable edge. After 5...Bb4 6.Bd2 Bxc3 7.Bxc3 d5 you reached a normal position. White's 13.Bb4 attacked your queen but allowed 13...Nxb4!.
You were fine after that, but 19.Ba4 (19.Re3 was better) and 20.c3 were White's mistakes. But 19...Rad8 and 20...a6 both let the advantage go. 19...Ba6 was the way to profit.
The game kept swinging. 28.Nc6 opened the e-file against your rook and 29...Nxg2 was a blunder (29...h4 was needed), but 30.Qxg2 returned the favour and you found 30...Qxc6!, winning a piece.
You were doing well, but low on time 37...a3 dropped to -4.1 (37...Qa3 was best), and 41...Qbc1 allowed a forced mate (41...Qaa2 was the move). The game ended on the clock.

review.turning_point: 37...a3 swung the evaluation from +0.8 to -4.1; 37...Qa3 would have kept the extra material.
review.focus: Late in the game, watch your clock and your pieces' safety together, as with 37...a3 and 41...Qbc1. Simple checks and queen safety beat pawn pushes.

review.headline: A smooth Old Indian Attack where you punished one central push and converted with care

sections.text: You met the Zukertort set-up with a solid ...d5 and ...e6 plan. 7...b6 was only a small inaccuracy (7...h6 was a shade better). White's 8.e4 Bb7 then led to the key moment.
9.e5 forked the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6, but it was a blunder, because you replied 9...Nxe5! 10.Nxe5 Bxe5. You came out a pawn up, at +1.7.

11...Bxc3 slightly relaxed (11...Bd6 was a shade better). After 12.bxc3 and 13.Bxf6 Qxf6 you kept control, with 14...Rad8 and 15...Bxd5 coordinating your rooks and queen. Your edge grew slowly to +3.6.

23...Ra5 and 24...Qc5 were small inaccuracies, but 26...Qxa2 27.Qxa2 Rxa2 left you two pawns up in the endgame. 29...Rxc4 30.dxe6 Rxd1 31.exf7+ Kxf7 32.Rxd1 and 34.Rxc7 Rxc7 left you with a winning ending. White resigned.

review.turning_point: 9.e5 was a blunder, and 9...Nxe5! turned a calm position into a clear +1.8 for you.
review.focus: Your play was accurate. The small points were 7...b6 and 11...Bxc3; ask whether a move like 7...h6 would have kept the position simpler.

review.headline: A Scandinavian gambit where a good start collapsed into dropped pieces

sections.text: You went for the Boehnke Gambit-style line with 2.exd5 e6 3.dxe6 Bxe6 and developed naturally with 4.Nf3, 5.Be2 and 6.O-O. The engine rated you well, at +2.1 to +2.8.
9.h3 was a slightly loose move, and 10.Bxc6 bxc6 11.d4 Qd6 took the pressure out. 12.g3 was a mistake, as 12.Nc3 kept more of the edge and it dropped you from +3.1 to +1.6.
14.hxg4 was a blunder, where 14.Nc3 was needed. 15.Nh2 then left a piece to be won; the engine wanted 15.Nh4. Black missed 15...Rxh2 and played 15...Qf5, which gave you a chance to escape.
Instead 16.Qxg4 lost your queen to 16...Qxg4, and you resigned. 16.Re5 was the better try.

review.turning_point: 16.Qxg4 walked into 16...Qxg4 and lost the queen, turning a position at -0.6 into -6.5.
review.focus: At 14.hxg4 you captured a pawn with your king exposed. Before grabbing material, check whether 14.Nc3 develops and keeps your pieces protected.

review.headline: A Petrov where a pawn storm met an overextended Black position and you resigned from near equality

sections.text: You played the Three Knights Petrov with 2...Nf6, and White chose 4.h3. 4...Be6 was a little awkward at -1.3, and 5.d3 was a slip by White, but you did not take the advantage. 7.g4 and 8.g5 started a pawn storm.
After 11.exd5 cxd5 12.Bxb6 axb6 the structure was healthy but you were behind. 13.h4 was strong, and 13...Bg4 was a blunder, since 13...b5 was the move.
White then went wrong with 14.O-O and 15.Qd2. You answered with 14...Nc5 and 15...e4, but both were mistakes: 14...d4 and 15...d4 were better. Even so you reached about -0.5.

21.g6 was strong, but 21...Bxh4 was a mistake (21...O-O was the move), and after 22.gxf7+ Bxf7 you were slightly worse. The engine rated the final position close to level, so the resignation after 26.Ne2 looks premature.

review.turning_point: 13...Bg4 wasted your good position, dropping from +1.4 to -0.3.
review.focus: At 13...Bg4 the bishop was exposed to White's pawn advance. 13...b5 was the move, so check what your opponent's pawn storm can attack before you place a piece.

review.headline: A topsy-turvy game you won by punishing a queen blunder and a final queen swap

sections.text: White opened with the Van't Kruijs 1.e3 and then 2.Qh5, a mistake that you did not punish. 2...d6 was a little passive, and White built up with 3.Bb5+ c6 4.Bc4 g6 5.Qf3.

8...Bxe2 was a mistake (8...Be6 was better), and White returned the favour with 9.Ngxe2. 9.Qxe5+ was the right move. You played well in the middlegame with 12.fxe5 Bxe5 13.d4 Bd6, and then went wrong with 15...Be7 and 16...Qa6, which dropped to -2.0.
17.Qe1 was a blunder, and you found 17...Bxb4!, which pinned the knight on c3 to the queen. After 18.axb4 Qxa1 you had won material (+3).
19...cxb5 and 21...Nb6 were slips, but White's 21.Nbc3 and 22.Nf4 repaid you. You found 22...Nc4!, and 24.Qxf6 Qxf6! left you a queen up. White resigned.

review.turning_point: 17...Bxb4! pinned the knight on c3 to the queen and won material after White's blunder 17.Qe1.
review.focus: At 21...Nb6 you left a piece to be won; 21...Rhe8 was safe. Check what a knight move leaves undefended before you play it.

review.headline: A queen-trade middlegame you were comfortable in, until a time-pressure slip on move 23

sections.text: This was a Levitsky Attack where White's early bishop sortie invited you to chase it. After 2.Bg5 2...f6 3.Bh4 you pushed 3...g5?, which kicked the bishop but loosened your kingside for good; the engine preferred 3...Nh6. Following up with 4...h5 and 5...h4 won space, though it kept the structure a little shaky.

You settled down with 6...Nc6 and 7...e5, and then White erred: 13.e4? lifted your evaluation from +0.7 to +2.0. The reply 13...Nfe7?! gave a little back (+1.1), but after 14.Qxd7+ 14...Kxd7 you were still clearly the one pressing.
The simplified middlegame stayed healthy for you. Trading rooks with 20...Rxe1+ and placing the bishop actively with 22...Bf4 kept you around +0.3, with nothing for White to attack.

Then the clock bit. 23...g4?? dropped you from +0.3 to -3.7 when the calm 23...Bd6 was available. White returned the favour with 24.Nxf4??, and you found the right recapture, 24...Nxf4!, to get back to +0.2. A further slip, 26...Rh8?, where 26...f5 was better, left you slightly worse when time ran out.

review.turning_point: 23...g4?? swung the game from +0.3 to -3.7 in one move, and only White's 24.Nxf4?? rescued you; after that the clock decided it.
review.focus: With little time, prefer quiet, safe moves: 23...Bd6 kept everything protected, while 23...g4 created a weakness you had no time to calculate.

review.headline: A promising Italian that slid away through queen adventures and a king-side blunder

sections.text: You met 3...h6 with the strong central break 4.d4 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 and stood well. Then 6.Qh5?! took the queen out early; Black kicked it with 6...g6, and 7.Qf3 spent more time getting back.

Black answered with 7...Ne5?, a fork of your queen and bishop that looks scary but was a mistake, because the engine's 8.Qf6 would have hit the knight and the rook in the corner at once, with 9.Qxh8 to follow. Instead 8.Qb3?? 8...Nxc4 9.Qxc4 slid you from +2.1 to -0.4.
Black blundered right back with 10...c6?? (+2.9), but 11.N5c3?? let it go again (-1.4). The better try was 11.Qd4, where the queen pins the d6 pawn against the rook behind it.

Later 24...Qc8?? let you win material with 25.Qxf7! and 26.Qxh5. But with your king uncovered and the clock short, 27.Kg2?? and 28.f4?? allowed 28...gxf3+ and the evaluation fell to -5.7. You fought on, but the game ended on time after 31...Qxc2.

review.turning_point: 28.f4?? opened lines near your own king and allowed 28...gxf3+ with check, swinging the evaluation from -0.5 to -5.7.
review.focus: Before pushing a pawn beside your own king, look for pawn captures with check: 28.f4 allowed 28...gxf3+, while 28.R1d2 was the safe move.

review.headline: A textbook refutation of the Latvian Gambit, finished with a mating attack

sections.text: Black's 2...f5? is the Latvian Gambit, and you answered it exactly right. 3.Nxe5! took the centre pawn and after 4.exf5 you were two pawns up with a comfortable position. The engine agreed with both moves.
You then loosened your grip a little. 5.Nd3? allowed 5...Bxf5 and cut your lead; 5.Nf3 would have kept you near +1.7. 7.Qf3? was another inexact move, with 7.Nf4 the engine's choice.

Black gave it all back with 7...Bxd3??, and 8.Bxd3! recaptured with a developed bishop. The big moment came at move 11: 11...Nxc2+?? looked like a fork of king, rook and queen, but 12.Bxc2! simply took the knight, and after 12...Qxe3+ 13.dxe3 you had traded queens and were a clean piece up.
From there it was good technique. 17.Bxa5 picked up another pawn, 21.Bf5+ kept Black's king uncomfortable, and 27.Rxc7+ brought your rooks to the seventh rank, ending in 29.Ra7#.

review.turning_point: 11...Nxc2+?? was met by 12.Bxc2!, and the queen trade after 12...Qxe3+ 13.dxe3 left you a full piece ahead.
review.focus: On 5.Nd3 you gave back some of the advantage; 5.Nf3 kept your pieces better placed, so when you are ahead prefer the retreat that develops.

review.headline: A grinding Petrov where you were slightly worse and a time-trouble queen move decided it

sections.text: In this Three Knights Petrov, 4.Bc4 4...Be6 5.Bxe6 5...fxe6 gave you doubled e-pawns but an open f-file and a sound centre. The engine had you a touch worse (around -0.5), and you defended with sensible moves like 6...h6 and 7...c6.

Your first real slip was 11...e5? (-1.1); the engine wanted 11...c5 to challenge the centre before committing the pawn. After that you traded pieces to ease the pressure, with 17...Rxe7 and 19...dxc5, and kept the game within reach.
With the clock short, 23...Qb5?! and then 24...Qa6? (-2.7) misplaced the queen, when 24...Qa5 25.Rd1 was safer. After 25.Nxc5 you were a pawn down.
White missed the chance to finish it with 26.Ne6? (the engine wanted 26.Nd7), and you found 26...Re8!, the best reply. It was not enough to change the position's character, and 27.Rd6 ended the game.

review.turning_point: 24...Qa6? in time pressure moved your queen away from the action and led to 25.Nxc5 winning a pawn, taking you from -1.2 to -2.9.
review.focus: On 11...e5, look for a pawn break like 11...c5 before committing to a structure; and when short of time, as at 24...Qa6, keep your queen where it protects your pawns.

review.headline: A nine-move Scotch Gambit miniature ending in a queen mate on f7

sections.text: You went for the Scotch Gambit with 3.Bc4 and 4.d4. After 4...exd4 5.Nxd4?! Black grabbed a pawn with 5...Nxe4 and 6.O-O kept the position open. The engine slightly preferred Black here, so this was a game that needed Black to go wrong.

Black did. 6...Be7? missed 6...d5, which would have opened the centre and kicked your bishop. You answered with 7.Re1?, a natural-looking move, but 7.Nf5 would have kept more tension. Still, it set a trap that Black fell into.

7...Nxf2?? grabbed a pawn, and 8.Qf3?! aimed your queen straight at f7. Black needed 8...d5, but played 8...Nxd4??, and 9.Qxf7# finished it; your bishop on c4 covers f7 and the king has no squares to run to.

Be honest with yourself about the opening: 5.Nxd4?! and 7.Re1? were not best, and the engine would have been happy for Black to take over. The credit goes to you for building the bishop and queen battery against f7 and spotting the finishing shot.

review.turning_point: 8...Nxd4?? took a knight but allowed 9.Qxf7#; 8...d5 was needed to stay in the game.
review.focus: Compare your quiet move with the active one: on 7.Re1 the engine wanted 7.Nf5, keeping the knight active, so check forcing options before a routine developing move.

review.headline: A Center Game win: you took the queen on e2 and converted a mountain of material

sections.text: White opened with the Center Game and queen sortie, 2.d4 2...exd4 3.Qxd4 3...Nc6 4.Qe3. You answered with 4...b6?, a bit slow; the engine preferred 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 to develop first. Still, 5...Bc5 put your bishop on a good diagonal.
6.Qe2?? gave you a chance to take over. The strongest reply was 6...Nd4, hitting the queen and the bishop on b5 at once. You played 6...Bb7? (-0.3) instead, and White got away with it for a move.
You set the same trap one move later: 9...Nd4 attacked the queen again, and White's 10.Nc3?? ignored it. 10...Nxe2! won the queen for a knight, and the evaluation reached +5.4 after 11.Ngxe2.

The conversion was patient. 17...Qe3+ and 19...Rxd1+ traded and simplified, 22...Qxh2 and 25...Rxe4 won pawns, and your h-pawn ran home with 33...h3, 34...h2 and 36...h1=Q. White ran out of time while you were promoting again with 46...g1=Q+.

review.turning_point: 10...Nxe2! picked up White's queen for a knight, taking the game from +1.2 to +5.3 in one move.
review.focus: On 6...Bb7 you missed a forcing move: when the opponent leaves a queen and bishop on the same knight jump, check 6...Nd4 before developing.

review.headline: A winning position built on a clever opening shot, lost on the clock

sections.text: You played a nicely controlled Philidor. Black's 5...Bh5? walked into 6.Nxe5!, a discovered attack: the knight leaving f3 let your queen see the bishop on h5. After 6...Nxe5 7.Qxh5 7...Nxc4 8.Qb5+ 8...c6 9.Qxc4 you had won a pawn and held +2.0.

You kept control with 10.O-O, 11.d4 and 12.Re1. Then 15.Bxd6?! was not necessary, but Black blundered with 15...Bxd6??, and 16.Qxd6! led to 17.Qxd8 and a queen trade that left you comfortably ahead (+3.9).
22.Ra3? let some air out (+3.5 to +2.1), where 22.c4 was better, but you still collected pawns with 24.Rxc6 and 25.Rxb6 and the position stayed winning.
Then time ran down. 30.Rc5?? (+2.0 to +0.1) ignored the passed pawn, when 30.a4 was a calm alternative. 31.Kf2?? and 32.Rxe2?? followed, and 32...Raxe2+ turned a won game into a loss, -5.1.

review.turning_point: 30.Rc5?? began the collapse in time trouble, dropping the evaluation from +2.0 to +0.1; 31.Kf2?? and 32.Rxe2?? finished the job.
review.focus: In a winning endgame with little time, deal with the opponent's advanced pawn first: 30.a4 kept control, while 30.Rc5 let the e-pawn become dangerous.

review.headline: A French Exchange that went wrong with an early knight jump and a greedy bishop capture

sections.text: A French Exchange with a normal start: 4.Nc3, 5.Nf3, 6.Bd2 and 7.Bd3 kept things level. Black's 7...Re8+ put a check on the open e-file.

8.Ne5?? blocked the check, but left your knight stuck in front of your king on the open file, and 8...Nc6 piled on (-2.6). The engine suggested 8.Ne2. Black's 9...Bxc3+?? gave you a way back (-0.3), and you found the right recapture, 10.bxc3!.

You stabilised with 12.O-O and 13.Rfe1, and Black's 13...b5? looked like a mistake worth +2.0 for you. But 14.Bxb5?? took a pawn that was easily recaptured by 14...axb5, giving a bishop for two pawns after 15.Qxb5. The engine's 14.Qf3 kept the pressure and left Black with problems.
After 15...Ne7 16.Ng6 16...Qd8 17.Nxe7+ 17...Qxe7 you were still behind in material, with the evaluation at -3.7, and 19.Qb6 19...Rac8 did not change it before you resigned.

review.turning_point: 14.Bxb5?? gave up a bishop for pawns, turning a +2.0 position into -3.8 in one move.
review.focus: Before capturing a pawn with a piece, check whether it can be recaptured: 14.Bxb5 allowed 14...axb5, while 14.Qf3 kept your edge.

review.headline: A long French Exchange win with big swings: you lost and regained control several times

sections.text: A French Exchange where you developed naturally. 11.Bg5 and 12.Nxe6 12...fxe6 gave you the better structure, but 13.Bb5? (-0.5) was inexact; the engine preferred 13.Bg4. After 13...a6 14.Bxc6 14...bxc6 15.Rxe6 you had a pawn.

Black's 15...Be7?? was a mistake, and your 16.Qe2! reply kept +2.1. Then 17.Re1 17...Bc5 18.Bxf6? let some of it slip (+3.6 to +1.9), when 18.Rxc6 was cleaner. Black's 18...gxf6?? gave it back, and 19.Qg4+ was strong.

20.Re8+?? looked like a back-rank shot but it only simplified, from +3.9 to +1.6; 20.Qa4 kept more. Then 23.Nxd5?? dropped your knight for a pawn (-1.8). Black replied 23...cxd5? where 23...Rd6 was better, and 24.Qxd5! forked the bishop on c5 and the rook on e6, getting you back to equality.

26.f4? was another inexact move (-1.1), but Black's 26...Kf7?? was a big blunder, and 27.f5! made the most of it (+4.8). After 28.fxe6+ you collected pawns with 32.Qxa6 and 44.Qxa6+, and Black resigned after 47.h4.

review.turning_point: 26...Kf7?? allowed 27.f5!, swinging the game from -1.1 to +5.0 for you.
review.focus: On 23.Nxd5 you captured a pawn with a knight that would simply be taken; count the recapture first, since 23.g3 kept everything safe.

review.headline: A Petrov where an early pawn grab cost a knight and the game never recovered

sections.text: In this Three Knights Petrov, 4.Be2 was a quiet move, and 4...Nxe4?? grabbed a pawn that was well covered. After 5.Nxe4 you were down a knight for a pawn (-3.4); 4...c5 was the calm alternative.

You tried to make things hard with 5...d5, 6...e4 and 7...c5, hoping to harass White's knights. White's 8.Nb3? was inexact (-1.9), but 8...d4?? let it off the hook; 8...c4 9.Nd4 was better. After 9.Nxe4 and 10.Nexc5 you were two pawns further behind.
You kept fighting. 11...Nc6?! then 12...Bxc5 won a knight back and 14...bxc6! was a good reply to White's 14.Bxc6+?, bringing you to -1.6.
15.d3 opened the diagonal for White's bishop to hit your queen, and 15...Bd6?? ignored it; 15...Qf5 was needed. 16.Bxg5 won the queen and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 4...Nxe4?? lost a knight for a pawn on move 4, setting the course for the whole game.
review.focus: Before grabbing a pawn with a knight, check what recaptures: after 4...Nxe4 5.Nxe4 you lost material, and 4...c5 kept the position balanced.

review.headline: A wild Bishop's Opening where you were winning before time trouble handed it back

sections.text: White rushed the h-pawn with 3.h4, 5.h5 and 6.h6. After 3...Be6 4.Bxe6 4...fxe6 5...Nf6 you developed sensibly, but 6...Nxe4?? let White trade pawns open with 7.hxg7 7...Bxg7 8.Qh5+ 8...Kd7, dragging your king to d7.

White blundered with 9.d3??, and the best reply was 9...Nf6, with 10.Qf7+ to follow. But 9...Nxf2?? let White off (-2.8). You still fought on, and 17.Rhd1+?? gave you another chance; 17...Kc8?? was a miss, since 17...Kc6 was the right square.

Then 18.Rd3?? from White was a blunder, and you found the right reply, 18...exd3!, getting to +2.9. You played well from there, winning more material with 22.Ne5+ 22...Nxe5 23.Rxe5 and reaching about +4.

But time trouble hit. 26...Rc8?, 27...Kc7?? and 28...Qd7?? undid the work, though White's 29.Qc4+?? and your 29...Kb8! brought you back to +4.1. Then 31...Rc2?? allowed 32.Re8#, when 31...Ka8 had held.

review.turning_point: 31...Rc2?? from a winning position allowed 32.Re8#; 31...Ka8 would have kept the advantage.
review.focus: In time trouble, check every White check or rook entry before moving: 31...Rc2 allowed 32.Re8#, while 31...Ka8 kept you safe.

review.headline: A topsy-turvy Scandinavian that ended in a long rook mate after White missed several chances

sections.text: In the Mieses-Kotroc Scandinavian, 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 3...Qe6+ 4.Be2 4...Nc6 was fine for you, and after Black's 5...h6? you found 6.d4!, taking the centre with tempo (+3.1). But 9.Bxa6?? gave away some of that edge by trading your good bishop for a knight and fixing Black's pawns.

The middlegame became messy. 12...Bxf3 13.gxf3 wrecked your kingside, 15.Be3? was inexact (15...Nxe4 followed), and you were relying on Black's 16...Qh3? to give you chances. 17.Bxa7 won a pawn, but 18.Qa4?? was a mistake before 19.Qxa6+ brought the queen back.
The big moment was 21.dxe6??, which allowed a forced mate; 21.e5 was the safe move. Black played 21...Qxh2+?? instead of the winning 21...Bxh2+, and 22.Kf1! was the best reply, keeping you alive.

The following moves were a series of checks on your king. 26.e5?! 26...Qh3+?? 27.Kg1?? 27...Qg4+?? 28.Kf1?? shows how much both sides missed under time pressure. You regrouped with 30.exd6+!, and 36...Qg5?? let you take the rook with 37.Bxd6+. From there you won the endgame, finishing with 62.Rg8#.

review.turning_point: 21.dxe6?? allowed a forced mate, but 21...Qxh2+?? missed it and 22.Kf1! kept you in the game.
review.focus: On 21.dxe6 you opened lines near your own king while Black's queen was active; 21.e5 was safer, so check every queen check before capturing.

review.headline: A Reversed Mexican where a loosening pawn push and a wrong recapture cost you the game

sections.text: In this Zukertort, you built a solid set-up with 3...Nf6, 4...Be7 and 5...c6, but 6...Bd7?! was passive (-0.9), and White grabbed space with 7.e4 and 8.e5. After 10.b4 10...b6 you were cramped.
11...f6? tried to break out but opened your king, and after 12.exf6 12...Bxf6 13.Nf4 the knight was strong. 13...Be8 was the better idea.

13...Bg5?? (-4.7) tried to counterattack but was a blunder, and White returned the favour with 14.Nxe6??, which forked your queen and rook. You then needed 14...Nxe6, which was worth +2.0 instead of -2.8; 14...Bxe6?? left your bishop on g5 to be taken by 15.Bxg5.
After that, White's pieces dominated: 15...Qd7 16.Ne5 16...Qd6 17.Bf4, 17...Qe7?! and 18...Nd7?! only kept you passive, and 19.Nxc6 ended it.

review.turning_point: 14...Bxe6?? recaptured with the wrong piece and let 15.Bxg5 win material, instead of 14...Nxe6 which would have kept you ahead.
review.focus: Before recapturing, check which piece keeps your others defended: on move 14, 14...Nxe6 kept your bishop supported, while 14...Bxe6 did not.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann Exchange win by tactics: a rook trade on e8 led to a queen-sacrifice mate

sections.text: In the Caro-Kann Exchange, 5.Bd3?! was a bit loose, but Black's 5...e6? let you play 6.Bxf5!, trading bishops and giving Black doubled f-pawns after 6...exf5.

Both sides played some loose moves. 7.Nc3?! and 8.Ne5?! gave Black chances, but 7...g6? and 8...Nf6? did not take them. After 9.Bg5? 9...Bg7 and 10.O-O 10...Nc6, you traded with 12.Nxc6 12...bxc6 and built pressure with 13.Qd3, 14.Na4 and 15.Nc5.

17.Qa6?! set a trap, and Black's 17...Re8?? fell for it: 18.Rxe8+! used the back rank, as the king on g8 had no escape square, and 18...Nxe8 was forced. You gave back a little with 19.c3?, when 19.Qc8 was more direct, but 20.Qc8 followed anyway.
The finish was neat. After 21.Qxe8+ 21...Bf8 you played 22.Nd7, and 22...Qf4?? allowed 23.Qxf8+! 23...Kh7 24.Nf6#, a mate with a queen sacrifice.

review.turning_point: 17...Re8?? allowed 18.Rxe8+!, which used Black's back rank and swung the evaluation to +3.1.
review.focus: On 19.c3? you spent a move when 19.Qc8 was available straight away; when the opponent's king is stuck, play the most forcing move first.

review.headline: A Philidor where an early bishop sortie left you under pressure all game

sections.text: You played a standard Philidor: 3.d4 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 5...Be7 6.Bc4 6...O-O. 7...Bg4?! was an early bishop move, and 8.f3 8...Bh5?! cost you more ground (-2.1). The engine preferred 8...Bc8.
9...c5?! opened the centre for White, when 9...Bg6 first would have kept the bishop safe. 10.Nf5 10...Nc6 11.O-O-O 11...a6 left you about -4, and White's pieces were well placed.

White's 12.Nxd6?? was a blunder, and 12...b5! was the right reply, but it only brought you back to -2.2. The engine preferred 15...Qe6 over 15...Qxd2+?!, which swapped queens and eased the pressure on White.
In the ending White's pieces worked together: 17.e5, 18.Nd5, 23.Rd7, and 24...b4?! only made it worse. 27.Bxe6+ was the end, and 27...Kf8?! made it -8.9.

review.turning_point: 8...Bh5?! and 9...c5?! set the tone, taking you from -1.0 to -3.4 in two moves.
review.focus: On 9...c5 the bishop was still loose; 9...Bg6 first would have secured it before opening the centre.

review.headline: A short Ragozin win where White grabbed a pawn and lost a rook

sections.text: In the Ragozin, 4...Bb4 5.Qa4+ 5...Nc6 and 6...Nxd5 were fine for you. 7...Qf6?! was a bit loose (-0.8), when 7...Nb6 8.Qb5 would have been more solid.
You traded off with 8...Bxd2+ and 9...exd5, and after 10.b4?? the d4 pawn was loose. 10...Qxd4! took it, the engine's top move, and your queen was suddenly centralised.

11.e3?? was the final mistake. 11...Qxa1+! was a skewer of the king and the bishop on f1, and it won a rook (+6.5). White resigned straight after. A very clean finish from a position that was equal a few moves earlier.

review.turning_point: 11.e3?? allowed 11...Qxa1+!, a skewer on the first rank that won a rook.
review.focus: On 7...Qf6, 7...Nb6 8.Qb5 was the safer idea; before queen sorties, make sure the queen has a way home.

review.headline: A Tennison Gambit game you won by punishing Black's mistakes after an unsound opening move

sections.text: 2.Nf3?? was a mistake, as 2.exd5 was best. Black replied 2...Bg4?, and you found 3.exd5!, the best reply, picking up the pawn. After 4.Be2 4...e6 5.Nc3 5...Qd8 6.d4 6...Bb4 7.Qd3 you were comfortable and developed well.
Some inexact middlegame moves followed. 11.Qb4? and 12.Bd6? let Black back in, when 12.d5 was better. But 13.Qc5! kept you at +1.4, and Black's 13...Qd7?? was a blunder (+3.6).

14.Bxb8?? was a mistake in return (+3.6 to +0.3), where 14.Ne5 was best, but Black answered 14...Rxb8?? when 14...Bxf3 would have kept equality. Then 15.Ne5! was excellent: a discovered attack, with your bishop on e2 now hitting the bishop on g4, and a fork of the queen on d7 as well.
After 16.Qxe7+ 16...Nxe7 17.Nxg4 you had won a bishop, and the technique was easy through 20.Nd7.

review.turning_point: 15.Ne5! attacked Black's queen and unleashed the Be2 on the loose bishop on g4, winning a piece.
review.focus: 14.Bxb8 spoiled a +3.6 position; 14.Ne5 was cleaner, so before a tempting capture, look for the forcing move that wins more.

review.headline: A Halasz Gambit in which your attack succeeded despite a series of risky moves

sections.text: You played the Halasz Gambit with 2.d4 2...cxd4 3.f4?! and stood a little worse. 5.Bb5?? (-4.2) walked into 5...Qa5+, a fork of king and bishop, but Black missed it with 5...a6??, and 6.Bxc6! 6...bxc6 7.Nxd4 got you out of trouble.

You then gave away a lot of your edge. 10.g3? was inexact (10.Ne4 was better), and 11.h4 and 12.h5?! started a pawn attack but at the cost of your own safety. After 12...dxe5 and 13.hxg6? (-3.5) you were worse.
Black's 13...Nxg6?? gave a lifeline, since 13...exd4 would have kept the lead, and 14.Qh5! was a good reply. But 15.f5?? left a piece to be won, and Black's 15...Qxd4?? missed 15...exd4.
16.Bxh6?? was another mistake, but 16...Bxh6?? was the final blunder, and 17.Qxh6! was the best reply (+5.6). Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 16...Bxh6?? took the bishop instead of the engine's 16...exf5, and 17.Qxh6! swung the evaluation from -2.8 to +5.6.
review.focus: On 15.f5 you pushed a pawn with your pieces undeveloped; 15.Nf3 would have kept the position under control.

review.headline: A Queen's Pawn game where you won a pawn early and then lost your way in an attack

sections.text: White played 4.e4? and you took 4...dxe4!, the best reply. After 5.Ne5 5...Bd6 6.f4 you had a good game, but 6...Nbd7? (+1.8 to +0.3) missed 6...exf3. 7...O-O?! and 8...b6?! kept things level, though 8.Qe2? was a mistake by White.
A good moment was 12...Bb7!, the best reply to 12.b3?. Then 13...Qh4+?!, 14...Qh3?! and 15...Nf6?! kept your queen active but gave away some of your edge.

16...Ng4?? was the big mistake (-4.1). White's 17.O-O-O?? gave you a chance to hit back, and 17...Nxe3 was the move, which would have forked the two rooks. Instead 17...Nxh2?? grabbed a pawn, 18.Rh1? allowed 18...Qxg3?, and 19.Rxh2 left you a piece down.
After that you tried 20...h5?? where 20...Bxh1 was needed, and 21...Bxe5! 22.fxe5 22...Bxh1 23.Rxh1 only slowed White. 25...Kh7? ended the game.

review.turning_point: 17...Nxh2?? grabbed a pawn instead of 17...Nxe3, which would have forked two rooks and won material.
review.focus: After 17.O-O-O the right move was 17...Nxe3; when the opponent errs, look at the forcing captures before taking a pawn.

review.headline: A winning passed pawn slipped away through one rook move and missed knight checks

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with a solid d5 and e6 setup, and White helped you with the slow 4.f3 and 5.c5. After 11.dxc5 11...bxc5 you pushed 14...d4, and once 16.exd4 16...cxd4 and 17.Bg5? came, your pawn reached d3 and the engine had you around +2.1.

The big swing was 20...Rc2??. It dropped your edge from +2.4 to +0.4 after 21.Rxc2 21...dxc2 22.Qxc2. The engine preferred 20...Nb4, keeping the rooks on and the pressure up. After that 25...Qf6?!, 26...Qg6?! and 27...Nd3?! slowly let White back in, and you were at -1.5.

Then White blundered: 28.Qc7?? jumped to +5.8 for you, and the right answer was 28...Nxc7. 28...Rf8 let it all go. After 30.g3?? and 31.Kg2? you had a second chance. 31...Ne3+ would have forked the king on g2, the queen on c2 and the rook on f1. You played 31...Qh6 and missed 32...Ne3+ as well after 32.Qd2.

The structure favoured you for a long time: after 18.Ng3 and 19.Qd2 your rooks went to the d- and c-files with 18...Rfd8 and 19...Rac8, while the pawn on d3 cramped White. That is a plan worth repeating, and it makes 20...Rc2?? hurt even more, because your position did not need a forcing idea at all.
33...f5 finished it; 33...Nxb6 was needed, and after 34.Nxd5 the position was lost.

review.turning_point: 20...Rc2 gave up a clearly better position, and 31...Ne3+ was the best chance to get it back.
review.focus: Before each move when you are ahead, list your checks and captures. 31...Ne3+ was a knight check hitting three pieces and you walked past it.

review.headline: A Danish Gambit where fast development and a rook raid overwhelmed the defence

sections.text: You opened with the Danish Gambit, 2.d4 2...exd4 3.c3 3...dxc3, offering pawns for quick development. 4.Bc4?! was fine practically, and 4...d6? let you off the hook, because 4...cxb2 was the critical answer. 5.Nxc3! was the right way to continue, bringing a knight out at once.
Black drifted. 8...b5? went wrong where 8...Bxc4 was needed, and 11...a5? and 14...a4? were loosening pawn moves. Meanwhile your rooks took the open d-file with 11.O-O-O and 14.Rhd1.
The crusher was 15.Rxd7!, taking the knight and putting you three points up with +4.4 on the board. 16.Ne5 and 17.Rxf7 kept the initiative, and you stood at +5.4 after 17...axb3.

The gambit worked because your pieces came out with tempo: 5.Nxc3, 7.Nf3, 8.Bf4 and 11.O-O-O all added attackers while Black spent moves on pawn pushes like 8...b5? and 11...a5?. Black never got the king to safety, and the open d-file did the rest. Gambit play like this is about speed, and you kept the speed up.
18.Qd3? was your one real slip, dropping from +5.4 to +3.4 when 18.Rd6 kept more pressure. It did not matter, since 19...Qd8?? allowed a forced win and your opponent resigned.

review.turning_point: 15.Rxd7! cashed in the open-file pressure and took you from a promising attack to a decisive advantage.
review.focus: At 18.Qd3? you had the stronger rook move 18.Rd6. When already winning, look for the move that keeps all your threats alive rather than a natural-looking queen move.

review.headline: A good Scandinavian that drifted level, then lost on the clock

sections.text: You handled the Mieses-Kotroc well: 2.exd5 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 3...Qe6+ 4.Be2, then 5.d4 and 6.Nf3 had you at +2.0 and more as Black's 5...h5 and 9...g6 weakened the kingside.

The first sign of trouble was 10.Qf3?!, but the real turn came at 13.Qxg5??. After 12.Nce4 12...Bxg5, 13.Nxg5 was the recapture that kept your +2.8, while 13.Qxg5 allowed 13...Qxg5 14.Bxg5?! 14...Nxe4 15.Bxe4 and the game was equal.
You got a chance back when 17...O-O?? jumped to +2.3 for you, but 18.Bxe7?? gave it straight back (+0.4); 18.Rhe1 was the move. Later 24.c4?! and 25.bxc4?! loosened your pawns.

The opening plan deserves credit. Against the early queen sortie you kept developing with tempo, and 7.Ng5 and 8.Bd3 made Black's queen keep moving. The lesson from 13.Qxg5 is that when your position is already better, the plain recapture keeps the pressure, and you do not need to simplify with a queen trade.
27.d5? came when you were low on time, and then the clock decided the result at move 29. The position was only slightly worse (-1.5), so time trouble turned a manageable game into a loss.

review.turning_point: 13.Qxg5?? allowed a queen trade instead of the 13.Nxg5 recapture, and that threw away a +2.8 edge.
review.focus: Clock management: by 27.d5? you were low on time and the position had already slipped. Spend less on routine moves such as 16.h3 so you have minutes for the middlegame.

review.headline: A wild tactical slugfest that you won on time with a big material lead

sections.text: You met 2.Bg5 with 2...f6 and built a big centre with 4...e5, though 5...Qd6?! and 7...Qe7?! cost you a little. Then 9.Bh4?? was a real blunder by White, and you were at +1.5 after 9...O-O-O. 10.Nd2? and 12.Ngf3? helped you further.

11...exd4? gave back some of that, since 11...h5 was the engine choice. But 12...dxe3! was the right follow-up and you steadied at +3.0. After 13.O-O 13...exd2?! 14.Qxd2 14...Bh6? 15.Qd4 15...Qe4 16.Qxa7 you were still ahead.

The mess began with 16...Qxc2??, which swung from +3.4 to -4.3, when 16...Qa4 was needed. 17.b4?? gave it back (+1.9), but 17...d4?? and 18...Qe4?? swung it again. Then 19.f3?? gave you 19...Qxd4+!, a check that also forked the queen on a7 and king on g1, bringing you to +5.2.

Your plan of 4...e5 and 10...g5 was ambitious, and White's passive 10.Nd2? and 12.Ngf3? let it work. The tactical moments at 16...Qxc2?? and 18...Qe4?? came from grabbing material without checking White's best answer, and both were rescued by White's own errors. After 20...Rxd4 you converted the endgame cleanly and kept a huge advantage to the end.
After the queens came off you were far ahead on material and kept making progress, even when 22...Rd7? and 29...Re2?! were not exact. White ran out of time at move 40.

review.turning_point: 19...Qxd4+! was the moment you took over, turning a messy game into a clearly winning endgame.
review.focus: After gaining an edge, look at forcing replies before captures. 16...Qxc2?? grabbed material when 16...Qa4 kept the edge, and 18...Qe4?? repeated the pattern when 18...Rxd4 was better.

review.headline: A clean punishment of an opening mistake, with a rook collected on the way

sections.text: White's 2.b3? was a strange start, and you answered perfectly with 2...Nf6! and 3...Bc5. After 4.Bb2 4...d5 5.exd5 5...Qxd5 6.Nf3 6...e4?! (a little hasty) 7.dxe4 7...Qxd1+ 8.Kxd1 8...Nxe4, the king on d1 was a target.
9.Bxg7?? was a blunder, and the right move was 9.Bb5+. You were at +2.7, and 9...Nxf2+ would have forked the king on d1 and rook on h1. 9...Rg8? was reasonable but gave away part of the edge.
10.Bd4?? gave you another chance, and 10...Bxd4! was exactly right. After 11.Nxd4 11...Nxf2+ 12.Kc1 12...Nxh1, your knight took the rook on h1, and the white king never got out of trouble.

The plan was simple and it worked: develop with 2...Nf6 and 3...Bc5, take the centre with 4...d5, and let White overreach. Once the queens came off and the white king stayed on d1, every capture near it came with check or threat, which is why 12...Nxh1 was possible. You played an accurate game with a 90.5 accuracy.
13.g3 13...Nc6 14.Bg2 14...Nxd4 15.Bc6+ 15...Nxc6 finished it, and White resigned.

review.turning_point: 10...Bxd4! followed by 11...Nxf2+ and 12...Nxh1 won the rook and ended the game.
review.focus: At 9...Rg8? you chose a safe-looking move, but 9...Nxf2+ was stronger. Whenever a knight can check the king and attack a rook, calculate that first.

review.headline: An early pawn grab backfired, and you nearly recovered before the clock ran short

sections.text: The game started as a Scandinavian: 2.exd5 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 3...Qe5+ 4.Qe2?! 4...Qxe2+ 5.Ngxe2. The queen trade was fine and you were level (+0.2) through 9.Bf4 9...O-O-O 10.Nb5.

11.Nxa7+?? was the key mistake. It took a pawn, but the knight ended up stranded and your position slid to -2.6. 11.Bh2 was the quiet move. After 12.Bxc7+ 12...Kxc7 13.c4 13...Nb4 14.Nb5+ 14...Kb8 15.O-O-O 15...Nxa2+ you were pushed back, and 16.Kd2?! and 21.Kd3? worsened it.
Black gave you a chance: 23...Nd4+?? was a fork of your king and bishop, but your own knight could just take it with 24.Nxd4, the engine choice. 24.Kd1?? instead put you at -5.6.

After the early queen trade the game was quiet, and 11.Nxa7+?? is what changed it. Give yourself credit for the fighting moves 27.fxe3! and 30.Bxd5!, which kept the game alive when the engine had you at about -3. The final lesson is the clock: 28.Kd2? and 32.Rd4?? both came when you were low on time.
You fought back well with 27.fxe3! and 30.Bxd5!, and when 31...Rd8? was played you were at +4.5. But 32.Rd4??, low on time, ended it. 32.d6 would have kept control.

review.turning_point: 32.Rd4?? threw away a position the engine rated at +4.5 after 31...Rd8?, and you were short on time.
review.focus: Check your moves for safety when low on time: 24.Kd1?? and 32.Rd4?? both came when a simple capture (24.Nxd4) or pawn push (32.d6) kept everything under control.

review.headline: A shaky bishop sacrifice that worked because the opponent cracked

sections.text: This was a Caro-Kann Exchange with sensible development: 4.Nc3 4...Bf5 5.Nf3 5...e6 6.Bd3 6...Bxd3 7.Qxd3 7...Nf6 8.Bg5 8...Be7. It was equal until move 14.

14.Bxh6? was the error. After 14...gxh6 15.Qxh6 the sacrifice cost a bishop for two pawns and the engine had you at -2.4. 14.Ne2 was the solid move. The attack with 16.h4, 17.g4?! and 18.g5?! was ambitious but risky.
The turn came when 17...Ne7? let you off, as 17...Nxd4 was the engine's best. Then 19.Qh5 19...Ng6 put real pressure on, though 20.Ne5?? ignored the better 20.Qg4 and handed Black the edge.

The opening plan of 8.Bg5 and 10.Bf4 was fine, but the sacrifice on h6 was premature because few of your other pieces were near Black's king. When you sacrifice a piece, count the attackers. Here only the queen and the h-pawn joined in at first, and 19.Qh5 added more pressure along the h-file. Your opponent's mistakes at 17...Ne7? and the resignation made it work out.

Even so, your opponent faltered, and after 21.dxe5 21...Qc7 22.Qe2 you kept the attack alive with 23.h5 23...Nf4 24.Qg4. Black resigned at -1.7 for you, so the engine would not call this winning, but the pressure was real.

review.turning_point: 14.Bxh6? changed the character of the game, giving up material for an attack that needed your opponent's help.
review.focus: Calculate sacrifices like 14.Bxh6 to the end: 14.Ne2 kept the equal position, and 20.Ne5?? gave away more than it gained.

review.headline: A messy QGD where tactics flipped back and forth, ending in mate

sections.text: You played a sound QGD exchange: 3.cxd5 3...exd5 4.Nc3 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 5...c6 6.Bd2 6...Be7 7.e3 7...O-O 8.Bd3 8...Bg4. 10...c5?! and 11...cxd4?! opened the position, and 12...Rc8?? was a real slip (-3.0).
Then White blundered with 13.Bg5??, as 13.Nxg4 was the right move. After 15.Bxh7+ 15...Kh8 16.Bxe7 16...Qxe7, 17.Rfe1?? put you at +2.5.

17...g6?? threw that away; 17...d4 was best. 19...Rg8?? was another miss for 19...Qh4. But 20.Qh6+?? allowed your best move, 20...Qh7!, and after 21.Qxh7+ 21...Kxh7 22.Nxd5 22...Bf3! was best even though the bishop was en prise.

Overall this was a sharp game that you won by finding the counterpunches. Your pieces were active from the start: 8...Bg4 and 9...Nbd7 prepared the central break that White never quite stopped. Both 20...Qh7 and 22...Bf3 defended and counterattacked at once, which is the hardest kind of move to find.
23.Nf6+?? forked your king, knight and rook, but 23...Nxf6! just took it. After 24.exf6 24...Rxg2+ 25.Kf1 25...Rcg8 26.Re7+ 26...Kh6, 27...Rg1# was a back-rank mate, with the king on f1 trapped.

review.turning_point: 22...Bf3! and 23...Nxf6! turned a messy endgame into a won position, ending in 27...Rg1#.
review.focus: Spot the quiet defensive moves: 17...g6?? and 19...Rg8?? both gave away large advantages when 17...d4 and 19...Qh4 were available.

review.headline: A calm Petrov where one clean slip by White decided it

sections.text: You played Petrov's Defense against the Three Knights, with 3...d6 and 4...Be6. After 5.Bxe6 5...fxe6 6.d4 6...exd4 7.Nxd4 7...e5, 8.Ne6 8...Qd7 9.Nxf8 9...Rxf8 simplified into a healthy position for you.
10...Nc6, 11...O-O-O and 12...h6 got you safely developed. After 13.Bxf6 13...gxf6 14.Qf3 14...f5 15.Qc3 15...fxe4 you picked up a pawn.
16...Qe6?? was your one slip: it went from +1.7 to -0.1, because 16...Qf7 was needed with 17.Qc4 to follow.

The opening was a solid answer to 4.Bc4: 4...Be6 offered a bishop exchange, and 5.Bxe6 5...fxe6 gave you the half-open f-file. That file mattered later, because 14.Qf3 14...f5 and 15.Qc3 15...fxe4 opened lines. It was a simple, clean win that could have been even cleaner with 16...Qf7.
White returned it with 17.Ne3??, going from -0.1 to +2.6, and you continued with 17...Rg8. White resigned soon after.

review.turning_point: 17.Ne3?? gave you a clear edge after 16...Qe6?? had given yours up, and White resigned.
review.focus: After winning a pawn with 15...fxe4, check what the opponent's best move is before moving your queen: 16...Qe6?? allowed 17.Qc4 and ruined the edge.

review.headline: A won game thrown away in time trouble, ending in mate

sections.text: You played the Stafford Gambit as White and won a pawn with 3.Nxe5, then punished 3...Nc6? with 4.Nxc6! 4...dxc6 5.d3 5...Bc5. 6.Be3? let Black trade, and 8.Qd2?! 8...Qh4+ 9.g3 9...Qg5 got messy.

10.Bg2?? was an error, but 10...Nxe3?? let you back, and 11.Nc3?? gave it away again (11.Ke2 was needed). Then 12...Nxc2+?? looked like a fork of your king and rook, but your 13.Qxc2! just took the knight.

From there you played well: 14.Kf1, 15.Re1 and 17.Rhf1 kept +4.6 to +5.0 for a long stretch. 28.Qxb5?? swung it to -3.8 (28.Rd2 was needed), but 28...Qxb5?? gave it right back, and 29.Rxb5! got you to +4.6.

Your opening choice paid off right away: 3...Nc6? let 4.Nxc6! win a pawn with a better structure. The long middle phase was calm, and you improved your pieces patiently with 18.Ne2, 19.Nf4 and 20.Qa4. At +4 or +5 you only needed to avoid blunders, and low time ruined that.
The end came in time trouble: 37.a5?? (37.Rd1 was needed), 38.Kf5?? and 39.a6?? allowed 39...Rf3#, checkmate.

review.turning_point: 37.a5?? turned a +3.8 position into a lost one, and 38.Kf5?? finished it.
review.focus: With a big lead, play safe moves: 37.Rd1 was safe, while 37.a5?? and 38.Kf5?? walked your king into a mating net. Ask what the opponent's checks do before pushing.

review.headline: Two missed mates, but you got there on the third try

sections.text: This was a Vienna Game: 4.Bd3 4...Bg4 5.O-O 5...Be7 6.Nd5 6...Nxd5 7.exd5 7...c6 8.dxc6 8...Nxc6. White's 9.Be4?? was a blunder, taking you to +4.9. You answered 9...Qb6??, dropping to +0.3 when 9...d5 was needed.
The middlegame was a struggle: 10...O-O?! and 11...Bh5?! were not accurate. Then 15...Rxf3?? gave up the exchange and left you behind at -2.6. 15...d5 was the cleaner move.

After 17.Qd5+ 17...Kh8 18.Be3 18...Ne2+ 19.Kh2 19...Qxb2 your pieces were active and White slipped with 23.Qxb7?, 24.Qe7?? and 26.Qe7??. Twice you missed the finish, 24...Qe4+ and 26...Qe4+, and played 24...Kg8?? and 26...Kg8?? instead.

Your kingside play had good ideas, such as 12...Bg6 and 14...exd4 opening lines, and 19...Qxb2 grabbed a pawn with tempo. The main lesson is the pattern: in all three mating chances the queen check on e4 followed by f3 and the queen capture gave mate, so once you see it on the board it is easy to find again.
Third time lucky: 27.a4?? let you play 27...Qe4+ 28.f3 28...Qxf3#, checkmate to finish.

review.turning_point: 15...Rxf3?? cost material and swung the game, but your opponent's later blunders gave you three chances at mate.
review.focus: Run your checks before quiet moves. At 24...Kg8?? and 26...Kg8?? the mate with 24...Qe4+ was waiting, and you needed three tries.

review.headline: A short Italian where a direct attack on f7 ended the game

sections.text: You opened with 1.e4 1...e5 2.Nf3 2...Nc6 3.Bc4 and met 3...h6 with the central 4.d4. After 4...Bb4+ 5.c3 5...Bd6 things got a little complicated.
6.dxe5?! was a discovered attack from the queen on the bishop on d6, but 6...Nxe5 7.Nxe5 7...Bxe5 simplified. It was slightly less than perfect (+1.0).
8.Qd5? aimed the queen and bishop at f7, and the engine would have preferred 8.f4. But Black's 8...d6?? failed to defend, so 9.Qxf7# was checkmate.

This game shows how fast a lead in development can punish a mistake. Black's 3...h6 and 4...Bb4+ used time without bringing out pieces, so after 5.c3 5...Bd6 you were ready to attack. The weakness on f7 was the target all along, and 8.Qd5? aimed straight at it.
Remember that 8...Qe7 was the best defence.

review.turning_point: 8.Qd5? set a trap, and 8...d6?? walked into 9.Qxf7#.
review.focus: Take care with early queen moves: 8.Qd5? worked here, but 8.f4 would have kept an edge without the risk.

review.headline: A good opening and a shaky middlegame, saved by the opponent's clock

sections.text: You played the Scotch Gambit setup as White with 4.d4 4...exd4 5.e5 5...Ng4. 6.Nxd4? was a slip (-1.4), since 6.O-O was needed. But Black returned the favour with 6...Nxd4??, and 7.Qxd4! put you back at +0.7.
8.exd6?! lost a little, but 9.Qe4+, 10.Bg5, 11.Bxf6 and 13.O-O-O kept things level while your rooks reached the e-file.
15...h6?? gave you +5.0, since 16.Bd3 was a discovered attack on the bishop on b4. You played 16.Rde1?? instead and it dropped to +0.0.

The early part was good practical chess: after the Scotch Gambit setup, 7.Qxd4! gave you a centralised queen, and 9.Qe4+, 10.Bg5 and 11.Bxf6 traded off a key defender. 13.O-O-O and 14.Rhe1 then prepared the e-file, which is why 15...h6?? was so costly for Black.
17.Qf4? was another slip (17.Bxf7+ was better), and 18.Ne4?? dropped you to -5.4. Your opponent ran out of time at move 20, but the board favoured them.

review.turning_point: 15...h6?? offered you +5.0, and 16.Rde1?? threw it away.
review.focus: After an opponent's blunder, look for the discovered attack: 16.Bd3 was the move that won material at +5.0, and 16.Rde1?? did nothing.

review.headline: A fine Petrov in which the clock decided the game

sections.text: You chose the Petrov with 3...d6 4.Nf3 4...Nxe4 5.Bd3 5...Nf6 and played steadily: 6...Be7, 7...O-O, 8...d5, 9...c6, 10...Nbd7 and 11...Nb6. By 14.Bf3 you were about equal.
15...Nbd7?? was the lone blunder (+0.2 to -1.9). 15...h6 was safer, avoiding 16.Nxf7, a knight capture that forked your bishop and queen.
White missed it with 16.c4??, and then 17.c5?? gave you +2.0.

The opening went well because you equalised comfortably with 8...d5 and 9...c6, and your moves were consistent with the plan. Time is the key point here: with 17.c5?? on the board giving you +2.0, a few spare minutes would have turned this into a good chance to win.
Sadly, you lost on time at move 17, though the board was in your favour. The clock was the real opponent.

review.turning_point: 15...Nbd7?? was the board mistake, but running out of time at move 17 decided the result.
review.focus: Manage the clock: you reached move 17 with a better position and lost on time. Speed up the opening moves like 6...Be7 and 8...d5.

review.headline: A good Scandinavian, undone by one careless pawn move

sections.text: As White you handled the queen trade after 4.Qe2?! 4...Qxe2+ 5.Ngxe2 and set up a good position with 6.g3, 7.Bg2, 11.b4 and 12.Bb2. 13.Ne4 13...f5 left you at +2.1.
14.h3?? was the key mistake (+2.1 to -2.5). 14.Nc5 was needed. After 14...fxe4 15.hxg4 15...Bxf2+ 16.Kh1 16...Bxe1 17.Rxe1, you were down material.
You fought on: 21.Rxe6?! was an ambitious try, 22.Nd5! was a strong response to 21...g5??, and you reached +0.0 after 23.Kg2.

The first twelve moves were good: your bishops on g2 and b2 aimed down the long diagonals and the rook on e1 supported the knight. That is why 14.h3?? was such a pity, because it dropped the whole advantage in one move. After that, 18.Bxe4 and 19.Nf4 showed good fighting spirit.
Then 23...Raf8?? helped, but 24.Rh6?? allowed a forced mate (24.Nf6+ was needed). After 25.Kh3! you were lost anyway at -4.2.

review.turning_point: 14.h3?? let Black strike with 14...fxe4, and you spent the rest of the game down material.
review.focus: Before a quiet move like 14.h3, check what is attacked. After 13...f5 your knight on e4 was under attack, and 14.Nc5 kept your edge.

review.headline: A short, sound Petrov cut off by the clock

sections.text: You played Petrov's Defense with 1...e5 and 2...Nf6, and then 3...d6 against the Three Knights. The structure was familiar and perfectly good.
After 4.Bb5+ 4...Bd7 5.Qe2 5...Nc6 6.d3 6...Be7 7.Bg5 7...O-O 8.O-O, each of your moves was sound, and the engine rated the position as level throughout.

You can feel good about the opening: 3...d6 headed for a solid Petrov setup, 4...Bd7 answered the check, and 6...Be7 and 7...O-O finished development before anything tactical began. All you have to work on is the clock, since the board was fine.
The game ended on time at move 8 with a level position, so this was a result that came from the clock, not the board.

review.turning_point: There was no turning point on the board: the clock ended the game at move 8 with the position level.
review.focus: Your accuracy was 91.5, so the work is time: after 8.O-O the clock ran out, so set a target for how many seconds to spend on opening moves.

review.headline: A Petrov that went wrong in the middlegame and ended in mate

sections.text: You played the Petrov: 3.Nxe5 3...d6 4.Nf3 4...Nxe4 5.Qe2 5...Qe7 6.d3 6...Nf6 7.Bg5 7...Be6 8.Nc3 8...h6. 9.Bh4 9...g5 10.Bg3 10...Nbd7?! started to loosen things, and after 11.Nb5 11...O-O-O 12.Nxa7+ 12...Kb8 the game stayed balanced.

14...c6?? was the first blunder, from +0.6 to -4.1, when 14...Nc5 was needed. White's 15.Nxd6?? gave you chances, because 15.Bxd6+ would have been a fork of the king on b8 and queen on e7. You then played 15...Ka8??.
17.Nd2?? gave you +4.6 but 17...Qxb2?? dropped to +0.6, as 17...Bxf5 was better. 19.Nxg7 19...Ba2?! 20.Rd1 20...Rh7?? 21.Nf5?? 21...Re8?? kept it going, and 20...Qc3 or 21...Qc3 was best.

The plan of 8...h6 and 9...g5 was ambitious, and it set up wild positions where the white knight on b5 caused trouble. The Petrov tends to look drawish, but those kingside pawn advances loosened your king, and 14...c6?? made that worse.
22.Ne4 22...Qxa4 23.Ra1 23...Nxe4?! 24.Rxa2 24...Qxa2 25.Qxa2# ended it, checkmate.

review.turning_point: 14...c6?? loosened your king and 17...Qxb2?? threw away a +4.6 chance.
review.focus: Keep your king safe before grabbing material: 14...c6?? and 20...Rh7?? both skipped better moves (14...Nc5 and 20...Qc3).

review.headline: A Sicilian that you won thanks to your opponent's errors and a finishing queen sacrifice

sections.text: You played an open Sicilian with 4.Nxd4 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 5...e5 6.Nf3, then 7.Bc4 7...b5 8.Bb3. Black's 8...Nbd7?? gave you +3.7, and 9.Ng5 was the strong move. You played 9.Bd2?? instead, and then 10.Qe2?? and 11.O-O-O?? passed up more chances.
Black kept erring with 9...Rb8?? and 10...Bb7??, and after 12.Bg5 12...Nc5? you played 13.Nxe5! 13...Nxb3+ 14.axb3. 15.Nf3 15...O-O 16.Rhe1 16...Rfe8 kept the initiative.
17.Nd5?? was a mistake, from +1.6 to -3.9, since 17.Bxf6 was better. But 19...h6?? gave you your chance.

The game shows how quickly a position can change. Black's 8...Nbd7?? and 9...Rb8?? handed you early chances, but 9.Bd2?? and 10.Qe2?? gave them back. Your strengths here were the central break 13.Nxe5! and the queen sacrifice at the end, both of which came from looking at forcing moves.
20.Qxe8+! was a back-rank trick: after 20...Rxe8 21.Rxe8# you had checkmate.

review.turning_point: 19...h6?? left the back rank weak, and 20.Qxe8+! won from a position where you stood at -4.0.
review.focus: You missed 9.Ng5 and 17.Bxf6. When the opponent stumbles, make the forcing move first, and check each move for tactics before moving pieces out.

review.headline: A trap in the Petrov that won the queen, followed by steady play

sections.text: You played the Petrov as White: 3.Nxe5 3...Qe7 4.Nf3 4...Nxe4 5.Qe2?! 5...d5 6.d3 6...Nc5 7.Be3 7...Na4 8.b3 8...Nb6 9.Nc3. It was balanced, and the engine had you roughly even.

9...Qb4?? gave you the shot: 10.Bc5+! was a discovered check, with the bishop attacking the queen and the queen on e2 checking the king on e8. After 11.Bxb4 11...Bxb4 you were way ahead (+4.6), having won the queen for a bishop.
13.O-O-O?? let off some pressure (+4.8 to +2.0), as 13.a3 was needed. But you recovered with 14.Nxd4 and 17.Ne4, and 19.Qxg7! took the g7 pawn.

The Petrov line you chose with 3.Nxe5 and 4.Nf3 is a good practical choice. 5.Qe2?! was a small inaccuracy, but your opponent went wrong at once with 9...Qb4??, and from then on you had time to play calmly. After 10.Bc5+ the position was effectively decided.
22.Qxh7?! and 24.Qa1?! were small slips, but the position stayed comfortably won, and 33.Nxd5 ended it at +7.6.

review.turning_point: 10.Bc5+! won the queen for a bishop after 9...Qb4??, and the rest was converting.
review.focus: 13.O-O-O?? walked into more trouble when 13.a3 kept things simple. When far ahead, pick the safest move.

review.headline: A messy Petrov where you let a big edge slip, then won a mating race anyway

sections.text: This began as a quiet Petrov-style position where you set up a solid Be7, Bg4-h5 and castling. White then drifted. 10.Qd3? and 11.Bg5? both handed you a lead, and by move 11 you stood about +1.8.

You gave much of that back at once. 11...h6? loosened your kingside when the stronger idea was to take on f3 and keep the e4 pawn in view. Two moves later 13...Nxe4? cashed in too early and the edge fell from +1.5 to +0.4.

White's 19.f3?? brought you back to +2.7, and you built on it well: 22...Nxg3, the rook trade on e8, then 25...Nxd4! after 25.g4?? left the d4 pawn to take. The lead grew past +5, which is where it should have stayed.

Then 32...Re6?? threw it away. The cleaner route was 32...Nf4+, which was a fork of the king on g2 and the bishop on g6 and would have kept you winning. White's 37.Kf2? let you back in with 37...Rxh3!, and the finish was lovely: 42...Ra1+! forced 43.Bb1 and 43...Rxb1# on the back rank.

review.turning_point: 32...Re6?? turned +6.2 into -2.2 in one move; 32...Nf4+ followed by 33.Kg3 Nxg6 would have kept the piece and the win.
review.focus: Before every move in a won position, check what your piece on d3 and the loose pieces can be attacked by; at 32...Re6 you needed to look for the forcing 32...Nf4+ first.

review.headline: A cool, accurate win after the Owen Defense went wrong on move 5

sections.text: Black's Owen set-up with 1...b6 and 2...Bb7 is a respectable choice, but 5.e5 hit the knight at once and 5...Be7?? walked into 6.exf6!. You took the knight, and after 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 you had a clean material lead (+3.7).

8.Be2?! was a little slow, since grabbing the pawn with 8...Qxb2 was not hard to stop, but you kept control by developing with 9.Nbd2, 10.O-O and 11.Ne4. That is the right way to cash in: finish development and let the extra material do the work.

12...Nd4? tried to trick you with a discovered attack on the bishop on b7 and your knight, but 13.Nxd4! was exactly right and Black lost more material. After 17.Qxc7 and 18.Qxa7 your queen took over the queenside and you were over +6 for most of the rest of the game.

In the long endgame you stayed patient, played 46.Rfg5+ with a pin along the fifth rank, and queened with 56.a8=Q. The finish was 68.Rh6#. The only real slip was 49.Bc6?, which gave back a couple of pawns' worth of evaluation but not the win.

review.turning_point: 6.exf6! right after Black's 5...Be7?? decided the game, taking a knight for free and leaving Black needing a miracle.
review.focus: At 49.Bc6? you gave up the chance to keep everything tied up; 49.Bf1 was the safer retreat, and in won endings it pays to pick the move that removes counterplay.

review.headline: A wild Winawer where you misplayed the opening but won the tactics

sections.text: You went into the Advance Winawer and early on played 5.Bd2?, which let Black take the d4 pawn. The sharper 5.Bd3 was the move, and after 5...Nxd4 6.Nge2? you were already worse at -1.7.

Black returned the favour right away with 9...f6??, which swung the evaluation to +1.9 for you. The correct reaction was 10.Rxd5, but 10.Qg4?? let Black off the hook. Your position was still playable, but 17.Rhg1? and 18.g5?! again let Black take the initiative.

Black then cracked first. 21...dxc3?? was a real blunder, and 22.Bxc3! was a good reply: moving the bishop from d2 uncovered the rook on d1 against the bishop on d7, a discovered attack. 23.Bxd7+? was inaccurate, but 24...Qxa2?? let you back into the game for good.
You finished sharply. 27.Qxd7+! Kb8 28.Qe8+ Nd8 29.Qxd8# is a tidy finish that came from keeping your rooks on the d-file.

review.turning_point: 24...Qxa2?? took a pawn but left the d7 rook hanging to the rooks on the d-file, flipping the game from -3.3 to +3.8.
review.focus: At 5.Bd2? and 6.Nge2? you let a piece into your centre; against the Winawer, keep the d4 pawn protected, since 5.Bd3 held it.

review.headline: You survived an inaccurate opening and punished White's d4 push

sections.text: This was a Bishop's Opening where both sides developed naturally. After 9.g4 Bg6 10.a4 the position was level, but 10...Qd7?? was a blunder, dropping you to -1.6. The simple 10...c6 would have kept things safe.

White returned the favour at once. 12.Ne2?? was a big error and brought you back, but 12...Nc6? was not the best use of it. 12...Nxg4 was available, and 13...Nd8? again missed 13...Nxg4. Still, you were back near equal by move 14.
The game turned with 19.d4??. You found 19...Ncxe4!, striking at the centre. After 20.Qe2 exd4 21.cxd4 d5 you had the stronger pawns and active pieces, and the evaluation was around +3.5.
You kept finding the best moves, 23...Qxf5 and 24...Qxh3, then 27...Rg6!, a rook offer that tied the white queen to the g1 king. White was lost at +7 and resigned soon after.

review.turning_point: 19.d4?? opened the centre for you, and 19...Ncxe4! turned a roughly equal game into +3.3.
review.focus: 10...Qd7? was the costly move. Before putting the queen on d7 with a bishop on b6 and White's Be3 in place, check what 11.Bxb6 does; 10...c6 was calmer.

review.headline: A slow Pirc where small inaccuracies built into a lost position

sections.text: You answered the Pirc with a flexible set-up using 3.d3 and 4.Bg5. 5.Qd2?! went a bit too early, and Black's 5...c6 and 6...Qc7 gave them an easy game. After 9.h3 Nxe3 10.fxe3 your structure was already awkward.

The next step was 12.dxe5?!, opening the centre while your king was still on e1, and 13.O-O-O?! put your king where Black's queenside pawns could attack it. 15.Kb1?! allowed 15...b5, and Black's pawns started to roll.

The real damage was 16.Qg3?. It took the queen from the defence of c3, and after 16...b4 the knight on c3 had no good way out. The better plan was 16.Bd3 with a calm structure, and from -4.5 you never recovered.
23.Rxd2! was the best practical try, giving up the exchange to stay in the game. But the position was already beyond repair, and resigning after 25...Bxg2 was reasonable.

review.turning_point: 16.Qg3? left the knight on c3 under attack by the b-pawn, and the evaluation dropped from -2.8 to -4.5.
review.focus: At 13.O-O-O? and 15.Kb1? you walked your king into Black's pawn storm; with queenside pawns already advanced, choose a safer king home first.

review.headline: Down a knight early, you bounced back when White gave it all away

sections.text: In the Three Knights Petrov, 3...Nxe4?? was a mistake. White simply replied 4.Nxe4, and you were a knight down for a pawn. 3...Nc6 was the safer move and would have kept the game even.
You fought back with 4...d5 and 5...e4, and 7.Nb3? from White let you off a bit. 7...a5? then gave some of it back, since 7...c4 was the more active idea. By move 9 you were still down about 4.6.
Then White blundered. 13.Nxf5?? looked greedy, but 13...Qxe4+! was a fork of the king on e1 and the knight on f5. That swung the game from -5.5 to +3.2.
15.Qh5+ Qg6 and 16.Qxc5?? finished things. You took with 16...Bxc5! and picked up the queen, so White resigned.

review.turning_point: 13.Nxf5?? gave you 13...Qxe4+! with a fork, turning a game you were losing at -5.5 into a win.
review.focus: 3...Nxe4 is the move to review. In the Three Knights, 3...Nc6 followed by ...Nd4 is the safer way to play for ...e4 ideas.

review.headline: A confident French win that missed an earlier mate

sections.text: Black's 2...Qe7 is an unusual reply to the French. You developed with 3.Nf3 and 4.Be2, castled, and already had the better game at +1.6. 6.e5?! was slightly premature, as 6.d5 was the stronger move, but you stayed ahead.
Both 8.Bf4?! and 12.Qd3?! cost a few tenths, but nothing serious. The position was good because Black had weak dark squares after ...g6, and your pieces were pointed at them.

Black's 15...Bd5? gave you the chance, and 16.Ne5! was the right reply. After 17.Nxg6 you won a pawn and the Black king was stuck in the centre. 19.Ne5+?! was a discovered check and attack from the bishop on h5, but it was less accurate than 19.Re1.
The big miss came at 24.cxd5?!. There was a forced mate with 24.Qxd5+ Qe6 25.Qxe6#. You still won at +5.5, but it is worth seeing why checks come first.

review.turning_point: 16.Ne5! after Black's 15...Bd5? launched the attack and took your evaluation from +3.0 to +4.4.
review.focus: At 24.cxd5?! you had a forced mate with 24.Qxd5+; before any quiet recapture, list every check and capture first.

review.headline: A topsy-turvy Three Knights where White's blunders decided it

sections.text: You played the Petrov Three Knights and offered a bishop trade with 4...Be6. After 5.Bxe6 fxe6 6.Ng5 you were fine, but 6...Nd5?? was a blunder, since the cleaner 6...Qd7 kept things under control.

7.Nf7 was a fork of your queen and rook, yet 7...Nxc3! was the right reply, and 8.dxc3?? by White was a real error. The best answer was 8...Kxf7, but 8...Qf6?? lost the plot and allowed 9.Nxh8, leaving you down material.
You stayed in the game and White kept making mistakes. 16.b4? and then 17.c5?? gave you back the initiative, and 17...Qh5! with the idea of ...Ng4 was a strong choice.
The finish was great. 18...Bxh4! put a piece en prise, 19.cxd6?? lost to 19...Bxg3!, and after 20.d7+ Kd8 21.fxg3 Qh2# you won.

review.turning_point: 17.c5?? gave you 17...Qh5!, and from then on White's king was under attack.
review.focus: 8...Qf6?? is the move to learn from: when a fork like 7.Nf7 can be answered by 8...Kxf7, always check the capture first.

review.headline: A long game full of swings that you won in the endgame
