sections.text: You played the Bishop's Opening as Black with a King's Indian-style set-up, and the middlegame stayed balanced. White's 21.Qh6?? was a blunder, taking you up to +3.3, but 21...Bxg3?? gave it away again, since 21...Rf4 was the move.
After the queen trade and rook trade, you reached a king-and-pawn ending. 28...h5+?? was a blunder, dropping to -2.2; 28...Ke6 was simpler. White then returned the favour with 33.Kh4??.

More errors followed on both sides. 40.cxd4?? gave you chances, but 40...exd4? was less precise than 40...cxd4, and 42...Ke5?? then turned +3.5 into +0.4. White missed their chance with 43.Kd3??, and you found 43...Kf4!.
From there your passed pawns decided it. You queened with 56...g1=Q and later 69...c1=Q, then finished with 76...Qfh2#.

review.turning_point: 43...Kf4! punished White's 43.Kd3?? and moved your evaluation to nearly +7.
review.focus: In pawn endings like 42...Ke5??, count the king moves carefully; 42...Kd6 kept the position under control.

review.headline: A quick Rousseau Gambit win where Black's greed ended the game

sections.text: Black chose the Rousseau Gambit with 3...f5, which is sharp and risky. You kept things simple with 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4, and Black's 5...fxe4?? was already a blunder.
6.Nc3?? gave some of this back, since 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qh5+ was the stronger idea. 6...Bb4?? then pinned your knight, but your position was still fine.
7.Qh5+?? was another inaccuracy. 7.Nxc6 would have hit the bishop on b4 and queen at once with a fork. But Black replied 7...Ke7??, and you had a forced win.
You finished neatly: 8.Nf5+ Kf6 9.Qf7+ Ke5 10.g3?! Bxc3+ 11.bxc3 d6 12.Bf4#.

review.turning_point: 7...Ke7?? walked the king into the open, and 8.Nf5+ started a forced mating attack.
review.focus: Look at 6.Nc3??: you had 6.Nxc6 available first, and in open positions the capture that forces matters over a developing move.

review.headline: A promising attack collapsed with one move at the end

sections.text: You met the Van't Kruijs with ...e5, ...d5 and ...Nc6. 8...d4?? was a blunder, since the quieter 8...c6 kept your pawns safe, and 9.Nxe4 left you slightly worse.
Then White blundered. 10.N4g3?? let you play 10...h5!, and you began a strong kingside attack with 11...h4. 12.Nh1? and 13.g3?? were both mistakes by White, and you were up +3.0.
You kept the pressure up well. 14...hxg3 opened lines and 15...gxh2+! was a strong follow-up to 15.Qe1??, with the evaluation at +4.9.
The decisive error was 18...Bd6??. After 18.d3 the c1 bishop saw your queen, and 19.Bxg5 won it. The correct move was 18...Qg4, which kept everything protected and kept the h-pawn ready to promote.

review.turning_point: 18...Bd6?? dropped the queen on g5 and turned +4.7 into -4.7 in one move.
review.focus: At 18...Bd6 you needed to check what White's last move opened; 18.d3 created a line from the bishop on c1 to your queen.

review.headline: A clean Italian win after Black's early bishop mistake

sections.text: You opened with the Italian, and after 4.d4 Black played the careless 4...Be6??. The bishop looked active, but it could be hit by a pawn.
5.d5! was exactly right: the pawn forked the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6. After 5...Nd4 6.dxe6 Nxf3+ 7.Qxf3 fxe6 8.Bxe6 you were comfortably ahead.
You then developed sensibly with 9.Bb3, 10.Qe3, 11.Nc3 and 12.Nd5, and traded knights with 12...Nxd5 13.Bxd5 to keep things simple. 14.Qa3 and 15.Qc3 took care of the king.
Your accuracy was nearly perfect, and White ran out of time at 16.Qc6 in a lost position.

review.turning_point: 5.d5! won material at once by forking two pieces after Black's 4...Be6??.
review.focus: No errors to fix here; keep watching for pawn forks like 5.d5 whenever Black puts a bishop on e6 while a knight sits on c6.

review.headline: A patient Petrov win capped by a brilliant queen sacrifice

sections.text: You played a standard Petrov: 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4, then built up with ...Be7 and ...d5. White's 9.b4? was the first slip, handing you a slight lead, and after 10.c5 Bf5 11.Bg5 h6 12.Bxf6 Bxf6 you had a comfortable game.
15...Bg4? was inaccurate, and 15...a5 was better. But White replied with 16.Ne5??, which let your bishop go to e2. 16...Bxe2! hit both the queen and the rook, a fork, and the lead went to +2.6.
You kept control through the trades with 21...Rxe5 and 24...Rxc5, and the d-pawn became a monster after 23...d4 and 25...d3.
The finish was beautiful: 28...Qe1+! forced 29.Rxe1 dxe1=Q#, a double hit on the back rank.

review.turning_point: 16.Ne5?? left the bishop on e2 free to take, and 16...Bxe2! gave you a fork that won material.
review.focus: At 15...Bg4? you let White play 16.Ne5; 15...a5 was the calmer way to keep your pieces coordinated.

review.headline: A smooth Petrov where you punished two inaccuracies

sections.text: You met 3.d3 with ...d6 and ...Bg4. White traded pieces with 6.Bxf6 Bxf6 and 9.Bxe6 fxe6, and the position was level. You castled and played 12...d5 to take space.
White's 14.Ng3? was the first slip, and 14...e4! was the right reply. 15.dxe4 dxe4 and your pawn on e4 attacked the knight on f3, a nice central break.
16.Nf5? made things worse for White. You took with 16...exf3!, and after 17.Qxf3 Re8+ 18.Ne3 Ne5 19.Qf4 Bg5 you were clearly better at about +5.
20...Kh8?! was the only inaccuracy, since 20...Nxc4 was a discovered attack from the knight that would have kept you at +8.8. White resigned soon after anyway.

review.turning_point: 16...exf3! won a knight after 16.Nf5?, taking you from +2.7 to +5.2.
review.focus: At 20...Kh8?! you stepped away from a strong move; after a check like 20.Qc4+, look at captures such as 20...Nxc4 first.

review.headline: A comeback win after a bad opening idea, finished with a clean mate

sections.text: In the Caro-Kann Classical you played 7.Ne5?! and 8.Bg5?!, then 10.Bh5??, which was a blunder that dropped you to -2.0. 10.h4 was the safer move. Black replied 10...Bxh5?, though 10...Nxh5 was stronger.
After 11.Nxh5!, the sequence 12.Bxe7 Qxe7 13.Qxh5 Qb4+ 14.c3 Qxb2 left you a pawn or two down, and 15...Qxc3 took more. You stayed in the game with 16.Qg4?! and 17.Rac1 rather than falling apart.

Black blundered with 19...Qe8?, and 20.Rg3! was an excellent answer. 21.h4? was less accurate, but 21...h5?? was a big mistake, and 22.Qxh5! was exactly right. 23.Qg5? and 23...f6? gave you another chance.
The finish was sharp: 25.Nxg6 Rg8?? was met by 26.Ne7+!, a discovered check from the rook on g3, and 27.Nxg8 won material. 39.Ra4# finished the job.

review.turning_point: 26.Ne7+! was a discovered check from the rook on g3 that won a rook, after Black's 25...Rg8??.
review.focus: 10.Bh5?? was the move that put you in trouble; before placing a bishop on h5, check whether Black can simply take it, as with 10...Bxh5.

review.headline: A lucky escape: you gave up a knight and still won in 14

sections.text: This game has the same early mistake as many Petrov players make. 3...Nxe4?? lost a knight for a pawn to 4.Nxe4, when 3...Nc6 was the safe move. You fell to -3.2 after only three moves.
White helped with 7.Nb3??, but you then played 7...d4?? and gave some of it back. 8.Nxe4 and 9.Bxc4 left you at nearly -6, and 10.d3 and 11.Qh5+ g6 kept you under pressure.
White then lost the thread. After 12.Qf3 fxe4, 13.O-O?? was a blunder and 13...exf3! won the queen, taking the evaluation to +4.2.
14.Re1?? finished it, because 14...Qxe1# was mate on the back rank.

review.turning_point: 13.O-O?? let you play 13...exf3!, winning the queen and swinging the game from -3.8 to +4.0.
review.focus: 3...Nxe4?? and 7...d4?? are the two moves to review; both left a piece loose, so ask what White's next capture does before pushing.

review.headline: A wild Two Knights attack that you won despite blundering the advantage

sections.text: In the Two Knights you played 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 b5 and went for 6.Bxb5?!, a sharp gambit-style idea. 6...Qxd5 7.c4?! allowed 7...Qxg2, and the game got messy.
8.Bxc6+?? was a blunder, since 8.Qf3 was better. Luckily for you, Black replied 8...Bd7??, when 8...Qxc6 was stronger, and the evaluation flipped to +7.2.
You then missed the best move again. 9.Bxa8?? was inaccurate, because 9.Bxg2 won the queen. You still stayed ahead, and kept the game going with 10.Rg1 and 11.Nf3.
12.d4?? was one more miss, as 12.Rxg4 was better. But Black's 14...Ng4?? was worse, and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 8...Bd7?? gave you +7.2 after your own 8.Bxc6+?? blunder, so Black's mistake rescued you.
review.focus: At 9.Bxa8?? you grabbed a rook instead of the queen; 9.Bxg2 was the right capture, so always compare captures by value.

review.headline: A tidy London Defense where White hung a piece

sections.text: Against the London you answered with the solid ...d5, ...e6 and ...Bd6, then 4...Nf6 and 5...Ne4. 6.Bxd6 cxd6 gave White the bishop pair but left you with a sound pawn structure.
7.Bd3 Qb6 hit the b2 pawn, and 8.b3 Nc6 added pressure on d4. These were natural moves and kept you active.
White then blundered with 9.Ng5??, attacking your knight on e4 but leaving the knight on g5 unprotected. 9...Nxg5! simply won it, taking you to about +4.4.
White resigned immediately. With no real errors, you played a very clean game.

review.turning_point: 9.Ng5?? left a knight undefended, and 9...Nxg5! took it for free.
review.focus: No mistakes to fix. A good habit shown by 9...Nxg5 is checking what the opponent's last move leaves undefended.

review.headline: A bumpy Scandinavian where your endgame technique made the difference

sections.text: In the Scandinavian you played 4.Nge2 and 5.g3?!, which was a reasonable approach. 5...Nd5? was a mistake by Black and 6.Bg2! was the right reply, and 7.dxc3 left you comfortable.
You then missed some chances. 8.O-O? let Black off the hook, because 8.Bxb7 was stronger. 10.Re1? missed 10.Nxc6, and 12.Be3?! and 15.b3?! let the evaluation drift towards equal.

20.Qh6?? was the biggest error, dropping to -2.0. But Black replied 20...Qd5??, where 20...Qxc2 was the move. After 21.Qg7 Rdd8?? you found 22.Qxf7!, which won material and brought the game back to +3.0.
The ending was handled well: 28.Re7, 29.Rxd5 and 30.Rxh7 ran down Black's pawns, though 36.f5? gave some back. You queened with 48.h8=Q and mated with 58.Qxb3#.

review.turning_point: 22.Qxf7! punished 21...Rdd8?? and returned you to a clear advantage after your 20.Qh6?? error.
review.focus: 20.Qh6?? is the move to study; when your queen goes deep, 20.Qe3 kept things safe and avoided losing the c2 pawn.

review.headline: A messy Petrov full of blunders that you won with one big tactic

sections.text: White chose 3.b3 against the Petrov, an unusual try. You took 3...Nxe4, and after 5.Qxe5+ Qe7?! the queens came off with 7.Qxe7+ Bxe7. The position was level.
White overextended on the kingside with 10.h4 and 11.h5. 11...Bxh5 won a pawn, and 12.g4?? was a blunder that 12...Bxg4! punished.
16.Be2?? was another mistake, and 16...Nxe2+! was a great reply. You were up about +2.4, but 21...Ng4?? gave it all away, followed by 22...Rfe8??, which left a piece to be won.
White returned the favour, and at the end 25.Rgh2?? allowed 25...Nxh2! and 26.Rxh2 gxh5 27.Rxh5 f6 28.Rh8+ Kxh8 won easily.

review.turning_point: 25.Rgh2?? allowed 25...Nxh2!, winning material and ending the game.
review.focus: 21...Ng4?? and 22...Rfe8?? let a clearly winning position slip; 21...Rfe8 was the safe move that kept your pieces protected.

review.headline: A Philidor where you built a solid edge, then lost your queen in a time scramble

sections.text: This was a Philidor that you played sensibly: 3.Bc4, 4.d3 and 5.O-O, then 7.Bg5 and 9.Bxe7 to remove Black's dark-squared bishop. Black's 12...Nd4 was a slip, and you answered it correctly with 13.Nxd4.
You then improved steadily with 17.Nb4, 20.Re2 and 22.Rae1, doubling rooks on the e-file, and stood around +0.9. That was good, purposeful play.

The first real damage came at 24.Ne3, which swapped off your useful knight and dropped the evaluation from +1.0 to -0.4; 24.d4 kept more tension. After 31.b4 Black's queen took a pawn with 31...Qxb4, and you were slipping again.
Black then blundered with 33...Qxc4, and 34.Qxh5 left you clearly better at +2.2, although 34.e6 was stronger. You held a +2 to +3 position for a long stretch.
With the clock low, 46.Qd4 and then 47.Qxa4 undid it all. 47...bxa4 took your queen, the evaluation went to -7.0, and the game ended on time soon after.

review.turning_point: 47.Qxa4 walked the queen onto a square where 47...bxa4 simply captured it, turning a clearly better position into a lost one.
review.focus: When you are ahead and short of time, play safe moves and check every capture for a recapture; 47.Qxa4 needed one look at the b5 pawn, and 46.Qf3 would have kept your advantage.

review.headline: A quiet Van't Kruijs where White's early queen and a bad knight capture handed you the game

sections.text: After 1.e3 e5, White brought the queen out with 2.Qh5. Your 2...d6 was a small slip, since 2...Nc6 defends the e5 pawn and develops at the same time, but you recovered quickly with a sensible setup of 3...g6, 4...Nf6 and 5...c6.
The game turned on 7.Nxd6+, where White gave a knight for a pawn. You took it with 7...Qxd6 and the evaluation jumped to about +5. From there you only had to play simply, and you did.

You kept trading into an easier position with 12...Nxd3 and 13...Qxd3, then 15...Bxe5 and 19...Nxd5, which swapped queens. Every exchange took away White's chances to complicate, and you stayed at +6 or better.
In the last phase your knight picked up pawns with 21...Nxa2, 23...Nxd3 and 24...Nxe1, and the rook finished with 29...Rd1#. A clean, accurate win.

review.turning_point: 7.Nxd6+ was a blunder, and 7...Qxd6 was the only reply you needed to take control.
review.focus: Your one inaccuracy was 2...d6; against an early queen sortie like 2.Qh5, develop with a threat, as 2...Nc6 does, instead of a quiet pawn move.

review.headline: A Philidor where you broke open Black's weakened kingside and finished with a rook invasion

sections.text: You went for the Italian-style setup with 3.Bc4 and 4.Nc3. After Black's 4...Be6, 5.Bb3 was the one inaccuracy: 5.Bxe6 would have damaged Black's pawn structure, while 5.Bb3 allowed 5...Bxb3 6.axb3 and a calmer game.
Black then weakened the kingside with 7...h6 and 9...g5. You reacted well: 8.d4, 9.Be3 and 10.dxe5 opened the centre, and after the trades on e5 you had the better position at about +2.6.
12.Qh5 put the queen on the weakened squares, and the pressure told. You won a pawn with 17.Qxh6, and the evaluation climbed to +3.9 after 17...Qg7.
The decisive blow was 21.Rd7, a rook on the seventh rank, followed by 22.Rxb7. When Black stepped 22...Bb4, 23.Rxb4 won a bishop, and 24.Qxe6 ended the game.

review.turning_point: 17.Qxh6 cashed in Black's loosening pawn moves and started the run of captures that decided the game.
review.focus: At 5.Bb3 you retreated the bishop into a trade; 5.Bxe6 was the more testing choice because it left Black with a worse structure.

review.headline: A game that ended on the clock before the opening was finished

sections.text: This one was over before it began: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d6 3.Nf3 Nd7, and then your clock ran out. The result was a loss on time after only three moves each.

On the board there is nothing to criticise. You took the centre with 1.e4 and 2.d4, developed with 3.Nf3, and stood a little better at +0.6 or so after 3...Nd7. Black's 2...d6 was a slightly odd way to go with the c6 pawn.

Because it was a clock loss and not a chess loss, the lesson is practical. Check that you are at the board and ready as soon as a game starts, since a flag this early gives away a perfectly good position.

review.turning_point: There was no turning point on the board; the game ended on time right after 3...Nd7.
review.focus: Nothing to fix in the moves of 3.Nf3 and the opening, so the work here is simply to be present and watching the clock from the first move.

review.headline: A Petrov where you stayed patient, punished a wandering knight and finished with a tactical flourish

sections.text: White chose the quiet 3.d3 against your Petrov, and you answered with a solid 3...d6. After 4.Bg5 Be7 5.Bxf6 Bxf6 you were fine, and 7...Bg4 followed by 9...Bxe2 traded off a good White bishop.
Things got harder after 12...d5 and 13.exd5 cxd5. White played the centre well with 15.Qe3 and 16.Qxb6 Nxb6, and by 17.dxe4 dxe4 the evaluation was around +2 in White's favor.

Then White blundered with 20.Nc7 and you found 20...Re7!, after which 21.Nxa6 bxa6 left you better in material. Your one real mistake came at 23...Bxc3, which let the advantage drop from +4.5 to +0.5; 23...Re7 was the stronger move.
White erred again with 25.Rxe4, and 25...Nd2! forked the rooks on e4 and f1. After 26.Rd1 Nxe4 you grabbed the rook and the finish was clean.

review.turning_point: 20.Nc7 was White's decisive error, and 20...Re7! exploited it to swing the game by about three pawns.
review.focus: At 23...Bxc3 you traded away your advantage in one move; before a capture ask what the recapture 24.Nxc3 does, and prefer a quiet improving move such as 23...Re7.

review.headline: A French Knight Variation where an early queen trip to e5 ran into trouble

sections.text: After 3.exd5 exd5 you played 4.Qe2+ and set up with 5.Nc3, 6.d4 and 7.Bg5. That is a reasonable plan, although 4.Qe2+ gave Black a comfortable game and the evaluation was already about -0.6.
The decisive mistake was 9.Qe5. After 8...Bb4, the queen on e5 is easily harassed, and 9...Re8 hit it at once. 9.O-O-O was the safer choice. The evaluation dropped to -3.4.

You then traded queen for rook with 11.Qxe8+ Qxe8+ and ended up behind in material after 12...Bxc3+ 13.bxc3, with your structure damaged too. You kept fighting well with 14.O-O, 15.Rfe1 and 16.Bb5 to build counterplay.

19.Bxd5 and 21.Bxa8 gave back some material, but Black always had a good answer, such as 21...Nxc2 and 22...Nxe1. 25.Re8 and 26.Rxg8+ finished the attack, but by then Black was well ahead and resigned the game to you only after 28.Ne7+.

review.turning_point: 9.Qe5 put the queen on an exposed square where 9...Re8 gained time and swung the evaluation by almost three pawns.
review.focus: Before moving the queen forward as in 9.Qe5, ask which rook or minor piece can attack it next; 9.O-O-O kept the game balanced.

review.headline: A wild Mieses game where you were ahead in the middle, then gave it back and ran out of time

sections.text: You met the Reversed Rat with 1...e5 and 2...d5, but a few quiet inaccuracies followed: 4...Bh5?!, 6...Nf6?! and 7...Bd6?!. White pushed on with 8.h4 and 9.f4, and after 9...Qd7? you were slightly worse.

The game came alive after 12.b4, 13.b5, 14.Bd2 and 15.Rb1, all inaccurate by White. Your moves 12...Ng4, 13...Ba3 and 14...Bb2 were also errors, so the evaluation kept bouncing, but 15...Bxc3 16.Bxc3 Nxe3! was a good shot: the knight forked the queen on d1 and the rook on f1.
By 20.g4 you were doing well at +3.4, but 20...Be6 let it drop to +0.4, and then 22...Qxf5 dropped it to -5.0. After 23.Bg4, 23...Qxg4+ 24.Nxg4 gave up the queen for a bishop.
You kept fighting with 24...d4 and 25...e3, but White was clearly better and the clock ran out around 35.Qa6.

review.turning_point: 22...Qxf5 recaptured on f5 without noticing that 23.Bg4 would attack the queen, turning a promising position into a lost one.
review.focus: At 22...Qxf5 you recaptured automatically; 22...d4 kept the pressure, so before each recapture look for a bishop or knight that can hit the queen.

review.headline: A Petroff-style gambit that turned into a kingside attack and an elegant mating finish

sections.text: After 1.e4 Nf6 you played 2.Nf3, which allowed 2...Nxe4 and a pawn lost; 2.e5 was the more testing way to meet Alekhine's Defence. Black was comfortably ahead (-1.4) after 7.Nc3 Bb4.

You fought back sensibly. 8.O-O-O and 9.bxc3 opened the b-file for your rook, and 10.Ne5 Nxe5 11.dxe5 gave you a pawn on e5 that cramped Black. Then Black wandered with 14...a4?, and 15.Qe4! found the right square for the queen.
Black's 16...h5?? was a blunder and 17.g4! was the strongest reply, ripping open the kingside. 17...f6?? then lost by force.
You missed the quickest win at 18.gxh5, because 18.Qxg6+ Kh8 19.Qh7# was available at once, but the attack was so strong that it still ended with 19.Qh7#.

review.turning_point: 17.g4! opened the kingside against Black's weakened pawns, and 16...h5 followed by 17...f6 left no defence.
review.focus: At 18.gxh5 you took a pawn when 18.Qxg6+ Kh8 19.Qh7# was mate; always check forcing moves against the king first.

review.headline: A crushing Philidor win that was thrown away by stalemate on the last move

sections.text: You played the opening well. After 3.d4 and 4.dxe5, you won a pawn, and 6.Bb5, 7.Nc3 and 8.Bf4 developed quickly. Black's king went to the queenside with 7...O-O-O, and you were at +2.7.
Your attack kept growing: 10.Qd3 Nxb5 11.Nxb5 Qb6 12.Qc4+ Kb8 13.O-O-O left you at about +4.5. Then 14.Bxd6+ was a blunder that dropped the evaluation to -0.5, since 14.Nxd6 kept the win simple.
Luckily Black blundered even more with 16...Nf6, and you took full advantage with 17.Rxb6!. After that you were up around +9, and the rest of the game was a technical win.
Sadly it did not end that way. After many accurate moves, 51.g6 left Black with no legal move and the game was drawn by stalemate. 51.Qe7 kept the win going.

review.turning_point: 51.g6 stalemated the Black king on the very move the win was within reach.
review.focus: On 51.g6 you gave Black no moves at all; whenever the enemy king is nearly boxed in, count its legal moves before you play, as 51.Qe7 showed.

review.headline: A Three Knights Petrov where an early knight grab put you behind for good

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3, you grabbed a pawn with 3...Nxe4. That was the decisive error: 4.Nxe4 simply won the knight back and left you a piece down. A move like 3...Nc6 would have kept the game balanced.
You fought on with 4...d5, 5...e4 and 6...c5, trying to harass White's knights. White handled it calmly with 5.Nc3, 6.Nd4 and 7.Nde2, and 8.Nxe4 took another pawn.
9...f5 and 10...fxe4 got some material back, but 11...Bf5? and 13...Qh4? were mistakes. 13...Qf7 would have held the evaluation near -3, while 13...Qh4 slipped to -6.0.
From there White simply collected material with 15.Bxb7 and 17.Bxa8, and your game ended on time after 22.Qxg3.

review.turning_point: 3...Nxe4 grabbed a pawn but allowed 4.Nxe4, which left you a piece down for most of the game.
review.focus: After 3.Nc3 look at what is defended before you capture; 3...Nxe4 failed to 4.Nxe4, so a developing move such as 3...Nc6 was needed.

review.headline: A Franco-Sicilian where 4.d5! punished an early slip and the attack finished with a queen mate

sections.text: Black's 3...e6? in the Sicilian was inaccurate, and you found the strongest reply: 4.d5!. After 4...exd5 5.exd5 Nce7, your pawn on d5 cramped Black, and 6.d6 pushed it deeper into their position.
You kept the initiative with 7.Qe2+ and 9.Bg5, and 10.Bxf6 gxf6 wrecked Black's pawns. A few moves were a touch loose (11.Nh4?!, 12.Qb5+?! and 14.Qd4?!), but your edge stayed above +3 throughout.
Black's 18...Be6? was a mistake, and 19.Qxb7 was the one real inaccuracy on your side, since 19.Qxa5 would have won more material. Still, you were at +4.0, and 20.Qf3 and 21.O-O stayed on track.
You finished with a flourish. 27.Rxe4+! fxe4 28.Qxe4+ regained the exchange, and 29.Qxc2 left you up a huge amount. 33.Qd8# ended the game.

review.turning_point: 4.d5! gave you a lasting space advantage, and Black never got out of the bind.
review.focus: At 19.Qxb7 you took a pawn when 19.Qxa5 was stronger, so after each queen capture look for captures that win bigger material first.

review.headline: A long Danish Gambit where you swindled your way from a worse game to a pawn-ending win

sections.text: You took the gambit pawn with 2...exd4, but 4...d6?!, 7...Bg4?! and 9...Bh5?! left you a bit worse. After 10.Nxe5 Bxe2 11.Qxe2 dxe5 and 12...cxd5?! the evaluation was around -2.
White's 14.exd5?? and 15.b3?? gave you chances. Unfortunately 14...Qxd5, 15...O-O-O and especially 17...Qc6 let them slip away again, and by 21...Qb5 you were at -6.0.
Then White blundered back. 22.bxc5 allowed 22...Qxb2!, and 23.Qd6+ Ka8! and 26.cxb7+ Qxb7! kept you in the game. Resourceful defending.

A pawn ending arose after 42.Rxa2+ Kxa2!, which equalised. At move 51, White's 51.Kg3?? lost the opposition, and 51...Ke6! began the winning king march. You promoted with 71...g1=Q+ and finished with 83...Qh1#.

review.turning_point: 42.Rxa2+ Kxa2! led to a pawn ending where 51.Kg3?? by White let your king and pawns decide.
review.focus: At 17...Qc6 you stepped away from 17...Qe6 and fell from -0.6 to -4.9; keep your queen safe and centralised before launching your own attack.

review.headline: A wild Mason Attack where you collected material early, then lost the thread under time pressure

sections.text: White opened with 1.f4 and 3.g3, and 4.Nc3? allowed 4...cxd4!, winning a pawn. You also played 5...Nc6 sensibly, and the game was fine for you through 8.Ne4.
9...Qa5+ was the first big error. 9...Bf5 would have been safe, while the queen check lost a lot of ground after 10.Bd2 and 11.hxg4.

You then had a spectacular chance with 12...Nbxc2+, which forked the king on e1 and the rook on a1, but 12...Nxg2+ was the stronger version. White's 16.Kf3?? was a blunder, and 16...fxe4+ and 17...Qc6+ put the king in danger of a skewer.
With the clock running down, 18...Qb5+ missed 18...Qxg2, 19...Qc4 and 20...d3+ made it worse, and the game ended on time after 22.Kf2.

review.turning_point: 18...Qb5+ gave up the chance to take the bishop with 18...Qxg2, and the position never recovered.
review.focus: At 9...Qa5+ you checked without a follow-up; 9...Bf5 kept your pieces developed, so ask what the check achieves before playing it.

review.headline: A short Giuoco Pianissimo where a pawn push on the kingside lost quickly

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 you played 2...Bc5, which allowed White to pressure your f7 square. 3.Bc4 was not the best, and you answered with the good move 3...Nc6!. Then 4.d3 g5 was where the problem began.
4...g5?? was a blunder that loosened your kingside. 5.Nxg5 took a pawn, and 5...Nd4 made it worse as 6.Bxf7+ followed. 4...Nf6 was simple and sound.
7...Qe8 was the final error: 8.Bxe8 took the queen and you resigned. After 7.O-O you were already worse, so a defensive move such as 7...h6 was needed.

review.turning_point: 4...g5 weakened the king and gave White an easy attack that you could not recover from.
review.focus: At 4...g5 you pushed a pawn in front of your king in the opening; 4...Nf6 develops a piece and keeps the king safe.

review.headline: A McConnell Defense where you won the queen early, then lost your own in a time scramble

sections.text: Black's 2...Qf6 invited trouble, and you found the right replies: 3.Nc3!, 4.Nd5 and 5.d4!. By 7.Bb5 your lead was +4.6, and 8.Nxb6 won Black's queen for a knight.
You kept the attack going with 9.Ne5 and 10.Nxf7, and 11.Bxc7 was greedy but still left you clearly ahead. 12.Qf3+ and 13.Bg3 were slightly loose, but Black's 17...Kf8 let 18.Bd6+! keep you winning.
After 20.Qe3+ and 21.Rhe1 you were at +5.8, but your play got careless. 22.Re2 and 23.Bb5 gave Black time, and 24.Qf3?? was a blunder that dropped you from +3.2 to -1.0; 24.Qf4 was the move.
Then 25...Bxa1 was a mistake by Black, but you replied with 26.Qa3+, which simply lost the queen to 26...Rxa3. 26.Qf4 would have kept the game alive.

review.turning_point: 24.Qf3 gave up a winning position, and 26.Qa3+ then finished the job by dropping the queen.
review.focus: At 24.Qf3 and 26.Qa3+ you rushed your queen moves; when you are far ahead, slow down and check what each of your pieces can be captured by.

review.headline: A Danish Gambit where an early knight move left g7 weak and a tempting capture on d3 allowed mate

sections.text: You accepted the Danish with 2...exd4 and 3...dxc3, then traded with 5...Bxc3. That is a sound way to meet it, but 6...Nc6?? was a big slip: 6...Nf6 was needed, because 6...Nc6 left the g7 pawn hanging to 7.Bxg7.
White missed it with 7.Nf3, and you found 8...O-O! after 8.Bd3, castling to safety. 9...d6 and 10...Bg4 followed sensibly, and the evaluation was close to level.
After 11...Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Ng6 13.Qg3, 13...Nge5? was an inaccuracy; 13...Qh4 was better. It put your knight in front of g7, where it blocked the long diagonal of the bishop on c3.
14...Nxd3 looked tempting because it attacked the rooks on c1 and e1, but the knight left e5 and 15.Qxg7# was mate. 14...Qf6 was the safe move.

review.turning_point: 14...Nxd3 hit two rooks but removed the knight that was shielding g7, which allowed 15.Qxg7#.
review.focus: At 14...Nxd3 you went for a double attack without checking your own king; always ask what the moving piece was defending, and consider 14...Qf6 instead.

review.headline: A long rook ending where a single slip by White let your king win the rook

sections.text: You played the Anti-Torre accurately, with 2...Bg4, 3...Nc6 and 4...e5. The trades 6...Nxf3+, 7...Bxf3 and 10...Nxf6 simplified into a level position, and you stayed equal for a long time.
A series of trades followed, with 14...Nxe4, 17...Rxe4 and 20...Bxe3. After 22...Rxa2 and 24...Rxc3 you picked up pawns, and the ending was balanced.

Your one real error was 38...Re5, which dropped you from 0.0 to -5.2; 38...h4 was right. White missed the best reply, 39.f4+, which would have forked the king on g5 and the rook on e5. Instead 39.Rc4 let you off.
The decisive moment came at 65.Rc5+??, a blunder. 65...Kxc5! won the rook, and you converted patiently with your rook and pawns, ending with 85...Rf1#.

review.turning_point: 65.Rc5+ was a blunder, and 65...Kxc5! won a whole rook in a drawn ending.
review.focus: At 38...Re5 you put your rook where 39.f4+ could have attacked it with check; before placing a rook next to your king, look for pawn checks.

review.headline: An Italian where an early knight grab backfired, you swung the game, and then stalemated on the last move

sections.text: 4.Nxe5 was a blunder in the Two Knights: 4...Nxe5 left you a piece down, and 4.Ng5 was the main line. You recovered with 5.Bb3 and 6.d4!, which forked the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5.

Black erred with 5...Bc5 and 7...Qe7, and 8.Qe2 was a slip because 8.O-O was better. After 11.f5 Qxe2+ 12.Kxe2 the queens came off, and Black's 12...Nf4+?? gave you the chance to play 13.Bxf4; 13.Kf3 missed it.
You did well after that: 15.Rxd5!, 20.Rxe8+ and 21.Bh6! kept you around +4. 28.h4 was a blunder that dropped you to -1.9, and Black took advantage with 28...Rxd2 and 30...Rxg2+.
Black missed 34...g5 and played 34...d5, and you slowly won back control, reaching +7.4. But 57.Kxf7 left Black with no legal move, a stalemate. 57.Ke7 kept the win.

review.turning_point: 57.Kxf7 stalemated the Black king when 57.Ke7 would have kept a winning endgame.
review.focus: On 57.Kxf7 you were low on time and captured the last pawn; in king and pawn or bishop endings, count the enemy king's legal moves before taking the final pawn.

review.headline: A Vos Gambit where a quiet pawn move allowed White to win a pawn and you resigned early

sections.text: You met 1.d4 with 1...e5?!, a gambit, and 2.Nf3 was actually not White's best because 2.dxe5 was stronger. Your best answer was 2...e4, with a good game.
2...d6?? was the error that cost you: 3.dxe5 took a pawn, and the evaluation dropped to -1.6. 3...Qe7?! then put the queen on an awkward square.

After 4.Bg5 f6 5.exf6 Nxf6, you were behind by a pawn or two with development roughly equal, at -2.2. That is not lost, but you resigned after 6.Nc3, so you never found out how much counterplay there was.

review.turning_point: 2...d6 gave White an easy capture on e5 instead of keeping the pawn with 2...e4.
review.focus: At 2...d6 you defended the e5 pawn too late; after a gambit pawn is offered, 2...e4 kept the extra pawn and gave you a lead.

review.headline: A Petrov where a queen move on the e-file gave White time and you were pushed back

sections.text: You played the Petrov correctly: 2...Nf6, then 4...Nxe4 after 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3. White's 5.d4 and 6.h3 are normal, and 5...Bg4 6.h3 Bh5 was fine too.

7...Qe7 was the blunder. It dropped the evaluation from -0.7 to -2.8 because the queen and knight ended up awkwardly on the e-file once the rook arrived. 7...d5 was the right way to challenge White's centre.
After that 9...c6 and 10...Nd7 gave White time, and 10.Re1 and 11.cxd5 cxd5 12.Nc3 built more pressure. 13.Qa4+ and 14.Bb5 ended the game when you were at -6.6.

review.turning_point: 7...Qe7 put the queen on the e-file in front of White's pieces and let White take over the centre.
review.focus: At 7...Qe7 you stepped into the e-file; in the Petrov, challenge the centre with 7...d5 before moving the queen.

review.headline: A winning attack thrown away by two careless moves

sections.text: This started as a model Italian. After 4.c3 h6 you took the centre with 5.d4, recaptured with 6.cxd4, and developed smoothly with 7.Nc3, 8.O-O and 9.Re1. By 9...Bg4 you were about +1.4 with a healthy centre and nothing to worry about.

10.d5 was the first slip. It shut the centre and let the black knight hop to d4, and the evaluation fell from +1.4 to -0.7. The sharper idea was to open the position while Black's king was still in the middle.

Black missed 10...Bxf3 and played 10...Nd4, and after 11.Be2 the move 11...O-O was a big error. You found 12.Nxd4, a discovered attack: the knight leaves f3 and your bishop on e2 suddenly looks at the bishop on g4. After 12...Bxd4 13.Bxg4 Nxg4 14.Qxg4 you were about +5 and a clear three points up in material.

Then 15.Bd2 threw it all away, dropping the evaluation from +5.1 to -2.1. 15...Bxf2+ was a fork of your king on g1 and rook on e1, and it also gave a discovered attack on your knight on c3 from the queen on f6. You held on with 16.Kh1, but 20.Nxe4 walked into 20...Qf1+, which the engine says leads to a forced mate. 20.h3 was needed.

review.turning_point: 15.Bd2 turned +5.1 into -2.1 by allowing 15...Bxf2+, a fork of king and rook.
review.focus: Before every move in a winning position, ask what the opponent's most forcing reply is. At move 15, 15.Be3 was safe, while 15.Bd2 allowed 15...Bxf2+.

review.headline: Steady play and a knight-and-rook finish that ends in mate

sections.text: Your opponent chose the unusual Carr Defense, 1...h6 and 2...g6, and you handled it with simple principles: 3.Bc4, 4.d4, 5.Nc3 and 6.Bf4 gave you a big centre and active pieces. 8.d5 cleverly chased the knight to b4, though 9.Qd2?! and the trade after 9...Nxd3+ 10.cxd3 took some of the shine off.

Then Black stumbled with 12...Rc8, which pushed the evaluation to +4.2 because 12...Bxd5 was the right capture. You grabbed the rook with 13.Rxc8, but it let the advantage drop to +1.6. 13.Bc7 was stronger, keeping everything under control while the Black king was stuck in the centre.

Even so you kept pressing with 14.Nxb6 and 15.Qb4. 17.Ne5 was another loosening move (+3.0 to +1.0; 17.Nd4 was cleaner), but Black answered with 17...Qd6, which let you play 18.Qxd6 and trade queens into a very comfortable position.
The finish is lovely. After 28.Nxf7 and 29.Nxh6+ your knights and rook swept the king upwards: 30.Nf5+, 31.Ne7+, 32.Rf5+, 33.h3+ and 34.Ng6+ forced the Black king to g3, and 35.Rf3# ended it.

review.turning_point: After 12...Rc8 you were at +4.2, but 13.Rxc8 let that fall to +1.6. You recovered when Black's 17...Qd6 allowed 18.Qxd6.
review.focus: At move 13 you grabbed the rook straight away. Spend a moment on quieter, stronger moves such as 13.Bc7 before you cash in a capture.

review.headline: A messy win where both sides gave the game away

sections.text: A Petrov Three Knights where you traded off the light bishops with 4...Be6 5.Bxe6 fxe6. The recapture gave you the half-open f-file but doubled your e-pawns. You then went for kingside space with 8...h6, 9...g5 and 10...Nh5, which is ambitious but loosening, and the evaluation was near equal.

11...O-O and 12...Nd7 were both small mistakes (11...Nf4 and 12...Ng7 were better), and your king was getting airy. White could have punished you with 12.Nxe5, but 12.O-O? and 13.Nd2 let the pressure slip, though 13.Nd2 did open the queen's line toward your knight on h5.

That turned out to be a trap for you: 13...Qb6 dropped the evaluation from +0.5 to -5.0 and left your knight on h5 hanging. 13...Qe8 was the solid answer, keeping everything covered. White did not take it, and 14.b3 gave you the chance back.

You found the best reply with 14...Nf4!, and after 15.Bxf4 Rxf4 the knight on h5 was gone but the rook was active. 16...Rh4 was another wobble (16...Kg7 was safer). Even so, after 17.Qg6+ Kh8 18.Qxe6 White resigned. Take the win, but know it was a lucky escape.

review.turning_point: 13...Qb6 left your knight on h5 hanging and cost about five and a half pawns. White's 14.b3 handed the game back.
review.focus: At move 13 your knight on h5 was loose with the queen on d1 aiming at it. Before moving your queen, check what that piece was defending, then play 13...Qe8.

review.headline: A shaky opening, a long endgame and a win on the clock

sections.text: A normal Italian turned sharp at once: after 4.c3 Nf6 you went for 5.Nxe5, which the engine called a blunder (+0.2 to -3.3). It left you worse on material, and after 5...Nxe5 6.d4 The quiet 5.d3 and 6.O-O was the principled setup.

Black returned the favour. 6...Nxe4 was inaccurate (6...Nxc4 was better), 7...Qh4 gave away more, and the queens were soon traded with 10.Qe2 Qxe2+ 11.Kxe2. In the endgame 14.Kd1?! walked into 14...Rxe1+, a skewer and a back rank problem for your king, but Black's follow-up 15...Nxd2?? let you recover with 15.Kxe1 and 16.Bxd2.

You then outplayed Black from 17.Kf2 on, and 25.Rb7! and 26.Rxb5! were fine rook moves. The worst miss came at move 32. 32.Kg5 let the win slip, because 32.Ra8+ was a back rank mate: Rb8 33.Rxb8+ Kh7 34.Rh8#. At move 33 you missed the same idea again with 33.Kh6, when 33.Ra8+ was still winning.

After that the game drifted to a drawn bishop ending. You kept making safe moves such as 47.Bc7+ and 48.Bxa5, then shuffled the king between e3 and f2 until move 86, when Black ran out of time. A lucky win.

review.turning_point: 32.Kg5 missed a forced mate with 32.Ra8+, and 33.Kh6 missed it again.
review.focus: At move 32 your rook on a5 could check on a8 against a king with no escape squares. Always look at every check first, especially when the enemy king is boxed in on its back rank.

review.headline: A greedy bishop grab, then a wild finish that went your way

sections.text: A flexible English opening with 2.a3 and 3.b4 from White, and you answered it well: 2...d6, 4...Bf5, 5...Be7, 6...O-O and 8...c6 kept everything solid. 9...d5?! was a little ambitious and 10.c5 e4 cramped White's queen's bishop, but 11.Ne5 Nxe5 12.Bxe5 left you in a good position.

After 12.Bxe5 White had blundered (the evaluation went to +2.3 for you), but 12...Re8 let it slip back to -0.1. 12...exd3 was the right capture. After 13.dxe4 Nxe4 14.Nxe4 Bxe4 15.Bd4 the game was equal again.
Then you went pawn hunting: 15...Bxg2 dropped the evaluation to -2.4 and 16...Be4 to -5.5 after 16.Rg1. 15...Bf6 was the move, challenging the bishop on d4 and lining up the rook on a1 behind it.

White then went wrong with 17.Bxg7 (17.Rxg7+ kept the edge). You answered with the accurate 17...Bg6!, and 18.Bh5 blundered again. After 18...Kxg7! you were up material and the attack was over. 19.Qd4+ Bf6 20.Qf4 Bxa1 followed, and White resigned after 21.Bxg6 fxg6.

review.turning_point: 17...Bg6! and 18...Kxg7! punished two White errors in a row. Your own 15...Bxg2 had nearly lost you the game first.
review.focus: At move 15 you took a pawn with 15...Bxg2 and the bishop was trapped by 16.Rg1. Before grabbing a pawn with a bishop, check whether it can still get out.

review.headline: An aggressive pawn storm that left the pieces hanging

sections.text: Against the Caro-Kann you chose the sharp 3.Nd2 and 4.Ne2, followed by a pawn storm with 5.f3, 6.g4 and 7.h4. It was a bold plan, and Black helped with 7...dxe4, which pushed the evaluation to +3.5 for you.

Your recapture was the problem. 8.fxe4 took the advantage down to +1.4, when 8.h5 was stronger, hitting the bishop on g6 before Black could sort things out. Still, 12.e5! was a good reply to Black's 11...Qc7 blunder, and you were comfortably better at +2.1 to +2.6.

Then the game turned. 13.Bf4 was imprecise (13.e6 was stronger), and 14.Nd6+?! gave up your good knight for a bishop. 16.c4 dropped the evaluation to -2.1 because 16...Nxf4 traded off your bishop and left your d-pawn weak, and 16.Bd2 would have kept things together.

The decisive blunder was 18.c5. After 17...Qxd6 you had to look after the knight on f4, which 18.Qd2 would have done. 18.c5 left it hanging, and 18...Qxf4 left you four points down in material. Your king had no safe home after 19.Rf1 Qe3+, and 23.Rc1 Rd8+ ended the game.

review.turning_point: 18.c5 left your knight on f4 unprotected, and 18...Qxf4 left you far behind.
review.focus: On move 18 you pushed a pawn instead of securing the knight on f4. Before any pawn move, count your loose pieces and make sure each one is protected.

review.headline: A wild Petrov where your tactics held up and the king walk almost ruined it

sections.text: A Three Knights Petrov where White chose the sharp 4.Bb5+ and 5.Bc4. You pushed 5...d5 and after 6.exd5 cxd5?! 7.Bb3 d4? 8.Ng5 Qb6? you drifted into trouble, and by 10.Bxf7+ Kd8 11.Bc4 the engine liked White at about -2.0 for you.

Then White cracked. 13.Nxh8 was the wrong capture (13.Nxe5 was safer) and you found 13...Qxc4!. After 14.d3 Qg8 15.Bg5? Qxh8! and 16.Bxf6? gxf6!, you were right back in the game at +1.7. Nicely calculated.

But your king walk 21...Kc7?! and 22...Kb6?? was a blunder (+1.1 to -4.7). 22...Bd7 followed by 23.O-O was the safe route. After 23.Nxd6 Nb4 24.Nc4+ Ka7 you were in trouble, and only 33.Qe4 and 34.Ra1 gave you the game back (34.dxc4 was best).
After 34...Ba6 35.cxd4? Nxd4+! the check opened everything, and the finish was clean: 36.Kc3 Rc8+ 37.Qc6 Rxc6#.

review.turning_point: 34.Ra1 gave you a lifeline, and 35...Nxd4+! turned a lost position into a mating attack.
review.focus: At move 22 you walked the king forward with 22...Kb6. Keep your king covered when the opponent still has checks, and develop with 22...Bd7 first.

review.headline: A shaky opening that fell apart, saved by the clock

sections.text: A Queen's Gambit Declined where you played a slightly odd setup with 4...Nc6 and 5...Bd6?!. After 5.Bf4 Bd6?! 6.Bg5 h6 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 the position was still level, and 8.e3 e5? began your trouble by opening the centre before your pieces were ready.

9.Nf3? was a gift (the evaluation went back to +0.1 for you), but 9...e4 gave it right back (+0.1 to -2.1), and 10...Be6 slid to -5.7. 9...dxc4 and 10...dxc4 were the sensible ways to keep control of the centre.

White returned the favour with 11.f3, blowing a winning position (-5.7 to -0.1). Even so, 11.cxd5 would have been a fork of your bishop on e6 and knight on c6. 11...exf3 gave away some of the advantage (11...Qh4+ was stronger), and after 12.Nxf3 Bg4?! the position was roughly equal.

You then played 13...O-O? (13...dxc4 was better) and 14...Rfe8??, which dropped back to -2.9, with 15.cxd5 Ne7 leaving you worse. The game ended with a win on time after 15 moves, so take the point, but your development and centre play need work.

review.turning_point: 10...Be6 took the position to -5.7, but White's 11.f3 immediately gave the advantage back.
review.focus: At move 9 you pushed 9...e4 instead of taking on c4. Resolve centre tension (9...dxc4) before launching pawn advances.

review.headline: A king walk in the opening that ended the game in eight moves

sections.text: A very short game that began as a French-style structure after 1.d4 d5 2.e4 e6 3.e5. 3...f6?! was the first inaccuracy, because it weakened the e8-h5 diagonal and your king's cover.
After 4.Nf3 fxe5 5.Nxe5, 5...Nd7? was the next mistake (-0.6 to -2.0). 5...Nf6 would have kept the knight developed and the king safer, and the engine suggested 6.Be3 as White's best reply.

White then checked with 6.Qh5+, and 6...Ke7?? dropped the evaluation to -7.1. The king on e7 had no good squares and walked into trouble, whereas 6...g6 would have blocked the check. 7.Bg5+ was strong, and after 7...Kd6? a discovered attack followed, as your king stepping off e7 let the bishop on g5 hit your queen on d8.
8.Nf7+ ended it at -8.7. Early checks like 6.Qh5+ should always be met with a block rather than a king walk.

review.turning_point: 6...Ke7 moved the king into the centre and the game was effectively lost after 7.Bg5+.
review.focus: At move 6 you answered the check with 6...Ke7. Always look for a block (6...g6) before moving your king into the open.

review.headline: A chaotic Ruy Lopez Berlin that you out-blundered yourself in

sections.text: You chose the exchange line with 4.Bxc6 bxc6 and then 5.Nxe5?! Bd6 6.Nf3?!, which wasted time. Black answered with 6...Bf4, which the engine called a blunder, and you got a comfortable edge after 7.d3 Bxc1 8.Qxc1.

11.Qf4 and 12.d4 built a strong centre, and you held about +2.6 at 12...Qe7. Then 13.O-O-O was the first big slip (+2.6 to -1.0). 13.O-O was safer, and Black missed the right reply, 13...Nxf2, which would have forked your rook on d1 and h1. Instead 13...Ba6 gave you chances.

But 14.h3 threw them away (+4.3 to -1.4). 14.Qxg4 won material outright, since the knight on g4 was hanging. After 14...Nxf2 15.Na4 Nxh1 16.Rxh1 and 17.Nc5! you fought back well, and 24.Rf1 was a good defensive move.

Move 22 (22.Ng5) was another big miss, and 26.Rf2 and 27.e6 gave up the advantage again. After 30.Qxh6 Black could have tried 30...Qe1+, which would have been a back rank problem for your king, but you were already far behind. You played on to move 37 but lost on time while still worse.

review.turning_point: 14.h3 missed 14.Qxg4, which would have won a piece or more, and the whole game turned.
review.focus: At move 14 your queen could simply take the loose knight with 14.Qxg4. Before a quiet move, scan for undefended enemy pieces.

review.headline: A calm Petrov win after your opponent threw away the queen

sections.text: In the Petrov, Modern Attack, after 3.d4 exd4 4.c3?? was a mistake by White, because 4...Nxe4 was the best reply; 4...Nc6 only gave back some of your edge. After 5.cxd4 Nxe4 6.Bd3 d5 7.O-O, you developed with 7...Bg4?! and 8...Ng5 and the position was still pleasant.

9.Be2 was inaccurate from White (9.Qe1+ was stronger), but then 9...Qf6?? was your blunder (+1.7 to -3.8). After 10.Nxg5 Bxe2 11.Qxe2+ Be7 you were struggling. The engine's choice was the safe 9...Ne6.
You fought on with 13...Nxd4 and 15...Qf6, and White got greedy with 17.Qxb7 and the fatal 18.Qxc6, which lost the queen. You found the best reply, 18...Qxc6!, and the evaluation jumped to +5.4.
From there you converted: 22...Qxc6 and 24...Qxc1 traded off White's pieces, and the later pawn push 42...a5, 43...a4 and 44...a3 gave a clean win. White resigned after 48 moves.

review.turning_point: 18.Qxc6?? lost White's queen, and 18...Qxc6! made it a won game.
review.focus: At move 9 you played 9...Qf6, leaving the knight on g5 loose. Check that every piece is defended before you move the defender.

review.headline: A clean attacking win that pounced on a Black blunder

sections.text: A sharp opening where you traded the centre with 2.d4 and 3.dxe5, then 4.Bf4 d6 5.Bxe5?! dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8. 5.Nc3 would have been a little better, but forcing the queens off meant Black's king could not castle.

Black developed with 7...Bb4+ 8.c3 and then 8...Bc5?, a mistake that allowed 9.Nxe5!. The sneaky point was that 9...Bxf2+ lost to the simple recapture 10.Kxf2!, and you were already +5.1. Black's king stayed in the middle for the rest of the game.
After 10...f6 11.Nf7+ Ke8 12.Nxh8 you won the rook, and you kept it simple: 14.Nd2, 15.Be2, 17.Rad1 and 18.Rhe1 developed every piece. 19.Nxe4 and 20.Kxd1 traded off the rooks.

21.Nf6+! was a fine finishing blow: it was a discovered check from the rook on e1, and a fork of the king on e8 and knight on d5. After 22.Nxd5 you were about eight points up in material. Black ran out of time at move 23.

review.turning_point: 9.Nxe5! took advantage of 8...Bc5?, and 10.Kxf2! won material by force.
review.focus: Only one small slip: 5.Bxe5 gave up a good bishop for a knight and let Black recapture easily. 5.Nc3 was better.

review.headline: A reckless knight grab that you survived and then punished

sections.text: The King's Head Opening saw White play 2.f3 and 3.Ne2. You grabbed a pawn with 3...Nxe4?, which the engine called a blunder (+1.0 to -2.6). 3...d5 4.d4 was calmer. After 4.fxe4 Qh4+ 5.g3 Qxe4 the position was messy and White was better.

White kept the upper hand with 6.Rg1, 7.Bg2 and 8.Rf1, but you stayed active with 8...Qh5?! and 9...Qxh2. 12...Bh3?! and 13.Rf2 Bg2 14.Rxg2 Qh1+ looked risky, but 15.Rg1?? was a blunder (-4.9 to +0.4), and you spotted 15...Qxf3!.

Then you made your own mistake: 18...f6?? dropped the evaluation to -4.0 (18...Nc6 was stronger). But White missed that again with 21.Qd5? and 22.Bf4??, which you punished with 21...Re8! and 22...Rxe6!, bringing it back to +1.7.
23.Rd1 allowed 23...Qxc2!, and 24.Qxb7 ended it with 24...Qxe2#. Great persistence, but you owe your win to White's errors.

review.turning_point: 15.Rg1 let you win back the position with 15...Qxf3!. The game swung from -4.9 to +0.3.
review.focus: At move 3 you captured 3...Nxe4 without checking the reply. 3...d5 was a safe developing move. Check what a capture does for your king and development first.

review.headline: A good opening that unravelled on a loose knight

sections.text: Against the Hungarian Opening you played 1...d5, 2...e5 and 3...dxe4, then used the bishop with 5...Bc5 and 6...Qd4?!. White fell for it with 7.Be3?, and 7...Qxb2! took the pawn and left you comfortable (+1.9).
After 8.Nd2 Bxe3 9.fxe3 Qb6 you were better. 10...Ng4?! put a knight on the rim, and though 13...Be6?? was only a small slip (13...a5 was best), you were still ahead on the board at +0.4 to +2.2.

The real mistake was 14...Bxb3, which dropped the evaluation from +1.3 to -2.5. Your bishop on e6 had been guarding the knight on g4, and capturing with it removed that defender. 14...Nd7 would have kept the advantage. White returned the favour with 15.Qxg4??.
After 15.Qxg4 you needed 15...Bxc2, but 15...Qc3+?? and 16...Qxc2+?? (-4.1) followed. 16...Bxc2 was safer. 17.Rd2 Qxd2+?! 18.Kxd2 Bxa2 was a loss of material, and 19.Qc8+ Ke7 20.Qxh8 ended the game.

review.turning_point: 14...Bxb3 removed the defender of your knight on g4, and the game never recovered.
review.focus: At move 14 your bishop on e6 was guarding the knight on g4. Before a capture, ask what that piece is currently protecting.

review.headline: A sharp French that ended in a queen mate on h7

sections.text: A French-style opening where you played 4.e5?! and 5.c3, building a pawn chain. Black grabbed space with 5...a6 and 6...b5, and your 7.O-O, 8.cxd4 and 9.Nc3 got the pieces out smoothly. At 10.Be3 you were slightly better.

The turning moment was 12.Nxb5!. It looked like a sacrifice, but 12...axb5 13.Qxc6 left you up material and the queen landed in the middle of Black's position. 11.Qc2?! was a slight inaccuracy, but you used it well.
17.Bg5? was the only real mistake (+0.8 to -0.6). 17.a4 was the engine's choice. But Black answered 18.Nxg5 with 18...Nxd4, and then you played the strong 19.Qd3, threatening mate on h7.
Black replied 19...h6?? instead of 19...g6, and you finished with 20.Qh7#. Good vision to see the diagonal opened after the knight left f5.

review.turning_point: 19.Qd3 threatened mate on h7, and 19...h6?? allowed 20.Qh7#.
review.focus: 17.Bg5 was a mistake that swung the evaluation from +0.8 to -0.6. Look for a quiet improving move such as 17.a4 before trading your bishop.

review.headline: A brilliant attack and a loss in the endgame under time pressure

sections.text: Against the Hungarian Opening you set up 3...d4 and 4...f6, then developed with 5...Nc6 and 6...Bg4. 9...Bh3?? was the first mistake (+2.7 to +0.7), and 9...Nb4 was a better way to use the c2 weakness. Still you played a creative kingside attack with 10...g5, 11...h5 and 12...h4.

13...hxg3?! and 14.fxg3 Bxg2 gave you an initiative: 15.Kxg2 Qh3+ 16.Kg1 g4 17.Nh4 Ng6 18.Rxf6 Nxh4 19.gxh4 Rxh4 were all active moves, and the engine rated the game roughly even. 20...O-O-O?! gave White a small edge.

22...Be7? and 24...Rf8? both missed 22...Qxg3+ and 24...Qxg3+, the best way to keep an edge. Luckily White answered 25.Nxe5?? and you found 25...Qxg3+!, a fork of the king on g1 and knight on e5. After 26.hxg3 Rxe5 you were ahead.
Then 30...Rf8?? dropped the edge (30...Rxh1 was best), and with little time left 41...Rf7?? ended it. 41...Rxc2 was the better move. After 42.Rxf7 Nxf7+ 43.Kf6 Ne5? 44.Kxe5 you resigned.

review.turning_point: 41...Rf7?? under time pressure turned a balanced endgame into a loss.
review.focus: At move 22 you played 22...Be7, but the stronger 22...Qxg3+ was available. Check every check before you make a developing move.

review.headline: A comfortable edge thrown away in a long middlegame

sections.text: A Scandinavian where you traded queens with 4.Qe2 Qxe2+ 5.Ngxe2, then built a kingside attack with 9.Bf4, 11.h4, 12.h5 and 14.h6. After the exchanges 7.Bg2 Bxc3 8.dxc3 and 12...Nxf4 13.Nxf4 you were about +1.0 and White's king seemed safe.
15.Rh2? was a slightly passive choice, but you kept a plus with 16.Nd3, 18.Rxe5 and 19.Nxe5, and your position was about +2.3 at the best moment, after 23...Nf8. 24.Bh3 Bxh3 25.Rxh3 simplified.
26.Nf2? was the first big slip (+2.0 to +0.5). 26.Re3 was better. 28.Ng4? then lost a pawn after 28...Nxg5, and 29.Nf6+ Kf8 30.Rd3?? dropped the evaluation to -4.2. 30.Re3 was the right square.

34.Nxg6? (-3.4 to -5.5) was another miss: 34.Nc4+ was the better move. Black returned the favour with 34...Ne4??, but 37.Rd7?? ended any hope. After 37...Rg1+ 38.Rd1 Rxd1+ 39.Kxd1 Kxf4 you were lost and resigned a few moves later.

review.turning_point: 26.Nf2? and 28.Ng4? let a +2.0 position slip, and 30.Rd3?? finished the job.
review.focus: At move 28 you moved the knight with 28.Ng4 and lost the pawn on g5. After a long advantage, check every pawn and piece is protected before each move.

review.headline: A sharp sacrifice that Black failed to answer, ending in mate

sections.text: A Scandinavian where you built a good position with 4.d4, 5.Nf3, 6.Bc4, 7.O-O and 8.Re1, then used 9.Bf4 and 10.Bb3 to develop. Black pushed 9...b5 and 10...a5, and 12.Ba2 kept the bishop aimed at e6, with +2.3 after 12...Nbd7.

13.Qe2? was a small slip (+2.3 to +0.8). 13.d5 would have kept the pressure. Then 14.Bxe6?? was a blunder, going from +1.1 to -0.8, because 14.Rad1 was simply stronger. 14...fxe6 15.Qxe6 left you a point down in material.
Black answered with 15...Nb6??, which let the evaluation soar to +4.4. 15...Nf8 would have defended. You found the best reply with 16.Ne5!, threatening 17.Qf7#.
16...Bc8? (16...Rf8 was the only chance) lost at once, and you finished with 17.Qf7#. Well done to spot it, but 14.Bxe6 was not sound.

review.turning_point: 15...Nb6?? allowed 16.Ne5! and 17.Qf7# in two moves.
review.focus: 14.Bxe6 was a speculative sacrifice that the engine rated as a blunder. Before sacrificing, check whether a quiet move like 14.Rad1 keeps your edge.

review.headline: A shaky 1.e3 game where you recovered from an early slip and finished with a mating attack

sections.text: You met 1.e3 with 1...e5 and built a sound centre with 2...d5 and 3...e4. The trouble started at 5...Qa5+, which looked forcing but took you from +0.4 to -1.6. The calm 5...cxd5, with 6.Ne2 to follow, kept everything under control.

White returned the favour with 7.b3, a real blunder, and you found the best reply in 7...cxd5. You then developed sensibly with 8...Nf6, 9...Qd6 and 12...Nc6. After 13...Bxb4+ and 15...Qxb4+ White's king was uncomfortable, and 16.Rc3 was another inaccuracy. Your 16...Bxc6 put you clearly ahead at +2.3.

Then you slipped. 17...Bxa4 dropped the evaluation from +2.3 to +0.4, and 17...O-O was the safer move. White answered with 18.O-O, a blunder, instead of 18.bxa4, and after 18...Bb5 you were back at +4.3. With 19.Qb1 and 19...Bxe2 you were well ahead in material.
From there it was technique. 26.Rc8 and 26...Qxd2 started the finish, the checks after 28.Rc8+ drove the king forward, and the game ended with 32...Qe1#.

review.turning_point: 18.O-O was the decisive mistake. White could have played 18.bxa4 and stayed close, but after 18...Bb5 the evaluation jumped to +4.3 and never came back.
review.focus: Before 17...Bxa4 and 5...Qa5+, pause and ask what your opponent's best reply does. Both were tempting moves that gave away a good position, and quieter choices like 17...O-O were stronger.

review.headline: A Petrov-style game won by punishing early slips, with a few shaky moments of your own

sections.text: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 and 2...Nf6 3.Nc3 and 3...Bb4 you took on c3 with 4...Bxc3 and grabbed a pawn with 5...Nxe4. White replied with 7.Nxe5, which swung the evaluation to +2.1 for you. Unfortunately 7...Qe7 gave most of that back, and 7...O-O was the cleaner move.

The next mistake was 8...f6, taking you from +0.9 to -1.9. White missed the best reply 9.Qh5+ and played 9.Nf3, and you pounced with 9...Nxc3. That is a discovered attack: the knight leaves e4 and opens the e-file between your queen on e7 and White's queen on e2. After 10.Qxe7+ and 10...Kxe7 the queens were off and you were comfortably better.

White's pieces were passive, and you improved steadily with 13...Kf8, 14...Bf5 and 15...Nd7. 19.f4 was a mistake, but 19...Nxd2 let some of the advantage slip, from +3.7 to +1.4. The engine preferred 19...Ng3 followed by 20.f5.
Even so, White blundered again with 21.Bxg6, and 21...Nxf1 settled matters at +5.7. White resigned soon after.

review.turning_point: 9...Nxc3 was the moment. White had just missed 9.Qh5+, and your knight capture opened the e-file against the queens and turned a bad position into an advantage.
review.focus: Look at 7...Qe7 and 8...f6. In both positions castling with 7...O-O or 8...O-O was safe, while the queen move and the pawn move each cost you about two pawns of evaluation.

review.headline: A long, error-filled Chigorin game decided by one strong tactic and a clean endgame

sections.text: You opened with 1.Nc3 and 2.d4, aiming for a Chigorin-style setup. 5.Ba4 pinned the knight on c6 to the king, but with 6.Qf3 and 7.g4 it left you worse, down to -1.8. Black answered 7...Be4 instead of capturing on g4, and you took your chance with 8.Nxe4. Black's 8...dxe4 was inaccurate, and 11.g5 kept the initiative.

The middlegame was a rollercoaster. 16.Qe5 was a blunder that took you from +2.0 to -1.5, and 16.gxf6 was the safer idea. Black gave it straight back with 17...Rg8, and you stood at +4.4. Then 18.Rb1 threw it away again, because 18.Qxe6+ forked the king and rook. 19.Bd2 and 20.Rc1 were also errors.
Black's 20...Nxe3 helped you, but 21.Bxe3 was another slip, since 21.Qxe3 was stronger. After Black's 21...b4 you found 22.Rxc7!, and the queen trade with 23.Qxb5+ left you a long way ahead.
From there you converted patiently. Your king hunted pawns with 38.Kxb4 and 40.Kxb3, the b-pawn advanced with 42.b4 and 47.b8=Q, and you finished with 68.Qh8#.

review.turning_point: 21...b4 and your reply 22.Rxc7! decided it. After the swings of the middlegame, that was the one tactic that settled the evaluation near +5 for good.
review.focus: On 18.Rb1 you missed 18.Qxe6+, a fork of king and rook, and on 20.Rc1 you missed 20.Nf3. When the opponent's king is stuck in the centre, look at checks and captures before making a quiet move.

review.headline: A loose Center Game where you took a lead, wobbled, and won on time

sections.text: White opened with 1.e4 and 2.d4, and after 3.Qxd4, 3...Nc6 and 4.Qe3 you chose 4...b6. That cost you a little (from +0.3 to -1.0), and 4...Nf6 followed by 5.Nf3 was more natural. White then spent time with the queen via 6.Qf4 and 8.Qf3, while you developed with 5...Bc5, 6...Nf6, 7...Bd6 and 8...O-O.

White's 10.Bd3 was a blunder and 11.Bb5 made things worse, so you were at +2.1. You answered with 11...Ne5, a strong move that attacked the queen on f3, and after 12.Qe2, 12...Nxe4, 13.Nxe4 and 13...Bxe4 you had won a pawn.

Then came the slip. 14...f5 turned a healthy +2.5 into -0.3, and 14...Qf6 was the engine's choice. A bigger error followed with 16...Bf3, which took you from +0.7 to -5.4, where 16...Rc5 was the safer try.
The game ended with a win on time after 16 moves, but the board was no longer on your side at that point.

review.turning_point: 16...Bf3 was the decisive error. The engine wanted 16...Rc5, and instead the bishop move dropped the evaluation to -5.4.
review.focus: At 14...f5 and 16...Bf3 you played active moves without checking what they left loose. Before each forcing move, list which pieces become undefended, because both of these swung the evaluation by around three pawns.

review.headline: A smooth, accurate Zukertort where you punished one greedy capture

sections.text: This was a very clean game, with 96.1 accuracy. You played 1.Nf3 and 2.d4, set up the fianchetto with 3.g3 and 4.Bg2, and added 5.e3, 6.Nc3, 7.b3 and 8.Bb2. Nothing there asked Black a hard question, but everything was in the right place.

Black picked a fight with 8...Bb4 and 9...Ba5, and you answered with 9.a3 and 10.b4. The bishop on a5 was in trouble, and Black's 10...Nxb4 tried to rescue it but was a blunder at +2.9 for you. The engine suggested 10...Bb6 11.Ne2.
You found 11.axb4!, the best reply. It is a discovered attack: the rook on a1 now looks at the bishop on a5 while your b-pawn attacks it too. Black took 11...Bxb4 and you simply castled with 12.O-O.
You kept control with 13.Ne5 and 14.Rb1. After 14...Bxe5 and 15.dxe5, Black's 15...Ng4 only made things worse at +5.4. Your 16.Qxg4 left you with a decisive material edge, and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 11.axb4! was the key moment. Black's 10...Nxb4 had grabbed material, but your recapture opened the a-file and left the bishop on a5 hanging.
review.focus: There is little to fix here. If you want something to sharpen, 14.Rb1 was the one move that cost about half a pawn, so check whether a more direct developing move keeps the bigger edge.

review.headline: A Petrov where you struck with a discovered check, then survived a messy middlegame

sections.text: In the Petrov you played 3...d6 and 4...Nxe4 after White's 3.Nxe5. White then tried 5.Qf3, a mistake, and your 5...Qe7 was also inaccurate because 5...Ng5 was better. Still, 6.Bd3 was a blunder, and you found the best reply.
6...Ng3+ is a discovered check: the knight moves away and your queen on e7 gives check along the e-file to the king on e1. After 7.Be2 and 7...Nxh1 you were far ahead on material at +5.

Then you let it slip with 8...Be6, which dropped you from +3.5 to -1.2, and 8...Nc6 was the safe move. After 9.Nc3 you played 9...Bxc4, a blunder that went to -1.4, and 10.dxc4 handed you chances to recover. You kept finding good moves like 10...c6, 11...Nd7 and 12...Ne5.

15...O-O-O was a small slip, but White's 17.Bd4 allowed 17...Nxc4!, another discovered attack because your queen on e6 now hits the knight on e4. You finished with 20...Qxa2, 22...Qxf7 and 24...axb6, and White ran out of time in a lost position.

review.turning_point: 17...Nxc4! was the turning point. After a long stretch of mutual errors, the knight move unleashed your queen against the knight on e4 and put you back in control.
review.focus: Look at 8...Be6. You were already ahead at +3.5, but the bishop move swung things by almost five pawns. When ahead, spend a moment checking which of your pieces are loose.

review.headline: A Ware Defense you won by building a kingside attack after Black overpressed

sections.text: Black met you with the unusual 1...a5 and 2...b6, and you played a straightforward 2.d4, 3.Nf3 and 4.Bd3. 7.Bg5 pinned the knight on f6 against the queen, and 8.Nbd2 and 9.Nc4 brought the pieces into play. 9.Nc4 was a blunder at +1.1 to -0.6, and 9.Re1 was the quiet move.
Black replied with 9...b5, which was inaccurate, and you traded pieces with 10.Nce5, 12.Ng4 and 13.Bxe7. After 14.Qxg4 and 15.e5 you had more space, and 16.Qh3 and 17.Qh6 headed for Black's king.
The blunder came from Black: 21...a4 jumped the evaluation to +6.7 for you. You found the strongest idea, 22.Rh3!, which pins the c3 pawn to the queen on a3 and threatens 23.Qxh7+.
That sequence ended quickly with 23.Qxh7+, 24.Qh8+, 25.Qxb8 and 26.Rf1, and you finished with 27.Qxc7+ and 28.Rh8#.

review.turning_point: 21...a4 was the moment Black cracked. Your reply 22.Rh3! turned the pin on the third rank into an unstoppable attack.
review.focus: Revisit 9.Nc4. It looked active but dropped the evaluation to -0.6. Black's reply gave it back, but a quieter move like 9.Re1 would have kept your edge.

review.headline: A solid English opening spoiled by one careless capture

sections.text: You answered 1.c4 with 1...e5 and 2...Nf6, and built a solid setup with 3...d6, 4...Bg4, 5...Be7, 6...Nbd7 and 7...O-O. It was patient, and the evaluation stayed within half a pawn for a long time.

White expanded with 8.b4, 9.b5 and 10.a4, and you responded with 9...Qc7, 10...Rfe8 and 11...Nc5, a fine way to use the queenside gap. After the exchanges from 14.exd5 through 17...Rxc5 the position was a little worse for you at +1.1, but still very much alive.

18...Rc2 put your rook on the second rank, and 19...Bf6 was slightly inaccurate. White then played 20.d4, a mistake, and you replied with 20...exd4, a blunder. That pawn capture opened the e-file for a discovered attack from the queen on e3 to your rook on e8.
21.Qxe8# ended the game on the spot. The engine's alternative was 20...e4, followed by 21.b6, which would have kept you in it.

review.turning_point: 20...exd4 was the decisive move. Taking the pawn pulled it off the e-file and exposed your rook to the queen on e3, which led directly to mate.
review.focus: Before 20...exd4, check what the pawn was blocking. A capture that opens a line toward your own rook or king needs the same scrutiny as a move your opponent might make.

review.headline: An Italian where a bold knight sacrifice backfired, then a long fight you could not hold

sections.text: You played the Two Knights with 4.Ng5 and 5.exd5. Black's 5...Ne7 was a mistake, but 6.Nxf7 was a blunder, even though it forks the queen and rook, because 6...Kxf7 simply took the knight. The engine suggested 6.d4. Black replied 7...Ke8, a blunder in return, and you found 8.dxe7!, another fork, this time of the queen and bishop.

That put you ahead, and 9.O-O and 10.Bb3 kept your position together. But 13.Qe3 was a blunder that dropped you from +2.5 to +0.3, because 13.Qxe5 was stronger. Black's 13...Bd6 gave it back, and 14.Qxb6 was acceptable.

More errors followed: 18.f4 and 20.g3 each cost you about two pawns of evaluation, and 22.Bd2 and 27.Kf2 moved the game against you. Black's 28...Bd3 gave you a chance, and 29.Na3 was the engine's choice, but 29.Nd2 missed it.
By 31.Bd1 the evaluation was -6.2. Black converted with 35...Nxd1+ and 36...Nxb2, and you resigned after 54 moves.

review.turning_point: 29.Nd2 was the missed chance. Black's 28...Bd3 had brought the game back to roughly equal, and 29.Na3 would have kept it close, but 29.Nd2 handed the initiative back.
review.focus: Look at 6.Nxf7. A fork only works if the capture is not simply recaptured, so count the defenders of f7 before sacrificing. 6.d4 would have kept you at +1.6.

review.headline: A Traxler-style attack where Black's mistakes outweighed yours

sections.text: You played the Italian with 3.Bc4 and 4.Ng5, and Black chose 4...Bc5, a mistake. The best answer was 5.Nxf7, a fork of the queen and rook, but 5.O-O was a small slip at +1.2 to -0.4. Black then played 5...d5 and you took with 6.exd5.

Black replied 6...Ne7, a blunder, and you should have played 7.d6. Instead 7.Nxf7 was another fork, though it gave away some of your edge. Black blundered again with 7...Rf8, and 8.Nxd8! took the queen.

You kept your advantage with 9.Bxd5, 10.Nxb7 and 11.Nc3. 13.Be3 and 16.Qh5+ were slightly inaccurate, but the evaluation stayed above +4. Black's 12...Nxg2 and 14...exd4 opened lines, and you brought the rook in with 15.Re1+.

After 17.Nd5 and 17...Nxe1 you stayed in control with 18.Ne7+, 19.Ng6+ and 20.Nxf8. 20...Rxf8 was a mistake, and your 21.Rxe1! picked up the loose knight. 22.Re8+ finished the game and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 8.Nxd8! was the decisive moment. Black's 7...Rf8 handed you the queen, and everything after that was a technical task.
review.focus: Look at 5.O-O and 7.Nxf7. Both gave away a stronger move, 5.Nxf7 and 7.d6, and cost evaluation. In the Traxler the fork on f7 is worth calculating before you castle.

review.headline: A Petrov where two inaccurate moves let White's knight take over

sections.text: You played the Petrov with 2...Nf6, then 3...d6 after 3.Nxe5, and took on e4 with 4...Nxe4. The opening went fine: 5.Qe2, 5...Qe7, 6.d3 and 6...Nf6 were ordinary and level, and 7...h6 asked the bishop a question.
After 8.Bxf6, 8...Qxe2+ and 9.Bxe2, you recaptured 9...gxf6, leaving doubled pawns but a sound position at -0.4. 10...Rg8 was a small inaccuracy at -1.0.

The real problem started at 11...Nc6, a mistake that took you to -1.8, where 11...Be6 followed by 12.d4 was preferred. White's 12.Nd5 then hit f6, c7 and e7 at once, and your 12...Be6 was a blunder, dropping to -4.3. 12...Kd8 was the best try.
13.Nxc7+ came with check and attacked your rook on a8. The evaluation sat at -4.0 and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 12...Be6 was the decisive error. After 12.Nd5 the c7 pawn was already weak, and instead of 12...Kd8 you allowed 13.Nxc7+ with check.
review.focus: At 11...Nc6 and 12...Be6, look at squares your opponent's knight can reach. When a knight can land on d5, ask which of your pawns, here on c7 and f6, it will attack.

review.headline: A short Scandinavian where Black's errors gave you a huge edge and you won on time

sections.text: You played 1.e4 d5 and 2.exd5, then 3.Nc3 hit the queen. Black replied 3...Be6, a blunder, because the queen on d5 stays attacked by your knight.
4.d4 was a missed opportunity, dropping from +5.4 to +1.2. The engine preferred 4.Nxd5, which keeps you far ahead. After 4...Qd8 you developed with 5.Nf3, a small inaccuracy.
Black then blundered again with 5...Nc6. You found 6.d5!, a pawn fork that attacks the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6. After 6...Nf6 you took 7.dxe6 and were up material.
Black ran out of time after 7 moves, so you took the win.

review.turning_point: 6.d5! was the key moment. The pawn fork on c6 and e6 left Black with no good way to save both pieces.
review.focus: Look at 4.d4. You had 4.Nxd5 available, which would have kept the large edge. When the opponent leaves a queen attacked, check whether you can simply capture before making any other move.

review.headline: A Petrov Modern Attack where you fought back well but gave away a winning position

sections.text: After 3.d4 and 3...exd4, White's 4.e5 attacked your knight. 4...Nc6 was a blunder, taking you from -0.4 to -3.5, and 4...Ne4 was the right move. After 5.exf6, 5...Qxf6, 6.Bc4 and 6...Bb4+ you stayed in the game.
White's 8.Nxc3 was a blunder, but you replied 8...O-O, a blunder of your own, instead of 8...Bxc3+. After 9.Bg5 and 9...Bxc3+ you were still fine, and 10.Nd2 was an outright blunder by White at +5.2.
11.Be2 was another mistake, and you found 11...Qxg5!. Then 12.bxc3 and 12...Qxg2, followed by 13...Qxh2, took more material. You were up by about +5 for a long stretch.
That fell apart at 21...d6, a blunder from +5.0 to -3.9. The engine suggested 21...Qa1+ followed by 22.Rd1. After 22.Rxa2 and the endgame, the f-pawn ran home with 50.f8=Q, and 59.Qfh8# ended it.

review.turning_point: 21...d6 was the turning point. You were clearly ahead, but the quiet pawn move let White play 22.Rxa2 and swing the evaluation to -4.2.
review.focus: Study 21...d6. When far ahead you should look at the strongest forcing option, here 21...Qa1+, before playing a quiet move.

review.headline: A Van't Kruijs game where early bishop moves cost time and one queen move cost the game

sections.text: You started with 1.e3 and then 2.Bc4, an early bishop outing that Black met with 2...d5. After 3.Bb5+, 3...c6 and 4.Ba4 the evaluation was already -1.8, because your bishop had been kicked around and Black developed with tempo.

You kept playing sensibly with 5.Nc3, 6.exd4 and 7.Qe2+, and 8.Ne4 set a trap. Black's 8...b5 was a blunder, and 9.Nd6+ is a discovered attack: your knight moves from e4 and your queen on e2 now hits the bishop on e7. The evaluation was around -0.2 after 9...Kf8.
Then 10.Qf3 was your blunder, dropping to -4.7. The engine preferred 10.Nxc8 followed by 11.Bb3. After 10...Bxd6 you were down material, and 11.Bb3, 11...Qe7+ and 12.Ne2 left you without a defence.
13.Qxc6 and 13...Nxc6 ended the game, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 10.Qf3 was the decisive error. After Black's 8...b5 you had a good chance, but the queen move allowed 10...Bxd6 and ended your counterplay.
review.focus: Review 10.Qf3. Your knight on d6 was attacked, and 10.Nxc8 was available. When a piece is attacked, count your options for saving it or trading it before you play a move that adds a second attacker.

review.headline: A Petrov that went wrong in the middlegame after a string of errors

sections.text: You met 1.e4 with the Petrov and played solidly with 3...d6, 4...h6, 5...Be7 and 6...c6. After 8.dxe5 and 8...dxe5 you castled with 9...O-O and developed with 10...Rd8 and 11...Nbd7. The game was balanced.

Trouble began at 12...Nc5, a blunder from +0.3 to -1.9, where 12...b5 was better. White missed the strong reply 13.Bxf7+ and played 13.Bd2, and you then went wrong with 13...Ncxe4, which dropped to -3.9. 13...b5 was safer.
White gave you a chance with 16.Rac1, a blunder, but 16...Rd8 was inaccurate. Then 17...Bf6 was another blunder, and after 18.Nxf7 you played 18...Kf8, a mistake, and the evaluation stood at -6.8.
21...Qxd8! was a good practical try, but the game was already lost. White went on with 22.Nxd8, 23.Ne6+ and 24.Qxe6, and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 13...Ncxe4 was the decisive moment. The evaluation went from +0.7 to -3.9, and the rest of the game was a losing fight.
review.focus: Study 12...Nc5 and 13...Ncxe4. In both cases 12...b5 and 13...b5 were available and kept the position balanced. Before you move a knight, check whether it leaves a piece undefended.

review.headline: A Sicilian won by a sharp tactical finish despite some wobbly middlegame moves

sections.text: You played the Open Sicilian with 3.d4 and 4.Nxd4, then 5.Qxd4, 6.Nc3 and 7.Bf4. The position was clearly better for you at +2.1, but 8.Bc4 was a blunder, dropping to -1.7, where 8.O-O-O was better.

Black's 8...Be7 gave it back, because 8...e5 would have forked your queen and bishop. After 9.O-O-O and 9...O-O, you found 10.Bxd6!, which pins the bishop on e7 to the rook on f8. By 12.e5 you were at +3.5.
Then you slipped with 15.Rd4, a blunder from +4.0 to +1.3, since 15.Qxd8 was better. Black's 15...Bxc4 and your 16.Rxc4 gave away more, and 16.Qxd8 was the right idea again.
Black's 23...fxe6 was a blunder, and you answered with 24.Qxe6+!, then 25.Qxc8, 26.Rd8+ and 27.Rxd8# to finish.

review.turning_point: 24.Qxe6+! was the decisive move. Black's 23...fxe6 opened the king, and your queen move led to 27.Rxd8#.
review.focus: Review 15.Rd4 and 16.Rxc4. In both positions 15.Qxd8 and 16.Qxd8 were the stronger moves, trading queens while you were clearly ahead.

review.headline: A Four Knights win where you recovered from a bad stretch and a bishop move decided it

sections.text: You played the Italian with 5.Nd5 and 6.c3, then 7.b4, and 8.a4 was a small inaccuracy. After 9.Nxb6 and 9...cxb6, 10.Bb5 was a blunder from +0.8 to -1.2. The engine preferred 10.b5.
11.c4 was another mistake, but Black's 11...Nd4 was a blunder, and you found 12.Nxd4! and followed with 13.d3, getting the position back to +1.1.

16.Qf3 dropped you to -0.8, where 16.Bxf6 was best. Black replied 17...Nd7, a blunder, and you found 18.Bxd8!. The knight left f6, which uncovered your bishop on h4 against the queen, a discovered attack, and you took it. After 18...Raxd8 you were well ahead.
You converted with 19.O-O, 20.Rac1 and 23.Rxc3, then 32.Qxc3! and 33.Qxc2! kept things simple. 47.f8=Q+ and 48.Qe6+ ended it, and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 18.Bxd8! was the turning point. Black's 17...Nd7 uncovered your bishop on h4 against the queen, and you collected it.
review.focus: Look at 10.Bb5 and 16.Qf3. Both moves left your position loose when 10.b5 and 16.Bxf6 were more solid. Check what your opponent's best reply does before you play.

review.headline: A Queen's Pawn game where you fought back but a hasty rook capture changed the result

sections.text: You answered 1.d4 with 1...d5, 2...e6 and 3...Nf6, with 4.cxd5 and 4...exd5 following. 6...Bd7 was a little passive, but you grabbed a pawn with 10.Qxb7 and 10...Rb8, and 11.Qa6 and 11...Ne4 kept the game close.

White's 12.Bb5 was a blunder, and 12...Nb4 was the engine's choice. Instead 12...Rb6 was a mistake. After 14.Bxc6 and 14...Bxc6, 15.Qc2 followed, and your 15...Qb8 was a blunder, dropping to -1.3, where 15...Bb5 was better.

16.b4 was a mistake, but 16...Nxc3, 17.Qxc3, 17...Bb5, 18.a4, 18...Bc4, 19.Ne5 and 19...Rxb4 gave you an active position. Then 21...Rxh1 was a blunder from +0.5 to -2.5, and 21...Rb3 was the engine suggestion.
23.Qxc4 was a mistake from White, but 23...Qa7 was a blunder, and 23...Qb7 was better. After 24.Rc1 and 25.Qxc7 the evaluation was -4.7. You ran out of time after 38 moves.

review.turning_point: 21...Rxh1 was the decisive moment. A promising counterattack slipped to -2.5 after the capture, and the position never recovered.
review.focus: Review 21...Rxh1 and 23...Qa7. In both positions 21...Rb3 and 23...Qb7 were the best moves. When you have the initiative, check what your capture allows before you play it.

review.headline: An Italian Game where a greedy blunder was answered by a kingside attack that finished in a clean mating net

sections.text: This was an open Italian Game with kings still in the center, and you got into trouble first. Your opponent played the slightly odd 3...a6 and 4...h6, which gave you an easy lead in development, but 6.Nxe5 grabbed a pawn that was defended and the knight was just recaptured. That swung the evaluation from +0.7 to -2.0, and 6.d4 was the sound way to open the center.

You were rescued by 7...Bc5, which walked into 8.d4!. That pawn push attacked bishop and knight at once (a fork on c5 and e5), and you spotted it immediately, which deserves credit because it brought you back to +0.9.
Black then grabbed on e4 with 8...Nxe4, and 9.Nxe4 was exactly right. After 10.dxc5 you were three points up and your opponent's king had no safe home.

From there you attacked the king directly. 12.Bxh6 broke open the pawn cover, 13.Qg4+ and 15.Qh5 kept the pressure up, and after 15...dxe4 the finish was forced: 16.Qxh6+, 17.Rg3+, 18.Rxg4+ and 19.Rxg5#. The rook lift with 14.Re3 was a nice practical way to bring the last piece into the attack.
