review.turning_point: 8.d4! forked the bishop and knight and erased the damage from 6.Nxe5, and after 9.Nxe4 you were just up material with the better position.
review.focus: Before capturing in the opening, check what recaptures. 6.Nxe5 gave up a knight for a pawn, whereas 6.d4 would have kept your good position.

review.headline: A cramped opening battle that you handled well until three tactical oversights in a row

sections.text: Your opponent chose a slow setup with 1.a3, 2.h3 and then a pawn storm with 8.g4 and 10.g5. You met it sensibly, claiming the center with 1...e5 and 2...d5 and getting your pieces out, and you were not worse for a long time. 9...Qd7 was a small slip (the engine liked 9...h6 to deal with the g-pawn), but nothing serious.

The first real problem was 13...a4, which dropped you from +1.4 to -1.5. Your opponent then returned the favor with 14.Nxd6+, and you correctly recaptured with 14...Qxd6!. After 15.bxa4 Rxa4 things were balanced again at +0.6.

Then 16...Nb4 allowed 17.c4?, which uncovered the queen on d1 against your rook on a4 (a discovered attack). It was a mistake by White, but you needed to see the idea. Instead 17...Nec6 left a rook hanging and the game turned decisively with 18.Qxa4, putting you about five points down.
The rest was damage limitation. White pushed with 21.h5 and 22.h6, opened the h-file, and 24.Nxe5 and 25.Qxd7 cleaned up. You resigned after 27.Rxh3.

review.turning_point: 17...Nec6 missed that 17.c4 had opened the d1-a4 diagonal, so after 18.Qxa4 you were a rook down with no compensation.
review.focus: After every opponent move ask what it uncovered. 17.c4 opened the diagonal toward your rook, and 17...Ra7 was the safe answer.

review.headline: A Petrov game where you were a piece down for most of it, then your opponent walked into a back rank mate

sections.text: The opening decided the shape of the game. In the Three Knights, 3...Nxe4 grabbed a pawn, but 4.Nxe4 just took the knight, and the engine immediately had you at about -3. Better was 3...Nc6, keeping the position healthy.

You fought on well. 4...d5 and 5...e4 gained space and chased the white knight around. Your opponent did not really consolidate: 7.Nb3 was a mistake, and a few moves later 9.Nd2 and 10.dxe4 let you trade down. Your 7...a5 was inaccurate, though, and you stayed worse.

A tactic gave you a chance. 14...Ba6 skewered the queen on c4 against the bishop on e2, but then 15...Bxe2 was the critical mistake because it allowed 16.Qxh7#. White missed it and played 16.Qxa8, grabbing a rook.

You then found the key answer 16...Re8!, hitting the queen on a8. White's 17.Ne4 ignored the danger, and 17...Qd1# was a back rank mate because the king on e1 was boxed in by its own rook and bishop. A great finish, even if you were lucky to get there.

review.turning_point: 16.Qxa8 grabbed a rook but missed the immediate 16.Qxh7# and then 17.Ne4 left the king exposed to 17...Qd1#.
review.focus: Avoid the pawn grab in 3...Nxe4. Against the Three Knights, develop with 3...Nc6 instead of giving White a free tempo and a piece-up position.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where you held an edge until a two-move slide in a tense middlegame

sections.text: You played the Scandinavian main line from the white side and handled it calmly. 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 and 5.Bd2 developed with tempo, and 7.Bc4 aimed at f7. You spent time on 8.h3 and 9.g4 to chase the bishop and 11.g5?! was a bit loosening, but 12.Nxg6 traded your knight for the bishop and you held a steady edge of about +1.
Both kings headed to the queenside. 17.Nxd5 and 18.Re3 were a touch slow, and your opponent's 18...Bd6 gave you +1.8. The right plan was 19.Bxd5, taking the pawn with a growing advantage.
Instead 19.Rc3 drifted to +0.1, and later you found 22.Bxd5!, the strongest move, but the continuation went wrong.

23.b3 was the decisive error. It dropped you from +1.4 to -4.8 because the bishop on d5 was left hanging, and 23...Nxd5 followed. 24.Qxd5 cxd5 gave up your queen for a knight, and the rest was a long defense. You were materially behind through to the resignation.

review.turning_point: 23.b3 left the bishop on d5 undefended against the knight, so 23...Nxd5 followed and the position collapsed to about -5.
review.focus: At 23.b3, check each piece's defenders first. 23.Bb3 retreating the bishop kept a small edge, while the pawn move left it loose.

review.headline: A short Philidor where your opponent stepped into a kingside attack and you finished with 9.Qxf7#

sections.text: A tidy, direct win. After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Nc3 Bg4, you played 4.Bc4, which was a small inaccuracy (the engine preferred 4.d4 exd4 5.Qxd4 to open the center while Black's pieces were loose), but the position stayed healthy at +0.4.

5.h3 asked the bishop a question, and 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 gave you the bishop pair and a queen aimed at f7. Black's 6...g6 weakened the dark squares, and your plan was simple: pile onto f7 with queen and bishop.
7.g4 was an aggressive and natural follow-up. Black responded with 7...Bg7, a blunder worth almost three pawns, because it ignored the pawn storm. Then 8.g5! hit the knight on f6.

Black's 8...Nh5 was the last mistake, and 9.Qxf7# was checkmate on the spot, with the bishop on c4 guarding the queen. You played every move cleanly after 4.Bc4: a calm developing game and a clear finish.

review.turning_point: 8.g5! forced the knight to move away from f6, and after 8...Nh5 the f7 square was defended by nothing, so 9.Qxf7# ended it.
review.focus: Your only inaccuracy was 4.Bc4. Against ...Bg4 early on, 4.d4 would have opened the center while Black's pieces were still undeveloped.

review.headline: A messy game where you built a huge advantage in the opening and middlegame and let it drift all the way to a stalemate

sections.text: Your opponent blundered early with 5...Nd7 and you answered precisely with 6.dxe5!. Then 7.Nxe5?? threw it away by dropping a knight to the recapture. The better move was 7.Bxf7+, which kept control.

You got another chance when Black played 10...Ng6 and 11...Nf6?? You found 11.Bxf7! and 12.Bxg6!, regaining the lost material and more. By 14.fxe5 you were four points up and 19.exf8=Q cleaned up the position beautifully.

By move 24 you were still around +4, but small slips like 24.Rg6? and 37.Re5?? let it fade. A rook endgame arrived with passed pawns on both sides. Your 42.g7 was good and kept you ahead, but 46.g8=Q?? let your advantage slip to equal.

The rook ending got messy. 49.Rg4+ and 51.Rg4+ drifted, and 56.Kb1 stepped into a position that was losing (-5.6), though your opponent let you out with 56...a2+. Then 61.Rxa2+ traded your last rook for a pawn and the game ended in stalemate.

review.turning_point: 7.Nxe5 gave back the entire opening advantage in one move, and the long rook ending never recovered your control.
review.focus: In the rook ending, 56.Kb1 turned a drawn position into a losing one; 56.Rg7 was the safe move. Keep your rook active behind the passed pawns rather than stepping the king into their path.

review.headline: A promising, quiet opening that ended when the clock ran out after only 7 moves

sections.text: Your opponent met 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 with the unusual 2...Qf6, an early queen sortie that the engine considers a mistake. You answered with 3.Nc3!, the right developing move, hitting the center and gaining time against the queen.

4.d3 was a little passive (the engine preferred 4.d4 exd4 5.Bg5, striking at the queen right away), but you remained comfortably fine. 5.a3 and 6.b4 gained space on the queenside and threatened to push the bishop around.

7.b5?! was the second inaccuracy, since the plan of opening the b-file did not help development. 7.d4 was the cleaner way. Black then played 7...g5?, and the position still stood at about +0.6 in your favour.
The game ended on the clock after just 7 moves, so the board result does not reflect the position at all. That is the lesson to take away.

review.turning_point: There was no board turning point; the position after 7...g5 was fine for you, and the clock decided the game.
review.focus: Play faster in the opening. Moves like 4.d3 and 7.b5 cost time for little gain; 7.d4 was the simpler choice and keeps tempo with the clock.

review.headline: A wild Ruy Lopez where both sides blundered repeatedly, until your attack and a passed pawn finished the job

sections.text: You played the Ruy Lopez with the Caro Variation. The opening went fine until 7.Nc3??, which allowed 7...Nxd4 and dropped to -1.5; 7.h3 was needed. But 8...Nxf3+ was Black's error, and you reacted well with 9.gxf3!, opening the g-file for your rook.
Black then blundered with 10...Qf6, jumping to +4.1. You missed the cleanest follow-up with 11.Nd5 (11.Bg5 was stronger), but still collected material through 13.Bxe7 and 14.Rxg7.

Both sides kept trading errors. 15.Bxd5 should have been 15.Qxd5, and 16...Bxf3 gave you +4.6. 18.Bxf7+ was a bit loose, but 18...Kd8 and your calm 19.Bd5! uncovered the rook on g7 against the queen (a discovered attack), keeping you way ahead.

Your biggest miss came on 22.Qxd8+. The engine found 22.Qf5+ Qd7 23.Qxd7#, a forced checkmate. Even so, you stayed far ahead and finished the game with the h-pawn marching: 37.h4 through 40.h7, and then 48.h8=Q put the cap on it.

review.turning_point: 10...Qf6 let you fight back from -1.7 to +4.1, and then 19.Bd5! kept the attack rolling with the queen on e7 under pressure.
review.focus: At 22.Qxd8+ look for forcing checks first: 22.Qf5+ Qd7 23.Qxd7# was checkmate. You took the safe route when the kill was on the board.

review.headline: A Danish Gambit where you accepted every pawn and then struggled to untangle your pieces

sections.text: Your opponent offered the Danish Gambit and you took everything: 2...exd4, 3...dxc3, 4...cxb2. After 5.Bxb2 you were two points up, which is exactly why the gambit is risky for White. The problem was your development: 5...Nh6 took you from +1.0 to -0.8, and 5...Nf6 was a much more natural square.

White returned the favor with 6.Nc3 and 8.Qd4, and you went for 8...Bxc3+, which looked like a big fork of the king, queen and bishop. But 9.Bxc3 just recaptured, and the better move was 8...Nc6, just developing. After 9...Qf6 and 10...Qd6? you were fighting for control.

You found a lovely resource in 12...Qxe5+! after 12.e5, regaining material, and held your own at about +1.3 through 14.O-O. But 16...Bh3? and especially 17...Nf5?? dropped you to -4.2, with 17...Be6 the sound move.
18...g6?? deepened the problem, and 20...Nb6 allowed a forced checkmate: the engine pointed to 20...Qf6 as the way to survive. After 21.Qxf7+ Kh8 22.Bc3+ you resigned.

review.turning_point: 17...Nf5 gave away the position after you had held the material edge, falling from -0.8 to -4.2.
review.focus: 8...Bxc3+ looked forcing but 9.Bxc3 just recaptured. Before cashing in a check, count the recaptures; 8...Nc6 kept everything protected.

review.headline: An even Colle-style game that stayed level for 40 moves before time pressure ended it

sections.text: A calm opening: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 and a fianchetto setup for both sides. After 8.c4 and 9.cxd5 exd5 you were on a firm footing, and 11...Ne4 12.Nxe4 dxe4 13.Ne5 Nxe5 14.dxe5 Bxe5 simplified to an equal position.
Your opponent then overpressed with 18.f4??, which handed you +3.1. The engine suggested 18...exf3, taking en passant. Instead 18...f5 brought the evaluation back down to +0.8 and the chance passed.

You defended well from there. 21...Bb7 was a small slip, but after 22...c5, 24.bxc5 Rxc5 and a series of trades the position came down to a rook ending around 0.0. Nothing much happened between moves 28 and 43.
The game turned only at the end. 44...Re3?? dropped you from -0.3 to -3.6, and 45...Be4?? left no defence against 46.g5#. The engine flagged both as moves played when low on time.

review.turning_point: 44...Re3 dropped the evaluation from -0.3 to -3.6, and with little time left 45...Be4 allowed 46.g5#.
review.focus: At 44...Re3, with the clock low, a calm waiting move like 44...Be6 would have kept it equal. Simplify your calculation when time is short.

review.headline: A Petrov line where you were behind from the third move, clawed back, then blundered a queen

sections.text: As in the Three Knights, 3...Nxe4 took a pawn but 4.Nxe4 took the knight, and you were down about three points for most of the game. 3...Nc6 was the standard solution.

Then your opponent made two big mistakes. 10.Qe2?? let you play 10...dxc3!, and 11.Qxe4+ was another error because you had the cool answer 11...Be7!, breaking the check and getting back to about equality.
The material was now roughly level and your king was safe after 12...O-O and 13...Re8. The engine rated the position as equal at 13...Re8, so you had fully recovered.
Then 14.Qd5 attacked your queen on d7 and 14...Nc6?? dropped to -5.6; 15.Qxd7 took your queen. The engine preferred 14...Rd8. You were out of time at move 15.

review.turning_point: 14...Nc6 ignored the attack on your queen, so 15.Qxd7 cost you the queen after you had worked your way back to equality.
review.focus: At 14...Nc6, check whether your queen is attacked before developing. 14...Rd8 kept the balance, and two checks per move pays off at speed.

review.headline: A Ruy Lopez where you played loosely but your opponent's blunders gave you a crushing attack

sections.text: Black chose the Alapin Defense, 3...Bb4, and you reacted with 4.c3 and then 5.b4?! and 8.b5?, pushing pawns without much purpose. After 8...axb5 9.axb5 Bxf2+ 10.Kxf2 Rxa1 you were on shaky ground, and 11.bxc6? left you at -1.3.

But your opponent blundered with 12...bxc6, where 12...Qh4+ would have kept the edge. 13.Nxf7 forked the queen and rook, though 13.Bxf7+ was a more precise way. Black then missed 13...Qf6+ and played 13...d5??, and you took the queen with 14.Nxd8!.

That pushed you to +3.9. 15.exd5 and 16.Qe2 kept things safe. Then 17.Kg1?? gave the advantage away, dropping to -5.5 because of 17...Rxc1+, but Black missed it with 17...Ng4 and you were saved again.
18.Qe1! was the best answer, and the end was straightforward: 21.dxc6+, 23.d5+, then a hunt of the king with 30.Be3+, 31.Qxg6+, 32.Bf4+ and 33.Qa6#.

review.turning_point: 13...d5 missed the saving 13...Qf6+, so 14.Nxd8 took the queen and gave you a winning game.
review.focus: 17.Kg1 nearly threw the win away: 17.Re1 was the safe move. Check whether the king step hangs a piece to a check such as 17...Rxc1+.

review.headline: A Petrov game where you were worse early, survived, and then punished a series of White errors with a mating attack

sections.text: 3.Bc4 d5?! 4.exd5 e4 5.Qe2 was a gambit-ish line, and 5...Nxd5?? was the mistake because 6.Qxe4+ took the pawn with check, dropping to -2.7. 5...Bb4 was the better move. You were behind for a long time after that.

White gave a lot back. 8.Qe5?? returned the advantage, 11.Na3?? was another slip, and you pressed with 12...b5 and 14...Qb6. Your good defensive move was 16...Be7!, a calm answer that held the balance.

Both sides then slipped: 17.Qb3? missed 17.Qxg7, and 17...Nb4? and 18.Bf4? kept things unclear. Your 18...h6?? went from +0.8 to -4.6 because the engine wanted 18...O-O to get the king out of the center.

Then came the key moment: 22.Re8+?? could be answered by 22...Rxe8!, and you were suddenly up seven points. 23.Nxe8 Kxe8 24.Ne4 Bxe4 25.dxe4 Qe6 26.Qc3 Qxe4 27.Qxg7 Qe1# finished the game with a mating attack. Well done converting.

review.turning_point: 22.Re8+ was a blunder and your calm 22...Rxe8! turned a worse position into a winning one.
review.focus: 5...Nxd5 gave up a pawn and the initiative; 5...Bb4 would have developed with a threat. Keep your king safe before taking pawns, as with 18...h6, where 18...O-O was needed.

review.headline: A Franco-Sicilian where good opening play punished early mistakes and you converted cleanly

sections.text: A clean, high-accuracy win. After 1.e4 c5 2.d4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6, the line 4.Nc3?! was slightly passive, but 4...Be7? by Black let you play 5.e5!, kicking the knight and gaining space.
6.Ne4 was your one mistake because 6.Nxd5 was stronger. Black answered 6...Nc6??, a blunder, and you found the right plan again with 7.c4!, attacking the knight on d5.
After 8.d5 exd5 9.cxd5 you pushed on with 10.d6, a strong pawn break. 11.dxe7 Qxe7 left you three points ahead, and you were comfortable at +4.7.
You then finished the job cleanly: 13.Bg5, 14.Qd6 to force the queen trade, and 16.Nxd6 left you ahead. 19.Bxd5 brought you five points up and Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 5.e5! seized space and 7.c4! kept the initiative against the knight on d5, and Black never got organized again.
review.focus: 6.Ne4 gave up part of your edge. 6.Nxd5 exd5 would have kept your advantage. Always look at captures first when a piece is offered.

review.headline: A long Petrov game where you defended a bad opening for fifty moves before the clock ended it

sections.text: It began with the familiar 3...Nxe4, a pawn grab that cost you a knight after 4.Nxe4 and left you about three points down. 3...Nc6 was the better move.

You fought back well. 10...h4! and 11...Bxf5! were accurate replies to White's slips (10.d3? and 11.Nxf5?), and you got within a pawn of equality. 13...Qe7 was a mistake that let White regain control.

17...Bd2+ was a discovered attack that opened your rook on the bishop on h4, and the game went into a rook ending where you were behind. Credit to you for 35...Rxb2! after 35.Rxc6, which brought you back to -3.6 from -9.2, and 39...Rxd3! after 39.Ra8, almost level.
Then 41...Kf4 dropped to -4.6 because the engine wanted 41...Rxh3 to take the pawn. 42...d3? and 43...Ke4 followed, and White queened with 47.a8=Q. You ran out of time at move 51.

review.turning_point: 41...Kf4 walked away from the h3 pawn at the moment you were nearly equal, and the passed a-pawn then decided the game.
review.focus: At 41...Kf4, grab the free pawn: 41...Rxh3 kept the game level. In rook endings, take material before king moves.

review.headline: A French-style game that was balanced for ages, then you missed a forced mate and still won on time in a long rook ending

sections.text: A Franco-Sicilian where 5.Bc4?! gave up a little, and after 6.Bxd5 exd5 7.O-O Nc6 8.Re1 the position was fairly equal. 11.Nfxd4? was a mistake (11.Bg5 was better), but 14.Qxb6 axb6 simplified into an endgame.

16.e6 was a blunder dropping to -0.2, while 16.exd6 kept things equal. Black took 16...Bxe6, but you recovered with 17.Bxb6. A series of quiet moves followed, with 18.Re3 and 19.Bd4 holding the position.
Then Black blundered with 24...Kf5, walking the king into a mating net. You missed it: the engine found 25.Rf3+ Kg5 26.Be3+ Kg4 27.h3#. 25.Kf3 let Black off the hook.

After that you were a bit worse around 34.Rf3?, but 41...Bh3?? gave you a huge chance, and 42.Rxh3! cashed in. You then ground the endgame down with 46.f5, 49.Rxf7, 55.Bxg7 and the queening 67.b8=Q, winning when your opponent ran out of time.

review.turning_point: 41...Bh3 hung a bishop to 42.Rxh3!, which swung the evaluation from -1.8 to +4.0 and set up the winning rook ending.
review.focus: At 25.Kf3, look for checks first. 25.Rf3+ Kg5 26.Be3+ Kg4 27.h3# was a forced checkmate.

review.headline: A Philidor where your opponent drifted into a tactic and you punished it with a knight raid

sections.text: A smooth win. After 3...Be6 4.b3 Bxc4 5.bxc4 you had traded bishops and left White with doubled pawns, and the game was close to equal at -0.2.

You missed two chances for more. 6...Be7? and 7...Nbd7? both let White get a better center; the engine would have taken the e4 pawn with 6...Nxe4 and 7...Nxe4. But White followed with 6.c3? and 7.d4?, both mistakes, so the game stayed close.
Then 8.dxe5? dxe5! was exactly the right recapture, and 9.Qb3?? was a blunder as 9...Nxe4 took a pawn and left you at +3.0.
The finishing sequence was great. 11.Qb5+ c6 12.Qb2 Nd3+ 13.Ke2 Nxb2 14.Bxb2 Nxd2 won the queen for a knight, and from there you converted easily with 16...Bxh4, 20...Qxd6 and 22...Qxb2.

review.turning_point: 9.Qb3?? let you take 9...Nxe4 and after 12...Nd3+ the knight hit the queen, ending in a decisive material edge.
review.focus: At 7...Nbd7, a free pawn was available with 7...Nxe4. Keep an eye on loose central pawns when your opponent plays a slow move.

review.headline: A reckless King's Knight game where sacrifices and mistakes flew, and your extra pieces finally told

sections.text: Black played 2...b6? and 3...c5??, and you took advantage with 4.Nxe5 and then the speculative 5.Nxf7. After 5...Kxf7 6.Qf3+, you took a rook with 8.Qxa8, but the engine was not convinced by these moves.
9.Ba6?? was a blunder that dropped the bishop to 9...Bxa6. After 10.Qxd8 Nxd8 the queens came off, but you were now worse at -2.9.

Black's 11...Ng4?? and 12...Nxf2?? let you recover, and 13.Kxf2! was the right capture. After 15.Bxd4 Nxd4 you were up some material and on the way to a win. 22.c5? and 23.cxb6? were small slips and 24.Rc3?? was a larger one, but your opponent kept erring with 23...axb6.
You finished with 25.Rc7!, then 29.d7 and 31.dxc8=Q+. The last moves, 36.Nd6+, 37.Rf7+ and 39.Rf8+, led to 40.Qf7#.

review.turning_point: 12...Nxf2?? gave the knight away and 13.Kxf2! left you well ahead for the rest of the game.
review.focus: 9.Ba6 just hung the bishop. 9.Bc4+ kept the pieces coordinated, so always check what a capture does to your piece before moving.

review.headline: A tactical Vienna where you had chances, let them slip, and lost on time in a drawn ending

sections.text: You went wild in the Vienna with 3...Qf6? and 4...g5??, a gamble that put you at -4.1 after 4.Nf3. White's 5.h3? gave some of it back, and after 7...Qxe4+ 8.Be3 exd4 9.Nxc7+ Kd8 the game was messy.
10.Nxd4?? was a blunder by White, and then 11...Nf5?? missed 11...Nxc2+, which forks the king and the rook on a1. After 12.O-O?? Nxe3! you were doing well again.
16...Bc5?? allowed a forced checkmate through 17.Qc7+ Ke8 18.Qxc8#, but White missed it with 17.Qf6. 21...Ne3 dropped to -1.0, 25.Rc1?? missed 25.Rg8+, and the game wandered to a drawn ending.
At the end you were low on time: 27...Nc6?? and 40...Kc6?? both slipped. 45...Kf7! was a nice save, but the clock ran out after 46.Rxa2.

review.turning_point: 16...Bc5 walked into a forced checkmate, but White missed it, and from then on the game slid toward a drawn ending decided by the clock.
review.focus: 27...Nc6 and 40...Kc6 both came when you were low on time. Spend less time earlier, and in the endgame play simple safe moves like 40...Kd6.

review.headline: Two Knights Defense where a greedy pawn grab walked into a pin and you rolled up the board

sections.text: You met the Two Knights with the classic plan: 4.O-O, then 5.d4 to open the centre. After 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 you had your pawn back and the position was roughly level.

Black went wrong with 6...Nxe4?, taking a pawn when 6...Ne5 was safer. Your reply was exactly right: 7.Re1! put a pin on the e4 knight against the king on e8, so Black's pieces were tied up straight away.

Then 7...Nxd4?? was the blunder (+5.0), and 8.Qxd4! was the best recapture: the queen created pins on g7 against the rook on h8 and on d7 against the queen on d8. After 9.Qxg7 and 10.Rxe4 you were clearly ahead on material (+3) and Black's king never found safety.

Your only slip was 11.Qxh6?!. It was still winning, but 11.Bxh6 followed by 12.Nc3 and 13.Rae1 would have brought more pieces in while the queen stayed active on g7. You still finished cleanly with 15.Rxe7+, 16.Rxf7 and 17.Rxf8, and the game ended on the clock with you far ahead.

review.turning_point: 7...Nxd4?? after your 7.Re1 pin: the evaluation jumped from +1.4 to +5.0, and 8.Qxd4 kept everything under control.
review.focus: On 11.Qxh6?! take the developing capture 11.Bxh6 instead. When you are already winning, bring the last pieces into the game rather than grabbing the next pawn with the queen.

review.headline: French Advance where a won middlegame slipped away with one wrong capture

sections.text: You chose the Advance French with 4.e5, which the engine called slightly loose (4.e5?!, 0.0), though nothing serious. After 5.c3 a6 6.Be2 cxd4 the centre was open and roughly level.

7.Nxd4?? was the first problem (-1.9): it left your e5 pawn without protection, and 7...Nxe5 was the right reply. Black took 7...Nxd4?? instead, and you answered correctly with 8.cxd4!, which brought the evaluation back to +0.3.

Black checked with 8...Bb4+, you blocked with 9.Bd2, and then came 9...Qb6?? (+5.4): 9...Bxd2+ was the right move. Now you had a strong shot, 10.Qa4+, a check that also hits the bishop on b4 and keeps a big edge.

Instead 10.Bxb4?? Qxb4+ recaptured with check and the advantage disappeared (+0.3). Then 11.Nc3 Qxb2 took a pawn, 12.Na4 Qb4+ kept the initiative, and you resigned soon after. This was a game you could have won in one move.

review.turning_point: 10.Bxb4??: the position was +5.4 until you took the bishop and allowed 10...Qxb4+ with check.
review.focus: At 10.Bxb4, look at checks and forcing moves first: 10.Qa4+ was available. Also before 7.Nxd4, recount which pawns lose their defender when a piece captures.

review.headline: Marathon where you survived a bad opening, struck with a fork, then ran short of time

sections.text: You were pushed back early: 4...Bg4?! and 5...Qd7?? (-5.0) gave White a large edge. 6.Nc3?? handed it straight back, but 6...c6?? (-2.9) gave it away again. After 7.Nxe4 dxe4 and 9.Nxg4 Qxg4 White kept the extra pawn and the better structure.
You held on at around -3 for a long time. The swing came when White went wrong with 23.Kg2?? and 25.Rh1?. You missed 25...Bxg5 and played 25...Rf8?? (-5.1), but 26.e4?? returned the favour (+4.6).
Then you found the best move of the game: 26...Rf2+! was a fork, attacking the king and the bishop on d2 at once. After 27.Kg1 Rxd2 and 30...Rxh1 you were ahead on material and heading for a win.

In the endgame you missed 32...Bxh8 after 32.Rh8+ and then 33...Kc8, but 39...Rg2+! was a skewer on the g-file: the king on g4 had to move and 40.Kf3 Rxg7 took the rook. 43...a1=Q put you massively ahead.
The last stretch was just technique, but the clock ended it as a draw even though you were winning by a mile. Simple, quick moves matter here.

review.turning_point: 26.e4?? answered by 26...Rf2+!: a fork turned a -5.1 position into a winning one (+4.0).
review.focus: At 25...Rf8?? the move was 25...Bxg5. When you reach a winning position like after 43...a1=Q, play the safest quick moves and watch the clock.

review.headline: Petrov where an early knight grab and a late bishop capture cost you good chances

sections.text: It began as a Petrov Three Knights. 3...Nxe4?? (-3.2) took a pawn, but 4.Nxe4 simply recaptured and left you down material. The calm 3...Nc6 4.Bb5 Nd4 was the engine's choice.
You fought back with 4...d5 5.Nc3 e4 6.Nd4 c5, and 7.Nb3?? gave you a chance (-0.7). But 7...d4?? (-4.0) wasted it: 7...c4 was the better try. After 8.Nxe4 you were down material again.
White returned the favour with 11.Nxc5?? (+3.0), and you found 11...Bxc5!. After 12.Qh5+ g6 13.Qh3 fxe4 14.Qxe6+ Bxe6 you were doing well, and you kept an edge of +3 for a long time.

30...Bxb4?? (-2.2) threw it away. The bishop pinned the c3 pawn to the king on d2, but a pinned pawn can still capture the pinning piece, so 31.cxb4 simply took it. The quiet 30...c5 kept control. 31...Rxb4?? followed, and 32.Rh8+ ended the fight.

review.turning_point: 30...Bxb4?? gave up a winning position (+3.0 to -2.2): the c3 pawn just captured on 31.cxb4.
review.focus: On 30...Bxb4, check the recapture before capturing: 31.cxb4 was legal even with the pin. When you are ahead, a quiet move like 30...c5 is enough.

review.headline: Reversed Sicilian where you outplayed a stronger opponent but settled for a repetition

sections.text: Against ARMY1719 (1359) you set up a classical e5/d6 structure and answered 11.d4 with 11...e4, closing the centre. After 13.cxd5 cxd5 14.Bb5 a6 15.Bxd7 Qxd7 the game was balanced.

18...b5? (-0.7) and 19...b4? (-1.5) were committal pushes; 18...exf3 was cleaner. Luckily 20.Ne2?? let you off and 20...bxa3! was a good practical answer. Then 21...Rc6? and 22...dxe4?? (-3.8) slipped again, where 22...Nxe4 was right.

You hit back with 23...Bxh3!, a discovered attack: the rook on c6 suddenly hit the bishop on f6 while the h3 bishop eyed g2. After 24.Bxe7 Qg4 and the trades on f2 you had huge counterplay, and 30.Qg3?? was a gift: 30...Qxe2! brought you back to level.

36.Qd6+?? was the decisive error by White: 36...Kxh5! took the knight and you were clearly ahead (+5.3). But your exposed king let White keep checking: 40.Qc6+ Kh5 41.Qf3+ Kg6 42.Qc6+ Kh5 43.Qf3+ Kg6 was a repetition while the engine had you at +5.4.

review.turning_point: 36.Qd6+?? Kxh5!: the queen check lost its point and you went from level to +5.3.

sections.text: You played the Petrov carefully but 9...Nxe4?! (-0.9) started a sequence of trades: 10.Nxe4 d5 11.Bxe7 dxe4 12.dxe4 Kxe7. By 20...Bxe4 you had grown a small edge.

review.headline: A fast Philidor win after your opponent missed a queen check

sections.text: You played the Philidor Exchange with 3.d4, 4.Nxd4 and 5.Nc3. 6.Nf3?! was slightly inexact, but 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Nc6 9.Bb5 was fine.
10.Ba4?? (+2.7 to -2.8) was a blunder; 10.Bxc6+ was better. Black answered 10...b5.
11.Nxb5! was a good try, but 12.Bxb5? (-5.2) was a mistake; 12.e5 was better.

Black missed 12...Qa5+, a fork of king and bishop on b5, and played 12...Be7??. 13.Bxc6+ was a fork of the king and the rook on a8, and you won. Winning like this was a good reminder that early forcing moves can punish an unprepared opponent, but 10.Ba4 and 12.Bxb5 each gave away more than you needed.

review.focus: At 10.Ba4 the pin on c6 looked tempting but 10.Bxc6+ was the stronger choice.

review.headline: A tactical win as Black where White's 13.fxe4 opened the door and you finished the job with a mate

sections.text: This Van't Kruijs opening quickly became a closed-center game, and you handled it with purpose. 3...e4 gained space, and 4...Nc6, 5...d5, 6...Bb4 and 7...Bg4 brought your pieces out without wasting time. White's 6.d4 was not the best (the engine preferred 6.dxe4), and from there you held a steady edge of around a pawn.

At move 12 you had a sharper option in 12...Bg3+, forcing White to deal with a check. You played 12...Rfe8?! instead and the lead shrank from +2.3 to +1.4. It did not matter much, because White cracked straight away with 13.fxe4??.

13...Nxg4! was exactly right, taking the bishop and coming out ahead on material. After 14.exd5 Bg3+ the white king was stuck in the center, and 15.Ke2? made it worse. 15...Bxd5! pins the g2 pawn against the rook on h1, so White could not untangle, and the evaluation climbed to +6.6.

16...Nxd4+?! was the one loose moment (16...Bxg2 was cleaner), but you stayed above +6 all the way home. 19...Nxa1, 22...Qxd2+ and 25...Qxc2 kept collecting material, and you closed it out with 30...axb2#.

review.turning_point: 13...Nxg4! after 13.fxe4?? won material at once, and after 15.Ke2? your 15...Bxd5! took the evaluation to about +6.6.
review.focus: 16...Nxd4+ at +8.5: the engine preferred 16...Bxg2. When you are far ahead, choose the simplest capture that keeps everything protected rather than a check that wins nothing.

review.headline: An even Bishop's Opening that fell apart once your kingside pawns started advancing

sections.text: You mirrored White early with 1...e5, 2...Nf6, 3...Bc5, 4...d6 and 5...Nc6, and the evaluation stayed near zero through move 5. White built a tidy center with 3.d3, 5.h3 and 6.c3, getting ready for d4.

The first slip was 6...d5? (-1.5). The quiet 6...a6 was the engine's choice. After 7.exd5 Nxd5 8.Qe2 you had opened the center before you had castled, while White's bishop on c4 was already aiming at the kingside. White's pieces were simply a bit more active from then on.
9...Nf4?! (-1.1) invited 10.Bxf4 exf4, which left the f4 pawn stranded and gave White time. 11.Qe4 then headed for your king, and 11...g5 with 12.h4 started to open lines around your own king.

12...h6?? was the decisive error (-1.0 to -6.7). 12...gxh4 13.Qxf4 would have kept the game level. After the pawn move, 13.Qg6+ could not be taken by the f-pawn because of the bishop on c4 aiming through f7 at your king. 13...Kh8 14.Qxh6+ Kg8 15.Nxg5 and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 12...h6?? (-1.0 to -6.7) left g6 open for 13.Qg6+, and White picked up the h6 pawn with check on 14.Qxh6+.
review.focus: 12...h6: before moving pawns around your own king, ask what checks the opponent's queen gets. The engine's 12...gxh4 captured on h4 and kept things level.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann where Black's queen excursion handed you a big edge, and the win came on the clock

sections.text: You met the Caro-Kann with 4.Bf4. 5.a3?! was a little loose (the evaluation dropped to 0.0) and led to 5...Bxc3+ 6.bxc3, but the doubled pawns did not hurt. 6...Nf6? was Black's first mistake, and your 7.e5! was the right punishment, gaining space and kicking the knight to e4.

8...Qa5?? (+1.0 to +3.9) was a real blunder. The queen pins the c3 pawn against your king on e1, which looks annoying, but it leaves Black's position loose. 9.Qd3?? then threw the edge away (+3.9 to +0.0). The engine's 9.f3 hits the knight on e4 immediately.
Black returned the favor with 9...b5??, and you found 10.f3! (+4.2). After 10...b4 11.fxe4 bxa3 you were a piece up, and 12.exd5 cxd5 kept the extra material.

From there you only had to stay tidy. 14...Bxd3 took your queen but 15.Nxa5 took theirs. Then 18.Bxa3+, 19.Nb7+, 20.Nd6 and 21.Bc5+ drove the black king around, and 22.Nxc8 won the rook as the game ended on time.

review.turning_point: 10.f3! after 9...b5?? was the strongest reply and won a piece with 11.fxe4. Without it, 9.Qd3?? would have been remembered as the big mistake.
review.focus: 9.Qd3?? when 9.f3 was there: if the opponent leaves a piece loose, look first for the forcing move that attacks it. That one choice cost you 3.9 pawns.

review.headline: A winning game as Black that slipped away on the clock after you out-calculated White's tactics

sections.text: A Center Game where you developed naturally with 2...exd4, 3...Nc6, 4...Nf6 and 5...Bb4. White's 7.a3? helped you, and 7...Ba5? set up a pin of the c3 knight against the king. The engine liked 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Nxe4 more, because it wins the e4 pawn.
Your own slips came with 10...d5? (-1.4) and 11...Nxd5?? (-4.1). 10...d6 and 11...Ne5 were the safe moves. After 11.exd5 you were simply a pawn down for little.

Then White gave it all back. 12.Bg5?? looked threatening, but 12...Nxc3! is a discovered attack: the knight leaves d5 and opens the d-file between your queen and the bishop on d3. 13.Bxd8? Nxd1! 14.Rfxd1 Nxd8 left you up material (+5.2).

You converted calmly. 18...Bxf3, 22...Rxf2, 23...Rxc2 and 25...Rxb3 piled up material, and even 36...Rb1+?!, a back-rank check that achieved little after 37.Kg2, did not change the evaluation much. But the clock ran out after 40.Ke5 with you far ahead.

review.turning_point: 12.Bg5?? followed by 12...Nxc3! swung the game from -4.1 to +2.6 in two moves.
review.focus: The clock: at 39...Rxf7 you were far ahead on material and had a huge evaluation lead, yet you lost on time. Simplify faster in won positions and keep a reserve of a minute or two.

review.headline: A slightly worse middlegame that flipped when White's queen walked into 20...Nxc6

sections.text: Against the Bishop's Opening you met 4.Bg5 with 4...h6 and 5...g5, chasing the bishop back with 5.Bh4 and 6.Bg3. That was ambitious, and it gave you a lot of space on the kingside, but it also loosened your own king.

The structure had a price. 8...Bh5?! pins the e2 knight against the queen on d1, but it cost time, and 8...Be6 was calmer. 9...Bg7?! (9...d5) pushed the evaluation to -1.1. White's 10.Bb5, 12.Ba4 and 13.Bb3 showed a steady, slight advantage.

You kept your composure. 14.Nd5 Nh5 15.Bh2 Nf4 led to 16.Nexf4 gxf4, and the position stayed around -0.5. 18...c6?! was another small slip (18...Ra7 was better), and it invited the queen into c6 after 19.Nb6 Qa7.
White took the bait with 20.Qxc6+??, and 20...Nxc6! won the queen for a pawn, swinging the evaluation from about -0.8 to +5.5. White resigned right after.

review.turning_point: 20.Qxc6+?? Nxc6!: the knight on d4 simply captured the queen.
review.focus: 8...Bh5?! and 9...Bg7?!: the engine preferred 8...Be6 and 9...d5, quieter moves that keep the position level. A bishop that eyes a knight on e2 looks forcing, but it needs a follow-up.

review.headline: A messy win: a knight dropped on move 5, then Black's blunders and 18.Nf6+ led to a queen mate

sections.text: Against 2...Bc5? the engine wanted 3.Nxe5, but you played 3.d4?. After 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 Qf6 the black queen and bishop both aimed at your knight on d4.

5.h4?? dropped it to 5...Qxd4 (+0.7 to -4.9). 5.Nf3 was the safe move. You were a full knight down, but you kept developing with 6.Qf3, 7.Bd3, 8.O-O and 9.Nc3, and 10.Be3?! set up a skewer on the queen on d4 with the bishop on c5 behind it, though 10...Qe5 sidestepped.
Black then helped you. 13...Na6?? (-3.8 to -1.2) let you back in. 14.Bxh6?? was a slip (14.Nd5 was better), but 14...g6?? gave it right back (-3.5 to +2.3), and 16.Nd5 set a trap.

16...Bxf2+ 17.Kh1 Bxe1?? grabbed your rook, but 18.Nf6+! was the point (+4.3 even though you were behind in material). 18...Nxf6?? 19.Qxf6! pins the f7 pawn to the rook on f8 and leaves Black helpless: 19...Re8 20.Qg7#.

review.turning_point: 17...Bxe1?? met by 18.Nf6+! turned a lost position into a winning attack, and 19.Qxf6! sealed it.
review.focus: 5.h4??: before pushing a wing pawn, check whether any of your pieces is under attack. The engine's 5.Nf3 would have kept the knight and the balance.

review.headline: A short Center Game win built on patient development and a queen blunder

sections.text: In the Center Game, the early queen moves 3.Qxd4 and 4.Qd1 cost you time (-1.0 after 5.Nc3). Black then wasted a move with 5...a6?, and you answered with 6.Nf3!, which put development first.

You played sensibly with 7.Bc4?!, 8.O-O, 9.Re1 and 10.Bd5. But 11.Qd3? (+0.1 to -1.5) was a mistake: 11...Nb4 would have been a discovered attack, the knight hitting your queen while uncovering the bishop on b7 against your bishop on d5. The engine preferred 11.a3.

Black missed it and played 11...Nxd5?? instead. After 12.Nxd5?! you were back to equal, and then came the blunder: 12...Qf6?? pins your b2 pawn against the rook on a1, which looks active, but it walks into your knight.
13.Nxf6+! won the queen and left you nine points up in material. Black's clock then ran out.

review.turning_point: 12...Qf6?? put the queen where your knight on d5 could take it: 13.Nxf6+! changed the material by nine points.
review.focus: 11.Qd3?: before placing the queen opposite an enemy bishop, look at what a knight move can uncover. 11...Nb4 would have hit both queen and bishop; 11.a3 was safer.

review.headline: A sharp Petrov won by a pawn storm and the finishing 19...Qb2#

sections.text: A Three Knights Petrov: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 g6 set up a fianchetto. White's 8.Bxf6?? was the first slip (8.Be3 was safer), and after 8...Bxf6 you got a nice diagonal. But 9.Nd5 and then your 9...c6? (9...Bg7 was better) allowed 10.Nxf6+ Qxf6 and the evaluation dipped to -0.9.

You found the right plan: 11...a5 and 12...a4 launched a pawn storm against White's long castle. 13.Kb1? was a mistake, and 13...a3! was the key move, because the pawn on a3 now hit b2 and cramped the king.

15.e5? dxe5! won a pawn, but 16...e4?? (+0.7 to -1.1) handed it back. 16...O-O was the engine's choice. 17.Qxe4+?? returned the favor, since 17.Nc7+ was the winning idea, and after 17...Be6?! the knight went for the rook.
18.Nc7+ Kf8 19.Nxa8?? Qb2#! The queen slid down the long diagonal to b2, protected by your a3 pawn, and the white king had no escape.

review.turning_point: 13...a3! hooked the b2 square, and the final 19...Qb2# shows how it paid off.
review.focus: 16...e4??: you were doing well but pushed a pawn that White could take with check. 16...O-O first would have kept the king safe and the edge intact.

review.headline: A wild attacking win where both sides swung the evaluation, ending in 40.Rf5#

sections.text: You got a good Italian setup: 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Ba7 8.Nc3 Nf6 9.e5 Nh7 gave you a huge center and space (+3.7 after 9.e5). Black helped with 3...h6 and 5...a5.

Then the evaluation became a roller coaster. 10.Qb3?? cut it from +3.7 to +1.5, 13.Rac1?? from +2.4 to -0.1, 14.Nd2?? from +3.5 to +0.1 and 15.Ne4?? from +3.0 to +0.6. Each time Black returned the favor with 13...b6??, 14...Rb8?? and 15...Nb4??. The engine's idea at move 13 was 13.Qxb7.

16.Ndf6+ gxf6 17.Bxe6? fxe6 18.Qxe6+ was a double sacrifice: you ended two points down in material but with the black king exposed. 18...Kh8? allowed 19.Bxh6!, your best move of that stretch. 20.Qg4?? (20.Qf7) and 21.Qh5? let Black back in.

23.Bg5+?? was a discovered check from the bishop, uncovering your queen on h5, but 23.exf6 was best. It dropped from +8.6 to -6.0. Fortunately 23...Kg7?? returned the favor, 24.Bxf6+ Kf8 25.Qh6+ Kf7 26.Qh7+ Ke6 27.Bxd8 won heavy material, and you finished with 40.Rf5#.

review.turning_point: 23.Bg5+?? threw away +8.6, but 23...Kg7?? gave it straight back and 24.Bxf6+ restored +8.0.
review.focus: 23.Bg5+: a check is not automatically best. At +8.6 you should pick the move that removes counterplay, and 23.exf6 did that.

review.headline: A strong opening trick gave you a big edge, which 15...Nh5?? threw back before the clock ended it

sections.text: Against 3.h3 in the Petrov you grabbed 3...Nxe4, and White's 4.Nc3? allowed 4...Nxc3! 5.bxc3. You came out a pawn ahead with White's pawns doubled. 5...d6, 6...Be7 and 7...Nd7 were sensible and flexible moves.
9...b5?! began a queenside pawn push that chased the bishop, and 11.a3? (11.a4 was better) helped you. 11...a4, 12.Ba2 e4 and 13.Nd2 d5 gave you space. By 15.f3 you were at +4.7, a large advantage.
15...Nh5?? lost most of that (+4.7 to +1.1). The engine's 15...e3 kept White cramped. After 16.fxe4 Ng3?! 17.Rf3 you needed 17...Qd6, but 17...Bh4? dropped you to -1.1, and 18.exd5 Qg5?! got worse.
19.Ne4?? gave you a lifeline and 19...Nxe4! won material back (+1.5). 20.dxc6 O-O 21.Bc1 left you still slightly better, but the clock ended the game after 21 moves.

review.turning_point: 15...Nh5?? let a +4.7 position slide to +1.1; from there the game became a fight.
review.focus: 15...Nh5??: the knight left the center right when the e4 pawn needed support. 15...e3 was the move that kept the bind.

review.headline: An Italian where the early queen trade went well until 13.Rb1?? turned the game

sections.text: Against 3...h6 you opened the center with 4.d4 d6 5.dxe5 dxe5, then traded queens with 6.Qxd8+ Nxd8. 7.Nxe5 won a pawn (+2.2), and 8.Nc3 Bb4 kept things comfortable.
9.Bf4?! f6 10.Ng6 Rh7 sent your knight on an adventure. 11.Bd3 Bxc3+ 12.bxc3 and you were still better by a pawn (+2.8), but the knight on g6 was sitting a long way from home.

13.Rb1?? (+2.6 to -2.4) was the error. The engine's 13.Nxe7 kept everything safe; after your move the black knight on e7 attacked the knight on g6. Black missed it with 13...f5??, and you were back at +4.1.

Then 14.Rxb7?? Nxb7 gave up the rook for a pawn (+4.1 to -3.0); 14.exf5 was the right move. You fought on through 18.Bxc7, 21.Be5+ and 26.Re6+?!, but 28.d5?? (28.Kd3 was better) lost another rook after 28...Nc4+ 29.Kd3 Nxe5+, and you resigned after 31.c4.

review.turning_point: 13.Rb1??, which turned +2.6 into -2.4 by leaving the g6 knight under attack.
review.focus: 13.Rb1??: before making a useful move, scan every piece you have advanced for attackers. 13.Nxe7 was the safe path.

review.headline: A recovery win: you survived 4...f6?? and then took White's queen with 11...Bxb4

sections.text: A Queen's Pawn Game with 1.d4 d5 2.e3 e6 3.Nf3 Nd7 4.Ne5. 4...f6?? was the error (+0.3 to -1.8): it allowed 5.Qh5+ Ke7 6.Qf7+ Kd6 and a king walk. The engine preferred 4...Bd6.
White overreached. 7.Bd2?? left the knight on e5 hanging, and 7...fxe5! took it (+2.5). 8.dxe5+ Nxe5 won a second pawn. The white queen on f7 was now far from home.
11.f4? let you finish the job: 10.Qb4+ Kd7 11.f4? Bxb4! won White's queen for a bishop (+6.8). After 12.Bxb4 Nc6 you kept developing with 13...Qe7, 14...b6 and 15...Bb7.

You kept a big advantage through the long middlegame, with 20...gxh6 and 21...hxg5 picking up pawns. 34...Ne4+?! and 37...Kb7?! were small slips. After 39.Ra3 a mate in one was available, but 39...a5?! missed it. You still won on the clock.

review.turning_point: 11...Bxb4! after 11.f4? won White's queen for a bishop and gave you a winning position.
review.focus: 4...f6??: it weakened e6 and the king. The quiet 4...Bd6 5.f4 kept things level.

review.headline: A gambit game that went from good to bad as both sides traded blunders until the clock ran out

sections.text: You played the Busch-Gass line and came out of the opening in good shape. After 2...Bc5? and 3...Nf6? you reached 7.Qxf3 at +1.7, despite your own inaccuracies like 3.Bc4? and 4.d3?.

The middlegame went through 8.Bg5, 10.Ne4 Nxe4 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 12.dxe4 b5 13.Bb3. Then 14.Qc3?? (+1.9 to -0.1) was the big error, since the queen on c3 is pinned against your king by Black's queen on b4. 14.c3 was best.

Black answered with 15...Qxg2??, and 16.O-O-O! was your best reply (+1.8). But 16...a5?? 17.d6?? c6?? 18.Qxe5?? and 19.d7?? were a string of mutual errors. 19.d7?? (+3.0 to -3.5) was the worst, because 19.Rdg1 would have hit the queen on g2.

After 20.Qd6?? and 21.Qe7?? you lost a bishop to 21...axb3. 23.Qxd8+?! was a back-rank check, but 23...Rxd8 simply took the queen. You played on, but down heavily, and the game ended on time at move 37.

review.turning_point: 19.d7?? (+3.0 to -3.5): you pushed the pawn instead of attacking the queen on g2.
review.focus: 19.d7: before pushing a passed pawn, check what your opponent's queen is doing. 19.Rdg1 would have kept your advantage.

review.headline: A long Caro-Kann grind won in the king-and-pawn finish after 39...Kd6??

sections.text: An Exchange Caro-Kann: 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Nf3 Nc6 6.Bb5 e6 7.Ne5 Bd7 8.Nxd7 Qxd7. 9.Bg5 a6 then 10.Bxf6? traded your bishop for a knight but left the b5 bishop to the a-pawn after 10...axb5. The engine preferred 10.Bxc6 first.
11.Bh4 Bb4 12.Qd3 O-O 13.Bg3?! Bxc3+ 14.Qxc3 b4 left you slightly worse. You held on, and 16...e5? gave you a chance. 17.dxe5! was a good reply and the engine's choice.
18.e6?! Rxe6, 20.f4?! h6 and 21.f5 Rf6 pushed forward, but 23.c3? (-1.4 to -3.1) was the real mistake. 23.Rxf5 Qxf5 was the move. After 23...Rxf1+ 24.Kxf1 bxc3 you were in trouble.

You stayed calm and Black slowly went wrong. 28.Qxa5, 30.Rxb7 and 31.Bxe5?! led to a rook ending. 36...Kg7? and then 39...Kd6?? left the rook on a5 hanging to your king. 40.Kxa5! picked it up, the a-pawn ran, and 45.a8=Q+ ended it, with Black's clock running out later.

review.turning_point: 39...Kd6?? and 40.Kxa5!: your king won the rook on a5 and the a-pawn queened.
review.focus: 23.c3? (-1.4 to -3.1): 23.Rxf5 Qxf5 was the move. When there is a capture on the board, count it out before making a quiet move.

review.headline: A short Center Game that went wrong at 8.Nf3?? and ended on the clock

sections.text: A normal Center Game: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qd1 Nf6 5.Nc3 Bc5 6.h3 O-O 7.Bd3 Re8. The queen detour cost a little time (-0.7 after 4...Nf6), but the position was fine.

8.Nf3?? (-0.1 to -2.1) was the first mistake. The engine's 8.Nge2 kept things solid. Black replied 8...Nxe4??, which was a mistake (-0.0), and then you missed the best reply, 9.Bxe4. Instead 9.Nxe4?? (-2.7) lost the thread.

After 9.Nxe4?? d5 the knight on e4 had no safe retreat, because the rook on e8 looks down the open e-file at your king. 10.O-O?! dxe4 made it clear, and you ended up a pawn down with Black's pieces more active. The game then ended on the clock after 10 moves.

review.turning_point: 8.Nf3?? (-0.1 to -2.1) set the trap, and 9.Nxe4?? walked into it.
review.focus: 9.Nxe4??: 9.Bxe4 was the capture that kept the extra material. Before taking with a knight, check what an open file does to your king.

review.headline: A game of swings: you won material early, nearly missed a forced mate, and won on the clock

sections.text: In the Petrov Italian, White's 4.c3?? allowed 4...Nxe4!, and 5.Bxf7+? Kxf7! gave you a lead in material. 6.Nxe5+ Kg8 7.Qb3+ d5 8.d4 followed.

8...Bd6?? (+3.2 to a forced loss) was a near disaster. The engine's 8...Bf8 was the safe move. After the move White had 9.Qxd5+, a fork of your king and the knight on e4 that leads to a forced mate. White missed it with 9.c4??, and you took 9...Bxe5.

10...Qh4?! 11.Be3 d4 12.c5+ Kf8 13.g3 Nxg3?? (+4.0 to -0.8) threw away your advantage, and 14...Qe4?? (14...Qe7) made it worse. White returned the favor: 15.Rf1+?? missed 15.O-O+, and 15...Bf5?? (15...Ke7 was better) did not help.
After 16.Nd2 Qxe3+ 17.Qxe3 dxe3 18.Rxf5+ the position became roughly balanced. 21.O-O-O?? and 21...Rad8?? were the last errors, but the game finally ended on time with you slightly ahead (+1.0).

review.turning_point: 8...Bd6?? was the near-fatal moment, since 9.Qxd5+ led to a forced mate that White missed with 9.c4??.
review.focus: 8...Bd6: after the early tactics your king was exposed on g8. 8...Bf8 was the safe move; check every forcing reply before moving.

review.headline: A fair opening ruined by a greedy knight on a2 that cost your queen

sections.text: Against the Mieses Reversed Rat you built a classical center with 1...e5, 2...d5 and 3...Nf6, then 4...Bb4+ forced 5.Bd2. 5...Nc6?! 6.Bxb4 Nxb4 7.h4 c6?! 8.h5 was odd on both sides, and the position was about equal.
8...Qa5? (+1.1 to -0.0) was the first real slip. The queen eyes the a2 pawn with the rook behind it, but the engine's 8...d4 kept the pressure. 9.c3 then attacked your knight on b4.

9...Nxa2?? (0.0 to -3.0) was the decisive mistake. 9...Na6 10.d4 was the safe way. After 10.Nc1 Nxc3 11.Rxa5 White took your queen, and although 11...Nxd1 12.Kxd1 got material back, you were worse (-2.6).
From there White built steadily: 16.Bb5+ Ke7, 18.Rxa7+, 20.dxc5+ and 21.cxb6 pushed on, and 23.Nc6+ ended the game, with you resigning at -7.3.

review.turning_point: 9...Nxa2?? (0.0 to -3.0): the knight grab lost your queen after 11.Rxa5.
review.focus: 9...Nxa2: knights on the rim are rarely safe. 9...Na6 10.d4 was the quiet way to keep the balance.

review.headline: A tactical miniature: you gave up a knight, then won it all back with 6...dxe4! and mated with 14...Qe1#

sections.text: A Vienna with 2.Bc4 Nf6 3.Nc3. 3...c6?! was a little passive, and 4...Nxe4? (-1.5) was a mistake because the engine preferred 4...d5 5.Bb3. After 5.Nxe4 you were down a knight.

5...d5 hit both the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4. 6.Bd3?? (-1.8 to +2.6) was White's blunder, since 6.Bb3 was needed. 6...dxe4! is a fork of the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3, plus a discovered attack from your queen on d3.
After 7.Bxe4 f5 8.Bd3 e4 9.Ne5 exd3 you were up material (+3). 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Nxg6 hxg6 12.Qxh8 grabbed your rook, but the white king was exposed and the queen had no help.
12...Qe7+ 13.Kf1 Qe2+ 14.Kg1 Qe1# finished it with queen checks down the e-file.

review.turning_point: 6.Bd3?? dxe4!: the pawn fork won the piece back with interest.
review.focus: 4...Nxe4?: snatching a pawn with a knight left you a piece down. 4...d5 5.Bb3 would have kept the center under control.

review.headline: A promising English Defense lost to the clock after a rough middlegame

sections.text: 1.c4 e6 2.d4 b6 3.e4 Bb7 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Bd3 Bb4 6.Qc2 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 gave you a big center. 7...Nc6 8.Ba3 d6 9.Rb1 O-O kept you at a modest +0.7.
10.c5?! dxc5 11.dxc5?? (+0.1 to -2.6) was the mistake. The engine's 11.Ne2 was safer. After 11...Ne5 12.Rd1 Nxd3+ 13.Rxd3 you traded your good bishop and Black was more active.
Black returned the favor with 14...Nxe4? (-0.6 to +0.5), and your 15.c6! was a discovered attack: moving the pawn opened the bishop on a3 toward f8. 15...Ba6? missed 15...Bxc6.
16.fxe4?! Bxd3 took your rook, but the position was still evaluated at +1.8. The game ended on the clock at move 16.

review.turning_point: 11.dxc5?? (+0.1 to -2.6) gave Black a free hand, and 15.c6! nearly turned it around.
review.focus: 11.dxc5??: the engine's 11.Ne2 kept the pieces protected. Before recapturing, ask what the opposing knight can do next.

review.headline: A quiet Center Game wrecked by one greedy capture, 9...Nxe4??

sections.text: A Center Game, Paulsen line: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 d6?! was slightly slow (-0.3), but 5.Bb5 Bd7 6.Nc3 a6 7.Bxc6 Bxc6 8.Nf3 Nf6 left the position balanced.
9.O-O Nxe4?? (+0.1 to -4.5) looked like a free pawn, but 10.Nxe4 left you a knight for a pawn down with your king still in the center. The engine's 9...Be7 10.Nd4 kept things level.
The game then ended on the clock after 10 moves, with you at -4.4.

review.turning_point: 9...Nxe4?? (+0.1 to -4.5) lost material and left your king in the center.
review.focus: 9...Nxe4: check the recapture before grabbing a pawn. 9...Be7 was the sound developing move.

review.headline: A Sicilian that swung wildly: an early queen blunder, a comeback, and a winning ending that ran out of clock

sections.text: The opening was fine. After 4.Bc4?! 4...cxd4 5.Nxd4 5...Nc6 6.O-O 6...Nxd4 7.Qxd4 you had a normal position, but 8.f4?! and then 9.f5?? pushed pawns in front of your own king while your queen stood on d4. The engine preferred 9.Be3.

That left the queen exposed to the bishop on c5. After 11...Bxd4 the material was at -8, and 12.Bxd4 only brought it back to -5. To your credit you kept playing, and the opponent handed you a chance: 18...Qc5+?? put you at +5.5 because 19.Nxc5 was available. 19.Kh1?? let that slip back to -2.0.

Your opponent's 30...Qxd2+ was a fork of your king on e3 and rook on e1, but 31.Kxd2! was the correct capture and it turned a lost game into a fight. With 31...Rd8?? and 32...Be6?? from Black you were comfortable again, and 35.Rxe2! led to an ending where you were clearly better (+4.0).

The clock hurt you in the ending. 46.Kf3?? and 47.Bf2?? were played while short of time, but 48.Rxg3! and 49.Bxg3! cleaned things up and you reached +5.5. The game ended on the clock with you at +7.3 after 54...bxc4.

review.turning_point: 9.f5?? left your queen on d4 to be hit by the bishop from c5 and cost most of your material; later 19.Kh1?? threw away the chance to punish 18...Qc5+.
review.focus: Before a pawn push like 9.f5, check where your queen can go once 9...d5 and 10...Bc5 arrive. Also, when a check like 18...Qc5+ appears, ask first whether you can simply take the checking piece with 19.Nxc5.

review.headline: A solid Petrov that turned into a winning rook ending, thrown away on the last move

sections.text: You met 4.d4 with 4...exd4 and played sensibly. After 8.Bxc6+ 8...bxc6 and the queen swap 11.Qxd8+ 11...Rxd8 the game was level, with a sound structure and an open file for your rooks.

14...Nd5?? was the first real slip (the engine wanted 14...Bxc2), and 15.Bxd8 put you at -5 on material. But the opponent answered 15...Nxc3 with 16.bxc3??, and 16...Bxc3+! was a fork of the rook on a1, the king on e1 and the knight on e5. After 17.Ke2 17...Bxa1 18.Rxa1 18...Kxd8 you were back to level.

19...Ke8?? dropped to -5.9 (19...Kd7 was better), but 20.Nd4?? gave it straight back. From there White drifted with 25.Kg4?, 28.a5? and 29.Re5?, and your 28...Ra4 pinned the f4 pawn against the king. By move 38 you stood at +5.6 with a dangerous passed a-pawn.

The ending slipped in stages: 38...Rxa5?? and 41...Ke4?? gave back a lot, then you recovered with 42...Ra7!. At 45...a3 you were at +6.5. Then 46...a2?? turned it around; the engine's 46...Rxg7+ kept a forced mate available. After 47.Rxa7 the material was -5 and the game ended on the clock.

review.turning_point: 46...a2?? pushed the pawn when 46...Rxg7+ was a check that kept a forced mate on the board.
review.focus: In the ending, look at checks and captures before pushing a pawn. At 46...a2 the rook capture with check, 46...Rxg7+, was the move; ask what your opponent's rook is attacking before you do anything else.

review.headline: A clean, accurate win: you let White's knight wander, took the pawns, and finished with a queen mating attack

sections.text: White played quiet moves like 2.e3, 3.h3 and 4.a3, and you simply developed with 3...Nf6, 4...Be7, 5...Nbd7 and 6...c5. After 8.dxc5 8...bxc5 9.Bb5 9...O-O 10.Bxd7 10...Qxd7 your position was healthy and the engine had you slightly better.

White's knight then spent six moves wandering (11.Ne5, 12.Nd3, 13.Nb4, 14.Nb5, 15.Nd4, 16.Na2) while you gained space with 12...c4 and 15...a5. 16...Qxb2?! took a pawn and 17.Bc3? 17...Qxa3! took another; the queen on a3 pinned the knight on a2 to the rook on a1, as 17...Qxa3 shows. That put you two pawns up.

19...Bc6 gave up some of the edge (19...d4 was the engine's move), but 20.Nc7?? gave you a chance and 20...Rac8! was the right answer. After 23.Ra1 23...Rxc7 you were five up on material. You kept your pieces coordinated and traded when it helped.
29.Qxc7? ended it. 29...Qxc3+! was a fork of the king on e1 and rook on a1, and from there the queen hunted the king all the way to mate.
sections.line: 29.Qxc7 Qxc3+ 30.Ke2 Qxc2+ 31.Kf3 Qxf2+ 32.Kg4 f5+ 33.Kh5 g6+ 34.Kh6 Qh4#

review.turning_point: After 17.Bc3? you played 17...Qxa3!, a pin on the knight that left White's queenside collapsing; 29...Qxc3+ finished the job.
review.focus: A very good game. The one clear slip was 19...Bc6; the engine prefers 19...d4, hitting the bishop and opening lines. Look for the active move when you are already winning.

review.headline: A Philidor where you punished early errors, nearly gave the edge back, and finished with a tactic

sections.text: Your opponent's 3...h6 and 4...Nf6? were slow, and 5.dxe5! was the correct reply. But 6.exd6?? (the engine liked 6.Qd5) let Black off the hook, and after 7.Qxd6?! the queens came off and the position was close to equal (+0.1).
9...Bf5?? was a mistake by Black and put you at +3.8, but 10.Nbd2?? gave it right back (10.Bd3 was the engine's move). After 10...Nxd2 11.Bxd2 it was level again.

Your opponent then went wrong with 14...Nxe5??, and 15.Rxe5! forked the bishops on c5 and f5. After 15...Bxf2+ 16.Kxf2 you were well ahead, and your rooks doubled on the seventh rank with 18.Re7, 19.Rxc7 and 20.Ree7.

22.Rxf7?? was greedy; 22.Be3 kept everything under control. But 23...Rxb2?? by Black gave you a nice finish: 24.Rxb7+! was a discovered check from the bishop on c4 and a discovered attack, and you won on time at +7.3.

review.turning_point: 15.Rxe5! forked two bishops after Black's 14...Nxe5??, turning an even game into a clearly winning one.
review.focus: Before grabbing a pawn, check what you are leaving behind. 22.Rxf7 threw away a lot of the edge; 22.Be3 first would have kept the rooks active. Likewise 10.Nbd2 ignored the knight on e4; ask what a developing move does to the position first.

review.headline: A quick win in the Philidor: White fell for the e4 knight trick and you took the queen

sections.text: You played 3...exd4 and then the slightly passive 4...d6?!, but the game stayed even after 5.Bg5 5...Be7 6.Bb5+ 6...c6. White's 7.Bc4?? was the first mistake; the engine wanted 7.Bd3.

7...Bg4?? was your own slip, since 7...Qa5+ was a strong check that attacked the bishop on g5. White replied 8.Nf3?? (8.f3 held on), and then 8...Nxe4! was a discovered attack: the knight moved and your bishop on e7 now attacked the bishop on g5.

9.Nc3?? lost more time (9.Bxe7 was best). After 9...Nxc3 10.bxc3 10...Bxg5 11.O-O 11...O-O 12.Nxg5, you played 12...Bxd1 and the material went to +10. White recaptured, you took on g5 with the queen, and White never got going.
From there you played simply and kept trading: 17...Nxd3, then 20.Rxe8+ and 20...Rxe8, and 21...Re1+ forced White to give up. You were at +9.5 after 22.Kh2.

review.turning_point: 8...Nxe4! used a discovered attack on the bishop on g5, and after 12...Bxd1 you were far ahead on material.
review.focus: 7...Bg4?? missed 7...Qa5+, which hits the bishop on g5 and the king at the same time. Before developing a bishop, look for checks that also attack something.

review.headline: A short Petrov where an early pawn loss and a premature queen move ended the game in eight moves

sections.text: You started well with 1...e5 and 2...Nf6, but after 3.Bc4 the move 3...Bc5?? left the e5 pawn with no defender (the engine wanted 3...Nxe4). 4.Nxe5 simply took the pawn and you went to -1.4.

4...d5?! and 5...Nxd5?! tried to open the position with your king still in the centre, but it only gave White more targets. 6.O-O was a calm move, and the engine's suggestion for you was 6...O-O to get the king safe.
6...Qg5?? is the move that finished it: after 7.d4 the queen was under attack and the bishop on c1 stood behind it. You played 7...O-O?! and 8.Bxg5 left the material at -10, so you resigned.

review.turning_point: 6...Qg5?? went to a square where 7.d4 attacked it with the bishop on c1 lined up behind. A queen that wanders out early becomes a target.
review.focus: Before moving your queen out, check which enemy pieces can attack it, as with 6...Qg5. At move 3 the engine liked 3...Nxe4, so look at central captures before developing the bishop.

review.headline: An attacking win in the Open Sicilian: you punished a loose queen and finished with a knight mate

sections.text: You played the main line 3.Nf3 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 and met 4...Qa5+ with 5.Bd2. After 5...Qb6, 6.Bc3?! was a bit passive, and Black's 6...Bb4?? is where the game turned, since it pinned your bishop on c3 against your king but allowed 7.Qd2.

7...a5? was another slip (7...Be7 was the engine's move). 8.Bxb4 and 8...Qxb4 traded your bishop for his and left you with a lead in development. 9.c3? was a small slip (9.Nc3 was stronger), but Black's 9...Qd6?? gave it right back and you went to +3.2.

Then you built the attack well: 10.Na3, 11.Nc4, 12.e5 and 13.Qf4 all kept your pieces active. 13...Nc5? let you hit hard with 14.Nd6+ and 15.Qxf7, and after 16.Qxg7 you had taken two pawns and had a huge attack.
The finish was precise: 17.Nf7+, 18.Nd6+, 19.Qf6+ and then 20.Nf7# ended it with a knight checkmate.

review.turning_point: 13...Nc5? let you play 14.Nd6+ and 15.Qxf7, which pushed your evaluation to +8.
review.focus: 9.c3? was the only real slip. The engine's 9.Nc3 develops a piece and keeps the attack going; make development moves before pawn moves when you are ahead.

review.headline: A Vienna Game where you hit back with accurate tactics and finally cashed in on the clock

sections.text: The opening was shaky for you. 4.f4 was an aggressive try and 4...Bc5?? (the engine wanted 4...Nxe4) let White take the initiative. But after 5.fxe5 5...Nxe5 6.d4 6...Nxc4 7.dxc5 you were fine, and White's 8.Qe2?? let you play 8...Qxc5!.

9.Na4? was another slip, and 9...Qb4+! was a fork of the king on e1 and the knight on a4. You followed with 10...O-O and 11...Qc5 and were doing well. White tried 12.b4, you retreated with 12...Qc6, and everything stayed in your control.

13...Re8?? gave up your edge (13...Nd6 was better) and 14...Qb6?? left a piece to be won; the engine preferred 14...Qxe4. Luckily 15.Nb3?? by White (15.Qxc4 was the strong move) gave you 15...d5!, and after 16.a4? you took a pawn with 16...Nxe4.
17...Qg6? (17...Qxb4 was the engine move) was inaccurate, but 18.Nxe4?? was a blunder and 18...Rxe4! left you up material. You won on the clock.

review.turning_point: 15...d5! after White's 15.Nb3?? punished an opponent mistake and gave you the central break and the e4 knight.
review.focus: 4...Bc5?? and 13...Re8?? both dropped your edge. At move 4, ask whether the capture 4...Nxe4 works first; the tempo spent on the bishop let White take over.

review.headline: A well-played Petrov where you outplayed White for 30 moves and then slipped in the pawn ending

sections.text: After 3.Nxe5 3...d6 4.Nf3 4...Nxe4 5.Qe2 5...Qe7 6.d3 6...Nf6 you reached a queen swap with 7.Qxe7+ and 7...Bxe7, and an equal ending. You developed with 8...d5, 9...c6 and 10...h6 and kept a solid position.

White's 14.O-O? let you play 14...Nxg4!, a discovered attack that put you ahead by 3 in material at +2.2. 15.Bxe7 15...Rxe7?? was a slip though (15...Nxh2 was best), but you still had a good position.
22.c3?? gave you another chance and 22...dxc3! was the answer, followed by 23.Nxc3 and 23...Rxb2. By 27...Rd1+ you were at +2.6, with the rook active and a pawn extra.

30...c4? and 31...b5?? let White back into the game, and after 43.Rxc3 43...Rxc3+ 44.Kxc3 the pawn ending was close. Then 44...Kf4?? was the error; 44...Ke6 was the move. White's king walked in with 45.Kd4, 46.Kd5 and 47.Ke6, and you resigned at move 54.

review.turning_point: 44...Kf4?? turned an even pawn ending into a lost one; 44...Ke6 kept your king in front of White's.
review.focus: In king and pawn endings, keep the king in front and calculate the race first, as at 44...Kf4. Also 30...c4? and 31...b5?? loosened your pawns; the engine preferred 30...Kf8.

review.headline: A comfortable ending against a much higher-rated opponent that slipped away under time pressure

sections.text: An Alekhine's Defence with the Two Pawns Attack. 5.Nc3?? let Black take with 5...dxe5 (the engine wanted 5.f4). You were then helped by 6...Bf5?, since 7.Qxd8+! 7...Kxd8 gave you a pleasant endgame and the evaluation went to +0.4.
You played the ending sensibly. 11.O-O-O, then trading rooks with 14.Rhd1 and 16.Rxd8, put you in good shape. 22.Nxf7+ took a pawn, and 24...g5? by Black let you push forward to +2.2.

Through the middle moves you kept the advantage: 26.Nh4?!, 29.Ng6+, 30.Nf4 and 32.Nd3 kept the knight active, and 34.Nxb7 took another pawn. After 34...Kg6 you were at +5.1, a clearly winning position.

Then the clock told. 35.Nd8?? gave up a lot (35.Kf4 was the engine's move), and 37.Kd3??, 38.Ke2?? and 39.Nd4+?? followed while short of time. After 39...Nxd4+ the material was -2, and the game ended on time after 40.Ke3 and 40...Nxb3.

review.turning_point: 35.Nd8?? threw away the grip you had at +5; from there the low clock produced one error after another.
review.focus: You were winning at 34.Nxb7 and ran short on the clock. Manage time earlier in the game, and when you have a safe plan like 35.Kf4, use it instead of looking for something fancier.

review.headline: An early knight blunder, a wild comeback with a promoted queen, and a winning position lost on time

sections.text: The opening was a normal Queen's Gambit Declined for six moves. Then 7...Nb6?? (7...dxc4 was the move) walked into 8.c5, and after 9.cxb6 9...Bxb6 you were down a knight for a pawn.

You fought on. 12...dxe4 and 13...Bxd4 opened the game up, and after 14.Nxf6+ 14...Qxf6 White tried 15.Bxh7+?, but 15...Kxh7! was the right reply. 16.Qc2+? 16...Kg8?? (16...g6 was best) was a slip, but 17.Ng5?? gave you the chance to break out with 17...Qg6? and 18.Qxg6 18...fxg6.

19.Rfe1?? let you play 19...Bxb2!, and the game turned. White missed chances too: after 25...Rac8?? the engine points to 26.Rh8+, a skewer on the back rank that forces a mate, and again after 28...c2?? with 29.Rh8+. But 26.g3?? and 29.f3?? let you off, and 29...c1=Q! put you up a lot.
You were then clearly winning (+6.4 at move 42 with a pawn on b2), but the clock ended it. The loss came from time, not the board.

review.turning_point: 29.f3?? let you queen with 29...c1=Q! when 29.Rh8+ would have been decisive for White.
review.focus: Two things: 7...Nb6?? cost a knight, so check where a knight retreats before moving it. And with a winning position at 42.Rb7, keep an eye on the clock; spend less time in the early moves.

review.headline: A model Italian win: you took the early advantage, kept the pieces coordinated and marched the king to promote

sections.text: After 3...h6 4.d4 4...d6 5.dxe5 5...dxe5 6.Qxd8+ 6...Nxd8 7.Nxe5 you were a pawn up with a safe position, and 8...f6? let you attack. 9.Ng6! hit the rook on h8 and the bishop on f8, and after 9...Rh7 10.Nd5 10...c6 you were at +5.3.

11.Ndf4?! was the only inaccuracy here (the engine's 11.Nc7+ forked the king and the rook on a8). Still, after 11...Nxf4 12.Nxf4 12...Bb4+ 13.c3 and 14.Bxg8 you had taken the knight on g8 and led by +5.2.
You then simplified with care: 16.Ne6 16...Bxe6 17.Bxe6, then 21.Be3 and 22.fxe3, and 25.Rd7+ and 26.Rxe7+ gave you an endgame with a bishop and a clear plan.

Your king marched to the queenside (27.Kg1 to 33.Ka6) while Black could do nothing. 41.hxg5?! was a small slip (41.e5 was cleaner), but 45.Kxa7 and 46.Kxb6 cleaned up and the a-pawn queened with 51.a8=Q#.

review.turning_point: 9.Ng6! attacked two pieces at once and left Black's rook stuck on h7, and you never looked back.
review.focus: A nearly perfect game. The one thing to review is 11.Ndf4?! versus 11.Nc7+; check for forcing moves that attack two pieces before settling for a quieter one.

review.headline: A Diemer-Duhm Gambit where White overreached and your queen ran wild

sections.text: White offered a gambit with 3.e4?, and 3...Nf6? was not best (the engine wanted 3...dxe4). Even so, after 4.Bg5? 4...dxe4! you were the one taking material, and 5.Bxf6 5...Qxf6 left you a pawn up.
6.f3? was a bad move (6.Nc3 was needed), and 6...e3? was a bit hasty; 6...Bb4+ was the engine's move. Still, after 7.Qa4+? you replied 7...Bd7!, and after 8.Qb3 8...Qxd4 you took another pawn.
9.Qd3? ran into 9...Qxb2!, and the queen kept grabbing material with 10.Qc3 10...Qf2+ 11.Kd1 11...Qxf1+. By then the material was +6 and 12...e2 threatened to promote.
You kept control with 13...Bxa3 and 14...Ba4+, and 17...Qxf3+ and 18...Qxh3 finished with the material at +13. You won on the clock.

review.turning_point: 9...Qxb2! turned a good position into a crushing one, as the queen took on b2, f2 and f1 in a row.
review.focus: 6...e3? let part of the advantage go; 6...Bb4+ kept the king stuck in the centre. When you are ahead, play the check that restricts the king.

review.headline: A messy Nimzo-Larsen where you harassed the queen but lost the thread, and then the clock

sections.text: A Larsen opening with 1.b3 1...e5. White's queen went out early with 4.Qf3, and you pushed it around with 6...h5, 7...h4 and 8.Qh2, a clear gain of time for you. With 5...Bg4 you were doing well.

10...Rf8?? let it slip; 10...d5 was the engine's move. After 12.Bb5? 12...a6?! 13.Bxc6 13...Bxc6 14.gxh4 14...Nd7?! you were still fine, but 15...Bxg5?? (15...Bd6 was best) traded your bishop and 16.hxg5 swung the evaluation from +1.1 to -1.5.
White made mistakes too (17.h4?, 22.O-O-O??), but 22...Ne5?? missed 22...Qxa3+, which would have taken a piece. 24...Qa3+ pinned the b3 pawn, and you kept fighting.
29.bxa4?? was a gift, but 29...Bxa4?? (29...Ne5 was better) threw it away, and 31...exf3? made it worse. The ending was bad on the board and then the clock ran out. 47...Kxd5! was a nice try.

review.turning_point: 15...Bxg5?? traded off your good bishop and the recapture 16.hxg5 shifted the balance for good.
review.focus: 15...Bxg5 and 22...Ne5 both missed a better move. Before an exchange, count what is left after the recapture. And play faster in quiet positions; this one ended on time.

review.headline: A wild Italian game where both sides blundered and you finished with a queen and a mating attack

sections.text: You went wrong early: after 4...Nxd4 the engine wanted 5.Bxf7+, but 5.Ng5?? 5...d5 6.exd5 6...Nxd5?? was a slip by Black. 7.Qh5?? was another miss (7.c3 was better), and 8.Nxf7? was a fork of queen and rook that Black simply captured with 8...Kxf7.

You were down material but the attack kept going: 9.Qxe5 9...Nxc2+ 10.Kf1?! 10...c6 11.Qxh8, then 12.Bh6 12...bxc4 13.Qxh7+. After 13...Ke8?? you found 14.Qxg6+!, a fork of the king on e8 and the knight on c2, and the evaluation moved back to +2.9.

15.Qf7+?? slipped again (15.Bg5 was best), but 17.Qxc2! took the knight and 18.Nc3 18...Nxc3 19.bxc3 kept you in the game. Black's 19...Ba6?? and 20...Qd7?? let you recover, and 23.Qxa8 put you well ahead.

The ending was easy. 25.Kf1! 25...Qe5 26.Qxa7+ 26...Bb7 27.Qe3 left you well ahead at +5 on material, and the h-pawn and a-pawn marched through. 42.a8=Q and then the queen and king finished with 55.Qh8#.

review.turning_point: 14.Qxg6+! forked the king and the knight on c2 after Black's 13...Ke8??, and the game turned around.
review.focus: Opening play: 5.Ng5?? and 7.Qh5?? sent pieces forward without a plan; 5.Bxf7+ was a better way to use the open lines. Develop before attacking.

review.headline: A Sicilian where Black blundered early and your queen and bishops finished with a king hunt

sections.text: 3...d5? was a bad move for Black (3...cxd4 was normal). 4.Nc3?? was your first miss (4.exd5 was stronger), and 4...c4?? returned the favour. After 5.Nxd5 5...b5 6.b3?? Black played 6...Bg4?, but 7.bxc4 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 8...Nxd4 left you a pawn up.

9...Qa5+? was a mistake by Black, and 10.Bd2! was exactly right. After 10...b4 11.Qxd4 11...O-O-O you were up 4 in material. 12.Bxb4? was a small slip (12.a3 first), but 12...Rxd5?? 13.cxd5! gave you +7.5.
The king hunt was lovely: 16.Qc3+, 17.Bxf8, 18.Bc4+, 19.Qf3+, 20.Qxf7+ and 21.Qxg7+ chased the king right across the board.
By 27.Qxh8 you were 15 up in material. 34.Qe3? was a mistake (34.Rd2 was cleaner), but the ending was still winning and you won on the clock at +9.

review.turning_point: 13.cxd5! after 12...Rxd5?? left Black with no counterplay and an exposed king.
review.focus: 12.Bxb4? and 34.Qe3? both gave something back. With a big lead, take a second to check that nothing hangs; the safer 12.a3 was available.

review.headline: A Petrov where you held a balanced middlegame and then lost the thread tactically

sections.text: After 3.a3 3...Nxe4 4.Qe2 4...Nf6 5.Qxe5+ 5...Qe7?! the queens came off with 6.Qxe7+ and 6...Bxe7. You then developed with 7...O-O, 8...Re8 and 9...d5, and the position was balanced.
White's 16.g4? gave you 16...Nxe2+, a fork of the king on c1 and the rook on g1, though 17.Nxe2 just recaptured. 18.Nd2? was another inexact move, and 20.f5 and 21.Nf4 followed.

21...Ne4?? was the first real error (21...Bd6 was best), and 22.Nxe4? 22...dxe4! saved you. But 24...Re5?? walked into 26.Bxe5 (the bishop on b2 had an open diagonal after 23.d5). White's 25.Kb1?? missed it, and 25...Rae8?? (25...Ree8 was better) followed.
After 26.Bxe5 the material was -5, then back to -2, and later 31...Bf6+?? and 32...Re7?? cost more. 33.Rxf6 ended with -5 on material and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 24...Re5?? put a rook where the bishop on b2 could take it, and you never recovered.
review.focus: Before putting a piece on a square like 24...Re5, check which enemy pieces see it, particularly long diagonals that opened with 23.d5.

review.headline: A sharp Two Knights Defence win: a sacrificed knight and clean tactics finished it in 17 moves

sections.text: You chose the sharp 4.Ng5 against the Two Knights, and Black replied 4...d5 5.exd5 5...Nd4 6.c3 6...Nf5. You answered with 7.Qe2, 8.d4 and 9.dxe5, and by 10.Qxe5 you were well ahead on material.
11.Ne6! was the key idea and the engine's top choice: it put a piece en prise, but Black could not take it safely. 11...Bxe6?? was a blunder, and 12.dxe6! gave you a strong pawn on e6.
13.Bxe6+?! was a fork of king and knight, but the engine preferred 13.Qxf5. It hardly mattered: 13...Rxe6 14.Qxe6+ 14...Kh8 15.Qxf5 left you 9 up in material.
Black played 15...Qe7+ but 16.Be3 solved it, and 17.Nd2 kept everything safe. Black resigned.

review.turning_point: 11.Ne6! offered a piece that Black could not safely take, and 11...Bxe6?? decided the game.
review.focus: Very good game. The small point is 13.Bxe6+?!; 13.Qxf5 was cleaner. When you are winning, take the simplest route.

review.headline: A Petrov Three Knights game where a pawn grab opened your queen to attack

sections.text: A normal start: 3...d6 4.Bc4 4...Be7 5.d4. 5...Bg4?! was a little loose and 6.d5 6...c6 7.O-O 7...cxd5 8.exd5 8...Nbd7 left things level. 9.Qe1 9...Qa5?! and 10.Ng5 10...Nb6?! were not best, but you were still fine.
11...Nbxd5?? took a pawn but missed that 12.Nxd5 was a discovered attack from the knight on c3 onto your queen on a5. White did not find it, and 12.Bd2?? gave you a reprieve.
12...Qb6?? (12...Qc5 was better) and 13...h6? kept things loose, and after 14.Nxf6+? you took back with 14...Nxf6!. Then 15...O-O-O?? (15...Qc6 was best) walked into more trouble.
16...Nxe4?? finished it: your queen on b6 was attacked by the bishop on e3 and you captured elsewhere. 17.Bxb6 17...axb6 18.Qxe4 left you -5 on material and you resigned.

review.turning_point: 16...Nxe4?? ignored the attack on your queen on b6, and 17.Bxb6 took it.
review.focus: Before every move, ask what your opponent's last move attacks, as with 16.Be3 hitting your queen. 16...Qc6 would have kept you in the game.
